DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. This space (8) is the atrium of this house. It is a large, very grand space surrounded by rooms with very high doorways. The reconstructed ceiling is very high. The entrance is centered along the southeast wall. There are matching doorways on each side of the entrance. At the south end of the southwest wall is a large doorway into dining room 3. Just west of this dining room is a doorway to a stairwell.To the west of this is a doorway to a small room (9). The open space in the western corner (10),which mirrors the space in the north corner (17), is an ala (wing). Between these, the northwest wall opens to the peristyle, with one broad central opening flanked by two smaller openings. East of space 17 is a doorway into room 18. At the eastern end of the northeast wall is a doorway to a small atrium and kitchen area. In the center of the room is a white marble impluvium. The rest of the floor is cocciopesto made of black stones with lines of large, white tesserae. At the center of the southwest wall is a large chest preserved under glass. At the center of the northeast wall are the remains of a fountain. The lower portion of the walls to the top of the doorways is of alternating courses of brick and stone. Above this level the walls are opus incertum with the top level being reconstruction. Remaining frescoes reveal a faux stone dado, a yellow frieze above it with figures on red backgrounds which are drinking or dealing with food on most of them. A black frieze above this shows puti frolicking with animals and sea creatures. There are architectural motives above the black frieze. The upper areas of painting are not preserved. Three rectangular windows are clearly spaced across the upper southeast wall. A fourth rectangular window is at the south end of the southwest wall, with a fifth window at the west end of the southwest wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The atrium is located directly northwest of the fauces (1). It is to the southeast of the peristyle (11).

DESCRIPTION:
This is the house of the Gladiators. We have identified room 12 as a dining room. This identification is based on the size, dimensions, decoration and location of the room. It is a rectangular room on the northwest - southeast axis. One enters through the door at the south corner of the southeast wall. The floor is only partially visible; however, it is entirely covered with a mosaic of small tesserae. The southeast one-third of the floor appears to have its own panel of decoration bordered by a band with a leaf pattern. Not enough of the central area shows to discern the motifs although we can see red tesserae in addition to the black and white. The rest of the room is divided from the southeastern third by a band of overlapping circles creating four-petal flowers. To the northwest of the band is a narrower band forming an all-around border for a carpet-like mosaic over the remaining two-thirds of the room. The corners of this are floral patterns with spiraling vines around a central medallion.

The threshold is reconstructed. The walls are opus incertum. There is a small rectangular window at the top of the northeast wall. The walls were frescoed. A plaster fluted pillar with the remains of a decorative capital aligns with a mosaic floor border to divide the space. Remains of the painting are extant on the northeast and southeast walls. The northern two-thirds of the northeast wall presents a third style/scheme with figures and statues on a white background. Tthe southeastern third of the room preserves a very different style of decoration with an almost life-size figure on a black background. This same sort of figure can be seen on the northeast wall and the southeast wall. The large figures are flanked by snakes. There is a frieze above with female portrait busts set on wings.
The ceiling is reconstructed, sloping inward from the northeast to the southwest. The condition of the room is fair.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the northeast of the peristyle and in the northern-most corner of the house.

I dare to disagree with my peers because there are pictures on the low walls if animals dying. They would have been eaten at the dinner table. DESCRIPTION:
Rectangular room on east-west axis opening through a large doorway with a variegated marble piece of revetment serving as a threshold. Tufa threshold in north door. Doors of medium height preserved to both north and east. Walls well preserved, 3 meters thick, leveled off, capped roof tile for protection. DESCRIPTION: We have determined structure 3-4-3 to be a house and room 30 to be a dining hall (one of nine dining spaces in the structure), based upon its size, its elaborate marble thresholds, and the possibility that it would have had an overlook to the garden below. The room is rectangular in shape and sits on a NE/SW axis. The room is largely reconstructed and low opus incertum walls currently exist on the northwest, southwest, and southeast walls. The northeast wall is currently a mixture of opus reticulatum (restoration) and opus incertum on the original 79 AD wall. There is a threshold of marble with door hardware inserts on the west end of the northwest wall. There is another similar door on the west end of the southwest wall and one more on the south end of the southeast wall. There is a large wide opening to dining room 29 currently in place on the east end of the southeast wall, but it is impossible to tell if there was a door or window there, or whether it was a solid wall. The current floor may have been restored. A black and red lining appears to be modern at the floor level on all the walls but in a consistent pattern (note: discoloration on the floor and ........ in the southeast wall indicate that the room may have been divided into two rooms).
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Dining hall 4394 is to the northwest of dining rooms 28 and 29 and to the northeast of space 31.

DESCRIPTION: This public fountain (4726) is on the south side of the via dell'Abbondanza. It is in front of 1.12.2, with its street side benches, and across the street from the House of Trebius Valens (3.2.1) The fountain is made of volcanic stone slabs, It has an added lining rounding off the wall / floor junction. The lining appears to have at least two layers. The interior dimensions of the basin are 0.89 m. by 1.25 m. and it is 0.70 m. deep. The pilaster is centred on the south east wall and is decorated with a male figure lying on his left side upon what appears to be a rocky orb. The figure raises his right arm over his head. It has been suggested that this is a satyr. The overflow is centred on the north west slab and the drainage holes centred at the bottom of the north east slab. This fountain has no functioning modern plumbing. BIBLIOGRAPHY: Pompeii in Pictures 1.12.2
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: in front of (north) of 1.12.2, immediately east of of the intersection with the vicolo della Nave Europa.

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is a commercial structure, a restaurant or perhaps, more likely, a wine bar. This space is identified as a kitchen due to it's size and features. It is a small, dark, rectangular space off the east corner of entry room #1. One goes up three steps to enter a narrow doorway. The kitchen is on a northwest-southeast axis. The southeast end is occupied by a latrine (4362). The west end of the southwest wall opens to an inset cooking platform (4361). No finished flooring is visible. The remains of plaster on the walls is seen just above the latrine on the southeast wall and very small vestiges on the southwest and northeast walls. There are three round openings across the upper portion of the northeast wall, possible little windows. An additional round hole is in the southwest wall above the cooking platform. The ceiling is reconstructed.

This wall returns to the east, constructed of masonry and Roman brick. Then the wall continues to the northeast, largely reconstructed, which joins with the house structure butting out from the step. The internal space contained by these walls is planted with 226 modern vines and stakes.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the House of the Geometric Mosaic in the so called complex of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14, 16) and part of the complex referred to by Eschebach as the complex of L. Aelius Magnus, which includes entrances 14-20. The area was under reconstruction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction, including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This room (7) has been identified as a dining hall due to its size and position in the house. We enter this room via a wide door from the atrium (2) in the northeast wall. The threshold is modern reconstruction in grey blocks with a step down to the floor level which preserves sections of marble with post holes for a door at either end. The floor shows remains of a large black and white mosaic - a black field with a double white banded border and a broad white edge. This appears to be laid over a previous white tesserae floor. The room is a large rectangular space. The southwest wall has no windows extant, but a window exists on the northeast wall to the atrium (2). The walls are brick and opus incertum, The southwest wall preserves a niche possibly for a lararium. The northwest wall has an arched opening at the base about halfway along the length. Plaster is preserved on all walls with black paint .....(obscured writing). The plaster is in poor condition. No ceiling remains.

Eschebach

DESCRIPTION: This is the house of the Vettii. The space (19) is a cubiculum/small reception room. DESCRIPTION: This street shrine consists of the masonry core of an altar, located on the vicolo del Labirinto, between 6.12 and 6.13. The altar sits on the sidewalk and consists of a concrete platform with a heavy pottery matrix that slopes towards the street. The altar itself consists of two upright stones, originally bonded by a concrete matrix containing large pottery shards and stone pieces. The height of the altar above the sidewalk is 0.985m. The width of the altar is approximately 0.75m and the depth is 0.34m. The south-eastern upright stone has fallen on to the sidewalk in that direction. Only the recessed top edge on the altar on the upright stone is extant. There is no external cladding. There is one layer of concrete matrix extant on top of the standing stone. There is extant wall plaster behind the altar.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Moralist and we have determined that its last usage was as a house. This room on the upper floor has been identified as a dining room due to its location in the house and the fine decoration and garden views. It is rectangular and on a NE/SW axis. We enter this room via a step down from dining room 4395 to the southeast. In the eastern corner of the southeast wall there is a doorway-sized opening blocked by a modern gate, which was probably a window in antiquity. Most of the northeast wall is a very large window providing a view to the garden (13) below. Some red painted plaster remains below the window and there is a drainage hole at the northern end at floor level. The northwest wall shows two very high windows overlooking the sacred grove of Diana (12) and the statue of Diana, which was white marble with possible metal accoutrements. On the northern end of the northwest wall beneath the window are two drainage holes to the exterior. Low down on the wall on the west and northern ends there are square holds whose purpose is unknown. The southwest wall shows a small portion of a black dado and tiny triangle of the red central register on the southern end of the southeast wall. The dado is missing but in the central register we see the remains of two panel pictures. On the southern end the panel shows Dionysus with a panther cape about to awaken a sleeping Ariadne to a new abundant life. Three putti, one armed with a bow, are assisting Dionysus. The central panel is mostly missing but elegant Egyptian columns remain, along with beautifully painted remnants of three figures. The floor shows small marble tiles inserted in concrete, modern cement floor overlays about half the floor. There is a good sized circular opening in a carved marble square, giving access to the floor below, possibly for transporting food from the kitchen on the lower floor. On the floor, level with the southeast end of the door opening, are two stone emplacements with sockets for a door. The ceiling is modern.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 31 (4395) is to the southeast.

DESCRIPTION: It has been determined that the Villa of the Mysteries is a commercial and residential structure. The room (67) has been identified as a preparation room due to its size, location, and features. It is a small rectangular structure on a southwest and northeast axis. One enters through a small doorway located in the south corner of the southwest wall. There is a white stone threshold with cuttings for a door. The walls are opus incertum, preserved to a great height on the southeast and northwest sides. The southwest and northeast sides are partition walls and are not well preserved. All walls have remains of plaster, but no paint. There are cupboard niches (6920, 6921) at the northern end of the northwest wall (6920) and at the eastern end of the southeast wall (6921). A rectangular stone preparation platform (6922) is located in the western corner of the room. No ceiling is preserved.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is northwest of peristyle 26 and is northeast of room 68.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so called House of Championnet. It is also known as the House of the Geometric Mosaics. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14,16) and part of the complex of L. Aelius Magnus, which includes entrances 14-20. This area was under construction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction, including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This room (19) in the House of the Geometric Mosaics is entered from the atrium (17) through a door in the center of the southeast wall. A marble threshold exists with fittings for a door. The floor is covered with a white and black mosaic with a white ground. A central emblem of a geometric flower shape is inserted into a lozenge shape which is bordered by black and white borders and a broad border of black stripes with checkerboard mosaic insertion. At either edge of the mosaic (northeast and southwest) there is a black rectangle on a white ground with an inserted black stripe delineating the edges. All walls show some white plastering. A large rectangular window is present high on the northwest wall. Eschebach calls this room an apotheka due to the wall holes for shelving (insert unintelligible bottom line here )...The upper sections of the brick and opus incertum wall are reconstructed. The southeast wall is brick and opus reticulatum. There is a modern ceiling.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Eschebach
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is in the north corner of atrium (17).

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so-called House of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrance 14,16) and part of the complex of L. Aelius Magnus which includes entrances 14 to 20. This area has since had modern reconstruction including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This is a large square room in the House of the Geometric Mosaics. Room 23 has been identified as a dining room due to its position in the house, its decoration and its views. We enter from atrium (17) via a doorway in the eastern corner of the northeast wall. There is a marble threshold with fixings for a door and .....
There is a wide doorway at the southern end of the southwest wall to the corridor (28), an extensive terrace that overlooks the sea. There is a limestone threshold with square cuttings for door posts. The floor is a white cocciopesto with an inserted emblema of black and white mosaic. A circle of black tesserae with seven geometric flowers also in black is on a white ground and bordered with a broad black stripe. A plastered drainage hole is present in the floor near the southeast wall. This room would permit bench placement in several ways. The walls are brick and opus incertum and reconstructed at the upper levels and all show some signs of plaster but no paint. There is no ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Corridor (28) is the the southeast and atrium (17) is to the northwest.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified this structure as a residential house with 3 entrances. Entrance 7 is the main entrance, entrance 3 is the secondary entrance and entrane 9 is the back entrance. We have determined the usage of the room as a dining room. This identification is based on the location of the room opening on the peristyle colonnade (29); the size and dimensions of this room, which is a fairly large rectangular space on a south west/north east axis. A wide opening almost the entire width of the north east wall would have provided a view of the colonnade (29) with two fountains between the columns towards the eastern end of the peristyle column. A smaller doorway opens to the corridor at the northern corner of the north west wall. This doorway has a white stone threshold and is restored to a lower doorway than the main door. The present condition of this room is very poor. The floor is completely gone exposing the lower level of the house (6789, root cellar). The walls are opus incertum with plaster remaining at the south corner of the south east wall, and the eastern corner at the north east side of the doorway and on the north west wall. There are two lines of holes cut through the south east wall; the lower comprised of three round large cuttings and with the upper row comprised of two smaller cuttings. The cuttings aline with each other. There are also two rows of holes cut into the south west walls. The bottom row comprises 1 rectangular hole in the south corner, a square hole in the middle, and a square hole in the west corner. The upper row comprises a central rectangular hole and a rectangular hole in the western corner.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the south west of area (29) of the peristyle and is south east of the corridor. Dining hall (24) is to the east.

DESCRIPTION:
This is a commercial establishment with a shop, vineyard, and processing spaces. This is an "L" shaped mansonry counter, the upper half of which is no longer extant. The lower half has extensive modern consolidation. The long arm of the counter faces the center of the room. The short arm of the counter faces the street to the south. At the north end of the long arm of the counter Eschebach reports a no-longer extant Hearth 5003, to the south of which are two dolia inserted into the counter: 5001 and 5002. Eschebach records a third dolium (5010), but no trace of it survives.

Bibliography: Eschebach p.70; PPP1, 190; PPM 920-921; Jashemski 57-58
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Shelf 5000 is to the northeast and Shelf 5008 is to the south.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified the structure of the Villa of Mysteries as a villa rustica type of structure. We have determined that the usage of this room is a reception hall.
The location is along the south side of the villa, adjacent to the diaeta, room (33). There is ample space for tables and chairs, with a splendid view of the "L" shaped garden. The floor is a huge rectangle of opus sectile with a wide black band for a border. The various pieces of marble are large, irregular shapes in browns, golds, reds, and black and blue.
On the north wall, there are two doors. One is a passageway (40) to the atrium (41). It has evidence of locks on threshold. Just east of this is a large door to the dining room 30 (6931).
On the east wall is a door to the farm manager's atrium (23). There is evidence of a lock in marble threshold. On the south side, there is a large passageway on east end that leads to the commercial part of the villa. The threshold shows signs of locks. There is one very large window area of this south wall with two engaged Doric columns on the ends and three free standing, all along the window sill. This overlooks the "L" shaped garden. There is one door to the diaeta (33) on the west wall. There is a large window on the north wall that overlooks the cult room (34)
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Diaeta 33 on west. Cult room 34 on north, passage (40) to atrium (41) on north, dining room 30 on north. Farm managers atrium on east (23)

DESCRIPTION:
It has been determined that this is a residential structure known as the House of the Priest Amandus. This room has been identified as a dining room due to its location, size, and decoration. This is a rectangular space on a northwest-southeast axis. A tall doorway is located at the eastern end of the south wall. The floor is opus signinum with a central tableau and a pattern of white lines of tesserae which appear above the areas of the room that would not contain the triclinia. According to the floor design, the couches would have been placed along the southwest, northwest, and northeast walls. The doorway is marked with a pattern of criss-crossing lines of white tesserae. A wide band with white and black tesserae in a floret pattern lines the southeast wall. To the northwest of this band is a band with white tesserae depicting squares and diamonds and other shapes. A wide band is located to the northwest of this with a diamond pattern. This band extends to the central tableau. The central tableau has bands of white tesserae with a band of florets and a central circle is outlined with bands of white and black tesserae and a band of white mosaic. The center of the circle is opus sectile, with four marble pieces also placed at the corners in the field outside the circles. The walls are well preserved with frescoes remaining on all four. A black dado with painted vignettes of birds and fruit (4252) is visible over most of the walls, with vertical panels above the dado. Another frieze of yellow panels with central paintings of fruit is in the top frieze.

The ceiling was vaulted (a modern reconstruction), with a window in the arch of the center of the upper southeast wall.

The red frieze on each wall is punctuated by a large painting panel with a mythological scene, with a scene of Bacchus (4253) on the southeast wall, Andromeda and Perseus on the southwest wall; on the northwest wall is Hercules, and on the northeast Icarus. The top yellow frieze contains central tableaux on each wall depicting food or drink (4251, 4250, 4249, and 4252). There are tiny accents on the red panels depicting figures with cups or jugs, such as 4254 on the southeast wall, which still depicts figures carrying jugs on their heads. This decoration scheme is fourth style. There is a great deal of restoration including the modern ceiling and a large portion of the southwest wall which is now plaster-filled.

There is a small rectangular window cut in the west corner of the northwest wall at the height of the top band of the dado and lower portion of the red frieze.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is off the west corner of the atrium (2) and directly northwest of the unnumbered stairway.

DESCRIPTION:
This deep public well is at the intersection of the Via Consolare and Vicolo di Narciso. It is Southeast of 6.1.18-19. The interior depth is difficult to discern because of restricted access. The superstructure above is barrel-vaulted. The vault runs northeast-southwest and appears to have several phases of construction. The superstructure sits on a tufa base slightly larger than the barrel vault. The lower section of the superstructure is made of tufa and volcanic stone, while the upper part is made of volcanic stone, tufa and some brick. Centered to the west in the exterior southeastern wall of the superstructure is a singular volcanic stone that has been mortared to the superstructure (F.Mazois 1824 and T. Dyer 1867 refer to this as a street altar.). The extant size of the stone is 0.57 meters by 0.65 meters with an extant height of 0.95 meters. There is a 0.22 meter by 0.15 meter wall of the barrel vault approximately 0.97 meters from the exterior northern corner. This opening is near the west corner of the adjoining water tower (4842).

F. Mazois Les Ruins De Pompeii, Second Partie. Paris:Firman Didot, 18. p 37 PL2,1
T. Dyer. Drawing of Fountain and Deep Well with Altar and Lararium. Painting London: Bell and Daldy, 1867: p. 38â€ƒâ€ƒ
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This public well is located at the intersection of the Via Consolare and Vicolo di Narciso, south of 6.1.18. It is northwest of fountain (4840) and abuts water tower (4842).

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified structure II-1-10 as a vineyard with a processing centre and room 7 as a processing room based upon its location immediately off the vineyard and the presence of what Eschebach defines as a water basin.

The room is entered from a door on the northwest from hallway 10 and sits on a southeast / northwest axis. The water basin (4283) sits in the western corner of the room. A square window centered on the southeast wall looks out to the garden (room 6). Higher up on the wall is a small opening which may have been a window in the past. The walls are opus incertum with some reconstruction and appear to have undergone renovations at various points in the past.

Bibliography: Eschebach page 87; Amadio, B., 'Regio II, Insula 1,' in Rivista di Studi Pompeiana 2 (1982), 192-5.

In particular, the west wall, devoid of any plaster, shows changed in both ancient and modern times. Plaster remains on the other three walls (red and white color appears to remain in some areas). The floor contains remains of cocciopesto surface.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Southeast of hallway 10, to the northwest and southwest of garden area 6.

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that the extended structure of 2.1.3,4,5,6,7 is a food distribution center based upon the interconnection of three shops, a house, a garden and space for storage of horses and carts. Room 1 is a counter room base upon the presence of a counter with dolia and hearth. The room has a wide marble entrance, a step up from the sidewalk on Via dell'Abbondanza. The door sill has indentations indicating the placement of a typical shop door closure. The room is rectangular in shape and sits on a north west - south east axis. The walls are opus incertum. The restored front entryway is opus mixtum. No trace of plaster exists on the walls, which are heavily recontructed. The counter (4292) is L-shaped - beginning on the north corner of the room and stretching through the middle.Behind the counter - in the working area - the floor rises by one step and is currently lapilli. The remainder of the floor around the counter is today lapilli but some traces of terracotta tiling remain by the door to the storeroom to the south east.

Jashemski 126; Eschebach 86
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: On the west corner of 2.1.1, to the north west of storeroom 2 and to the south west of sales room 3

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that 2.1.3-7 is a food distribution center and that room 13 is a combination of a garden area and space for carts. We base this determination upon the fact that entrance 7 on the side street abutting Via dell'Abbondanza is, today, a small metal gate but at the time of the eruption was a wide entranceway. Eschebach suggests that a stable and cart space was located here. Space 13 is a large garden-like area in a rectangular shape on a north west - south east axis. The south west wall runs along the side street and contains entrance 7. The south east wall backs to the neighboring property. The north east wall contains two wide doorways - one to space 14, with a rectangular window above the door frame (designated as a stable) and one to area 12. The north west wall has two wide rectangular windows and two large doorways, leading to room 4 (which is the back shop room of entrance 5) and room 2, which has been identified as the storeroom for the counter room (4291) at entrance 6. Walls are opus incertum. The doorways have jambs of opus mixtum and the floor is overgrown with weeds and it is impossible to determine its composition. The area is open to the sky.

Jashemski 26; Eschebach 86
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: to the south east of storeroom 2 and Tablinum 4, to the south west of stable 14 and space 12

DESCRIPTION: We have identified a residential structure and determined the use of this space as a dining room. This identification is based on: the large size of this rectangular space; the presence of a large couch niche [6845] in the southwest wall; the broad entranceway at the eastern end of the southeast wall; a large window on the northeast side overlooking [4]/ This is a large rectangular space on a northeast/southwest axis. The doorway at the east end of the southeast wall is the only door to this space. It is fairly high and is broad. No threshold is visible. The condition of this room is fair to poor with upper walls reconstructed and a modern ceiling. No flooring is visible. Over the large window in the northeast wall there is a small, central window. Painted plaster remains on all four walls. The northwest wall is intact to the ceiling in the northwest corner. The painting scheme is barely visible; however there is a dado which may have been black. The zone above is divided into large panels which appear to have been red, and the uppermost zone revealed slight traces of architectural spaces beyond the wall. This may have been fourth style. There may have been a tunneling hole in western half of the northwest wall, although modern plaster is covering this section of the wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is directly southwest of the garden [4] and northwest of spaces 6 and 7.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified this kitchen [6832] for the following reasons. There are two main entrances. One is a rear entrance to the street, the other to the gardens. Two others are two additional rooms. The kitchen is of a good size. On the southeast is a door to the prep room, then another entry on the southeast to another prep room. On the southwest wall there is a long hallway to the garden, then another entry steps down to a dining room. On the northwest wall there is a small rectangular space. There one sees a large cooking platform [6833] but most cooking platform attributes are missing. There was a tiled surface to cook on. There is a low wall connecting the platform with a water basin [6834] with a pipe. This basin is coated with hydraulic cement. Then one can see a latrine [6837] of good size, possibly for two people. The walls show small portions of painted plaster. There is no ceiling to the entire area described. The exterior door (to the street) has a stone threshold. The threshold shows indications for a large door and indications for a smaller door within the threshold.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: There is a cooking platform [6833] which shares a wall to the northeast with the water basin [6834] and another wall to the northeast with the latrine [6837]. There are two prep rooms on the southeast wall. A hallway and a dining room [6846] lie to the southwest.

DESCRIPTION:
This public fountain is on the west side of the Via di Mercurio at the intersection with the Vicolo di Mercurio. It is at the northeast corner 6.8.24. The fountain is constructed of volcanic slabs. There is a round lining at the wall/floor junction. The floor lining is no longer extant, revealing terra cotta tile pieces. The pilaster sits at the center top of the southwestern slab and is decorated with the image of a Mercury in high relief. The fountain has no modern plumbing. The interior dimensions of the basin are 1.21 meters by 0.91 meters and it is 0.78 meters deep. There are worn hand recesses on either side of the pilaster. There are worn hand recesses also at the western and southern interior corners of the basin. The overflow is in the center top of the northeastern slab, with the drainage hole near the northern interior corner.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This public fountain is located on the west side of the Via di Mercurio at the intersection with the Vicolo di Mercurio. It is at the northeast corner of 6.8.24.

DESCRIPTION: This is the so-called House of Championnet complex, also referred to as the House of the Geometric Mosaics. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14,16) and part of the complex of L. Aelius Magnus which includes entrances 14 to 20. This area was under reconstruction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction, including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This room (21) is identified as a small dining room. It is a small rectangular room on a northeast, southwest axis. The entrance to this room is through the southeast wall. This room is open to the atrium (17). A small, arched opening cuts through to the adjacent atrium (2) to the northwest, associated with entrance 14. The doorway has a broad white threshold flanked by two grey volcanic stones which underlie the ends of the wall. Both sides of the southeast wall are brickwork. The section to the east of the doorway reveals rectangular panels of opus reticulatum. The other corners of the room are also brickwork, extending from the north corner to the west, including the arched opening. The central areas of the northwest, southwest and northeast walls are opus incertum. Plaster remains on all walls, but no fresco survives. The upper portion of this room is reconstructed. The ceiling is reconstructed. The floor of this room is decorated with white mosaic with black decoration. The central area of the floor is defined by a wide border with ........... This central area is flanked by black lined borders which define side spaces at the southwest and northeast sides of the room, perhaps for couches. These defined areas do not extend to the southeast wall because of the features, now missing, which occupied the south and east corners of the room. These features are unidentifiable, but were rectangular with a stone border and a red cocciopesto floor surface. These spaces may have held storage chests.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: ?This dining room is to the northwest of the atrium (17). It is to the southeast of corridor 20.

DESCRIPTION:
This enclosure tomb is on the southern side of the cemetery road, with a house-like facade. It is the tomb of Aulus Veius Atticus. The facade is built in opus incertum and covered in stucco. There is a molded cornice and pediment with a molded ranking cornice and a marble dedicatory inscription in the center of the pediment. A large doorway goes through the center of the facade. The facade is the north-west wall. The remains of steps approach the entrance and there is a large raised threshold block. No remains of a door are visible. There are remains of plaster still visible on the north-west, south-west and north-east walls. The door-frame, like the threshold, is dark volcanic stone in large bricks. Behind the facade is a walled enclosure for funerary banqueting. No flooring is visible. The facade has a peaked roof, reconstructed with roof tiles. The white stucco facade has red painted borders around the pediment and molded cornice, and this also has red graffiti across the facade.

BIBLIOGRAPHY
Campbell 29
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This tomb is to the south-east of the cemetary road. It is adjacent to tomb 9, which mirrors it's facade and is to the south-west.

DESCRIPTION:
This house is not complete.

It has been identified that VII, 2, 16 is an early domestic house that may have been used as a commercial property or solely for domestic purposes. It is known by 4 names: House of Marcus Gavius Rufus, House of Theseus, House of the Seven Skeletons and House of the American Admiral. It has been determined that the last usage of Room 16 was as a dining room. This is based on size, location and decoration. It is a rectangular space on a northeast/southwest axis. One enters through a large doorway on the southwest side. This door opens out to the southeast ambulatory of the peristyle court. The flooring remains visible in the northeast half of the room. It is cocciopesto with a pattern of white and back stone tesserae. The pattern clearly delineates a space for three couches surrounding a circular motif. The walls are opus incertum with the doorways flanked by large stone masonry (tuff). On the whole, plaster is preserved on every wall with fresco remaining on the northeast and northwest walls. These frescoes are best preserved in the northeastern half of the room where they are covered by a reconstructed ceiling. The room is in fair/poor condition with reconstruction along the upper parts of the walls. The surviving fresco appears to be second style preserving large columns separating panels, with traces of garlands. The panel in the eastern corner of the northeastern wall preserves a face of a tragic mask. At the south end of the southeastern wall, a small doorway passes through to the entrance corridor leading to the kitchen. This, like the other doorway, does not preserve a threshold.

Eschebach p257
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
This room is located to the northwest of the corridor to the kitchen.
It is to the northwest of the ambulatory of the peristyle court (5).

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this room as a storage room. We base this identification on its location, proximity and accessibility from the ambulatory (11) and atrium (2). The presence of a large dolium (4571) supports this usage. This is a rectangular room with a north-south axis. There are two large doorways, each with stone (tufa) thresholds. The large doorway on the north wall opens into the atrium (2), and the large doorway on the south wall opens to the ambulatory (11). Two smaller doorways on the east wall open to two small rooms (9 and 10). On the west, there is a low wall with a large window opening into the tablinum (48). The floor is stone and rubble (lapilli). There are no remaining fresco surfaces.

BIBLIOGRAPHY ESCHEBACH PAGE 451

DESCRIPTION: It has been determined that this is a restaurant and vineyard (4363) known as the House of Lesbianus. This determination is based on the presence of a kitchen and at least five dining rooms along with the absence of cubicula. This space is identified as a dining room (1). One enters this space through a doorway from the street in the northeast wall. The space is rectangular on a northwest-southeast axis. The northwest section of this space provides room for a triclinium. The southeast side of this room serves as a passageway connecting the entrance to the kitchen (4360) and stairway to the southeast and stairs to the vineyard (4363) at the south end of the southeast wall, a doorway to a small dining room (3) at the south end of the southwest wall, and a doorway in the middle of the southwest wall into a larger dining room (2). DESCRIPTION: This is a rectangular press room on a northwest/southwest axis, entranced through the southwest wall through a partially blocked doorway to the corridor to the west, with stepped threshold and placings for a door. DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this structure is domestic and called the House of the Moralist. This space is identified as a dining room due to its size and location. DESCRIPTION:
Tomb 30EN is made of opus incertum and brick. Tomb face is towards the southeast and is comprised of two parts. At the bottom is a rectangle of opus incertum with three arched and plastered niches centrally located. Each niche has an indentation for a statue or columella of the deceased. The rectangular top is slightly smaller than the base with brickwork creating engaged columns on the two sides. A pediment fits between the two columns with a flat plastered area below and a marble inscription plaque above at the tip of the triangle. (See Campbell for a translation of the inscription.) The architrave and pediment had stucco reliefs of a hunt scene and ritual objects (see Feature 4916) per Campbell. The walls on the southeast and northwest are in poor condition but a projected plan indicates the depth of the tomb enclosure would have been about 3.24 meters.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the House of the Vettii. We have determined this space to be an ala due to its position off the atrium. This ala (4662) is located in the north corner of the main atrium of the house of the Vettii. This ala has three walls north west, north east and south east. DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this residence is a domestic structure known as the House of the Moralist. DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is a dining room within a residential structure. We have identified it as a dining room for servants. We have based this identification on the location of the room, which steps down from the large kitchen (1). This identification is also based on the large scale of this room and the features which include a high platform along the entire northwest wall and a stepped platform in the south and west corners. The condition of this room is very poor. The floor is not visible. A row of five horizontal beam holes across the southwest wall suggest a low ceiling. Two holes in the remaining portion of the northeast wall align with the holes in the southwest wall. There is a window above the level of the holes in the center of the southwest wall. The poor condition of this room makes it difficult to determine whether it had any painted decoration; the only plaster remaining is at the southwest wall, but this seems to predate the addition of the partition wall on the northwest and southeast sides. DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Geometric Mosaics in the so-called complex of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14,16) and part of the complex of L. DESCRIPTION: We are in the House of M. Pupius Rufus. We have identified this room as a dining room. The floor is not visible due to vegetation nor is the threshold to the west. DESCRIPTION:
This public fountain is located where the Via Consolare and the Vicolo di Modesto meet. It sits southeast of 6.13.19-20. It is constructed of volcanic stone slabs. There is a round lining at the wall/floor junction. It is probably lined with opus signinum, The interior of the basin measures 1.02 meters by 1.20 meters and it is 0.72 meters deep. The pilaster sits atop the enter of the northwestern slab and is decorated with an eagle holding a hare in its beak. The fountain has modern plumbing but it is not currently functional. The overflow is on the top center of the southeastern slab with the drainage hole below almost at street level, There is a well-worn hand recess on the northwest side of the pilaster and lesser worn hand recesses on the northeast side of the pilaster and part the interior northern and western corners.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This fountain is at the intersection of the Via di Consolare and the Vicolo di Modesto. It is immediately southeast of 6.3.19-20.

DESCRIPTION:
It has been identified that VII, 2, 48 is a commercial restaurant. It has been determined that the last usage of Room 11 was as a dining room. This identification as a potential dining room is based on the lavish decoration and single recess. The small room is entered through a high rectangular entrance door to the south of Corridor 15. The northern corner of the northwestern wall has a large rectangular recess that could have housed a couch. The room seems to have originally been painted with motifs of architectural structures and figurative motifs, such as (what looks like) a lion on the northern wall and a naked male figure on the southeastern wall. These motifs were later covered by another painted design, but only traces of red socle remain. The figurative motifs were framed on top by a frieze supporting a projecting semi-lunette which would also have been painted. Above the semi-lunette on the northern wall are six rectangular recesses which may have housed the beams to support the second floor. No traces are visible of such recesses on the opposite wall. The south wall is pierced by a small rectangular opening above the door opening. No traces are visible of the original flooring. From inside the room, the entrance door frames the window of the opposite Space 9.

Bibliography: Eschebach p763-764 and Jashemski p175
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Corridor 15

There is small potions of plaster and some painted plaster on the wall. There is no ceilings. The recess explains the 'L' shaped protrusion into the dining room. DESCRIPTION:
This is tomb sixteen identified by Campbell as the tomb of Numerius Alleius Auctus. It is an enclosure with three walls on opus incertum and the fourth wall ( southwest wall) being the exterior of tomb fourteen. There is an opening in the west corner. The enclosure space contains six collumella although Campbell identified nine and presumably one of the missing pieces was inscribed with the name given to this tomb.
Presently, four collumella are standing in situ along the northwest wall and north corner, as well as two more in the south corner.
We suggest that the remaining space would have been used for funerary banqueting.
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Campbell
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This tomb is to the northeast of tomb fourteen and the north of the cemetery road.

DESCRIPTION:
This space has been identified as a shop associated with the bakery at 5-4-1, although this shop is 5-4-2. It is a rectangular space on a northeast/southwest axis. There is a wide doorway to the street along the southeast side. The threshold is composed of three large gray blocks with a cut groove across all three. There is a doorway at the western end of the southwest wall with no threshold. There is a niche at the east end of the northeast wall which is presently open through to the adjacent property (5-4-3). There is a niche near the south corner of the southwest wall. Two large windows open to the serving room (14) to the northwest. The front of the shop was brick. The southwest wall and the northeast wall were opus incertum. The northwest wall is opus incertum below the window level with large cut block masonry along the west corner as far as the window and between the two windows. The floor was cocciopesto, which is preserved in part along the northeast wall and niche. The ceiling does not survive. Kneading basin (4633) is in the north corner. Four other artifacts presently stand to the west of this. One of these is a stone mortar. The other
three appear to be stone column fragments. Plaster with fresco (yellow turned red) surviving can be seen near the south corner on the the southwest and southeast walls.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The shop is to the southeast of serving room (14) and northeast of the fauces (1).

DESCRIPTION: Dining room lies in the southeast part of the house. It is entered from the anteroom (room 13) to the northwest. On the southeast wall is a long rectangular opening high up in the wall and one small ground level opening to the right. On the far end of the southwest wall in the entrance to the cubiculum (room 12). The black and white mosaic floor is divided into two sections which are separated by a band. The band is decorated in a scroll. The southeast portion of the mosaic is a plain white mosaic of tesserae. The northeast section of the mosaic is decorated with a grid of 3x3 square panels. The panels are ornamented with black and white geometric designs. The panels as a group are framed by one strand guilloche. The wall panels are divided into two sections along the lines of the mosaic sectioned divisions. The northeast and southeast sections are divided by long rectangular bands of different colors and widths. The southwest and southeast walls are decorated with three large red panels supported by a large band ornamented with a yellow structure that looks like a podium. The other half of the dining room is decorated with figurative panels containing life size figures. In the northwest wall is partly destroyed female figure sitting on a low support and wearing a long robe. In her right hand she is holding an unidentified object. In northeast wall is left only a male figure dressed in a white mantle. He is sitting on a low based support. He is looking right but at what is no longer discernible. In southeast wall represents to large elephants standing on either side of an alter. On the right elephant, on its back are two small figures holding indiscernible objects. This elephant is ornamented with a garland around its neck.

Room of irregular shape! (Rectangular-Have architects check) with a beveled southeast corner- presumably following contour of cliff. No indication of original floor covering. DESCRIPTION: Garden restaurant. Small dining room located in front of room 13. Window on north wall looks on to the garden (room 10). DESCRIPTION: One enters Room 2 from the south by ascending two steps. Directly to the west of the entrance is a cooking platform set back into the wall. The rest of the room is roughly rectangular with a north-south axis. On the north wall is a window that has been blocked up. On the south wall is a large window looking on to Room 1. Below the window is an irregularly shaped recess which may have been used for a couch or counter. The room was decorated in antiquity but not enough remains to say anything about it. On the north and east walls are places to insert ceiling beams to create what Eschebach calls a half floor or mezzanine, probably for storage. He refers to steps in this room but all indications of them are missing.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: None None Salesroom (Room 1) is to the west.

DESCRIPTION: Rectangular room with east/west axis. Doorway in center of west wall opens to small garden(room 14) Doorway at west end of north wall to 11. Painting survives in northeast corner along east and south wall. Red lower register, yellow above with a border. Indeterminate yellow decoration in lower register. DESCRIPTION: Rectangular room with east/west axis. Doorway in the northern wall to north. Step up to room 8 and doorway at Western end of southern wall to room 11. DESCRIPTION: This feature number, 3721 is a rubble and mortar basin for a mill. The top is smoothed with cement and the structure sits between 2 other mill basins that are aligned with the S.E. wall. The structure is approximately 1.5 feet high on the exterior, at it's highest point and is circular. The inner height is slightly less. The width of the ring surface from the outer portion to the inner portion is approximately 8 inches, similar to the size of a rim of a tire. The center is filled with rubble and debris.

DESCRIPTION: There is a small lararium situated approximately 5 feet from the ground on the Southeast wall in the mill room. The height from the bottom to the top of the lararium is approximately 1.5 feet and the width is approximately .1 foot. The top is arched and it is approximately 6-8 inches deep, at the bottom. There is evidence of plaster painted light yellow containing plants with green leaves and red berries. There is a broken lip/edge which protrudes along the bottom.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is contiguous to mill base 3721 to the N.E. and mill base 3720 to the N.W.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Done by Lisa Wernick and Fran Capo

DESCRIPTION: There is a large rectangular room, it is situated on an E/W axis. There is a wide open doorway, situated through the West wall to Atrium 7. There is no visible threshold. The floor is obscured by lapilli. The N, E, and S walls are under extensive restoration. Extensive plaster survives on the N, E and S walls with visible decoration on the N and S walls. The plaster is best preserved on the N. wall. Identified, is a 3rd style with a black lower register with yellow trim, white is seen above with red trim. Red trim survives in the S.W. corner, with trims of plaster moulding seen at the junction of the ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Atrium 7, to the West
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Carlos Avila

DESCRIPTION: On the S.W. wall of the kitchen, there is a beehive oven that has a square opening to the kitchen. The oven is constructed of mortar and cut stone slabs. The base is cut stone.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: There is a platform that extends from this oven (3706) along the N.W. wall. There is a stone slab covering a well (3707) situated immediately S.W. of this oven.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Done by the team of Fran Capo & Lisa Wernick

DESCRIPTION: This is a low, rectangular couch niche, situated at the E. end of the N. wall. The base of this niche is obscured by lapilli and debris. The plastered interior face survives at the W end of the niche.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: N.E. corner of the room.

DESCRIPTION: We see a great enclosed oven. At the floor level is a rectangular opening to store wood or charcoal. There is no dolium for water storage. There is a large slab and smaller stones inside a great restraining arch that encloses the beehive oven within. To the right of the archway is a rectangular space for the use of a lamp, good luck symbols, etc. The brickwork enclosing the beehive extends across one third of the oven. The other two thirds is plaster and opus incertum. This great oven extends on the north wall and has a large passageway where workers could pass through prepared bread loaves to the baker standing in part of the oven. He would insert the bread (as many as 80 loaves were removed from one Pompeii oven). On the right side of the oven there is a pass-through where the bakers would pass trough loaves into the processing room (4433) on the side of the oven.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the south is processing room (4582). To the north is processing room (4433).

DESCRIPTION:
Room 6 has been determined to be a storeroom, based upon its size and the presence of holes in the walls for brackets. This small square space is entered from a doorway from dining room 5 (4592). The doorway is on the southeast wall of the room. Walls are of opus incertum and heavily restored, so the size of the door cannot be determined. The northwest wall contains a high square window to the street, with a row of post brackets for ceiling supports above. Walls contain evidence of frescoed painting. Bracket holes at various heights on the northwest and north east walls suggest a shelf storage system. Floor is dirt and weeds.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Eschebach, Jashemski 116
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the northwest of dining room 5 (4592).

DESCRIPTION: At the entry to this bakery/restaurant; situated on the Southeast corner is a rectangular counter that is small in size. The surface and all the plaster is gone. This counter was added in the final years of the life of the city of Pompei.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The team leader is Terri Bruno.

DESCRIPTION: A solid lava block is shaped for a base as a meta. We see paving stones around this feature. There is no catillus. It is approximately 30 cm from the southeast wall which is confusing as there is no space for ananimal to walk around it.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: mill 3207 and kneading basin 3222 to the northeast; catillus 3226 and mill 3206 to the southwest; water basin 3225 and cistern 3216 to the northwest

DESCRIPTION: This is a square room with a doorway in the centre of the west wall with a modern lintel and no threshold. The floor is obscured by lapilli. There is undecorated plaster on all four walls. High in the centre of the east wall is a large window opening to the street, with a modern lintel. Three quarters of the east wall beneath the window is taken up by a large rectangular cooking platform 6197. In the southeast corner there is a latrine 6198.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: room 15 to the west

DESCRIPTION: We enter this larger dining room from the west from a narrow corridor off garden 11 to a no longer extant entrance. The floor is lapilli and rubble. There is little plaster or paint in this room except for a patch on the north wall. Here we can see the ubiquitous white/yellow so common in this insula. The adjoining dining room 12 (3279) is connected by a narrow doorway to the south wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: adjoins dining room 12 (3279) and overooks the colonnaded garden 11 and is alongside corridor 8 to the north

DESCRIPTION: On the north wall of dining room 12 there is a niche backing on to the east wall. It is a moderate size with a minimal indentation. It has been plastered and painted red.

Squarish room 2 opens to the north to salesroom 1. The doorway is narrow with reconstructed brick facing on both sides. The west wall is opus incertum with two high post holes near the north and south ends. At the southwest end are the remains of an embedded dolium 6508. The north wall contains slight traces of painted plaster (red and white?) The east wall has three brick structures at its current top, which may have been windows opening to the street to the east. There are two post holes, one at window height, one slightly lower. A brick arch in the masonry at floor level provided structural support. In the south east corner of the room are three stone steps. The south wall is masonry with faint plaster trace and brick facing around the doorway. There are two joist holes in that wall, one on either side of the door. Floor is obscured by lapilli. No ceiling remains. Eschebach says that this was an olive oil distributor.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: sale room 1 to the south

DESCRIPTION: Trace remains of a clay dolium are found in the southwest corner of preparation room 2. Eschebach suggests that a water basin was also present in the vicinity.

The northeast and west walls contain a series of post holes indicating the presence of display shelves around this shop. The west wall contains pairs of four and the east wall has two regularly spaced pairs. Another four holes are scattered with no regular patterns throughout the shop.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: all north of 6507 dolium

DESCRIPTION: Eschebach pp 184-185 refers to a second dolium in room 2 that is no longer extant.

This preparation/cooking platform is approximately five feet long along the southeast wall and on the northeast wall approximately three feet deep. At its highest point, it is approximately three feet high and is in the corner.

DESCRIPTION: This is the remains of a rectanguar basin in the south corner of the room. It is in very poor condition. It is visible to about six inches in depth and seems to have had ceramic tile lining along the northwest edge. The use of this basin cannot be determined.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: to southwest of dolium 3925, in the southern corner of the room

DESCRIPTION: Walking into this storeroom, north of us is a stairway to the second floor. We see a plastered rectangular storeroom on a north/south axis. On the west wall we see three post holes for shelves. The north wall has some plaster left and four post holes for a ceiling. On the east wall we see a low doorway to storeroom 18. This storeroom is under the stairway. The floor is pounded earth with some lapilli. This room would have had a ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: storeroom 17 to the north, dining garden 13 to the south

DESCRIPTION:
This house is not completed. This house identified as the House of C. Vibius preserves a large open space at the southeast end of the house. This space is identified as an exedra or dining garden. The exedra is in a portion of the house that shifts its axis from northwest/southeast to a slightly more easterly direction. There is a wide opening along the northwest side into this space; no threshold is visible. This may have been a garden. The walls are preserved to what would have been a second story level, but this space would have been unroofed. Small beam holes along the southeastern wall may have held an awning, and three small holes along the southwest wall may have held a small covering. The entrance is flanked by massive walls of alternating courses of brick and cut stone. The three other walls are opus incertum. The northeast wall is constructed with two large brick supporting arches within the fabric of the wall. Midway across this wall is a hole through the wall with an inverted roof tile serving as a rain spout. One feature remains in situ: Dolium 4556 which stands in the northern corner of the space. This space may have been a garden and perhaps an outdoor dining space.

Bibliography: Eschebach
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is to the southeast of the peristyle courtyard and to the east of the kitchen (Room 23)

DESCRIPTION: This is a cupboard located in the western corner of storage room 9. This appears to be about two feet deep, three feet wide and goes up to the ceiling. Holes in the northwest wall remain for shelving. Some pkaster remains over the rubble structure. Condition is poor. No floor can be seen.

DESCRIPTION: A catillus is in the middle of the room towards the northern corner. Excavation reports record that it is in situ. No extant meta, present.

This large dining room is entered through a large doorway from corridor 11. The room is rectangular with a north east/south west axis. The room is in poor condition, however much of the coccio pesto floor remains with assorted coloured stones embedded throughout. A small door in the southern corner along the south east wall enters to the adjacent preparation room (27). There is no plaster or paint on remaining on the walls. No ceiling remains. In spite of this poor condition, the view of the peristyle gives this room a sense of luxury.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the north east of corridor 11. It is south east of dining room 32 and is north east of preparation room 27.

DESCRIPTION: Latrine with masonry step. The floor to the North of the step is tiled draining down to the latrine to the South. The hole beneath the stone step allows drainage into the drain/sewer. The sewer is filled with earth. Square recess in the wall to the west of the drain above which is a second rectangular recess supporting a seat. The latrine is separated from eh rest of the room with a plastered partition wall. However, this does not survive to sufficient height to show any placing for the seat.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Southwest corner.

DESCRIPTION:
In the Vicolo dei Termo at an intersection region 9.4 and 9.5 and 9.6 and 9.3, a corner of a house or houses that has not been excavated.
At the outside of the new central baths, which were unfinished at the time of the eruption is a crossroad shrine. This consists of an aedicular niche, made of brick with an apparent ledge and beneath it is an altar.

DESCRIPTION: This house is not completed. This feature was not identified or completed.

This is a large sized Kitchen room. The kitchen is located on the Northeast side of the house at ground level. There are 2 entrances. There is 1 entrance on the street side. You can enter directly into the kitchen from the street. The rear entrance, rooms 6, 9 and 12, then proceed into the kitchen. The entrance from the street ha 2 post holes and evidence of a door. The other entrance is taller from the interior of the house corridor, that leads from the small garden. There is no ceiling or roof remaining and the floor is made up of dirt and debris.
The North wall is badly damaged and reconstructed with some traces of yellow paint or mold. It has a round recessed area situated high up that is blocked in now. On the North wall situated on the left side is a large hearth to be discussed (6366) cooking platform.
The East wall, the facing wall (entrance 12 from the street), there is a damaged wall with traces of plaster. The construction in the lower part of the wall suggests the presence of a sewer. On the East wall, high up there is a square or rectangular opening that is damaged at the top. The S. Wall is badly damaged, it is the facing wall on the left side (6568). There is a latrine located next to a cooking platform running the length of the wall. On the West wall, facing the wall on the far right is the large door, that is an entrance to the interior of the house, it is badly damaged!
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
The room contains 2 cooking platforms and a latrine and an arched opening at floor level in the corner of the East wall

There is a large entrance on the West side that opens at the corridor (40) and there is a smaller entrance situated to the East; it enters the street. (Vicolo del Fauno)

DESCRIPTION: Rectangular masonry cooking platform extending along the north wall from the west. The southern and eastern half is collapsed but the surface survives in the north west. Plastered surface contiguous with the plaster on the north and west walls. No visible lip or storage.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Latrine 6387 and water feature 6388 are to the east

DESCRIPTION: Latrine is in the south east corner of the room. Latrine itself is obscured by lapilli and debris. In the east wall behind the latrine is a terracotta down pipe inserted into a plastered recess in the wall. The plaster continues along the face of the wall behind the latrine. Directly against the latrine to the north is the masonry support of the water feature 6388.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: water feature 6388 to the north, cooking platform 6386 to the west

DESCRIPTION: Subterranean storeroom under room 32 is accessed to the south y stairs from peristyle 26. Narrow rectangular room, east/west axis. All walls are plastered with no visible decoration. Recess in the centre of the west wall may be a collapse. Plastered vaulted ceiling. An L-shaped cooking platform is found along the north and west wall. Plastered floor throughout, partially obscured by earth and debris.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: room 26 to the south

DESCRIPTION: one enters th dining room 16 through a large open doorway from corridor 11 or corridor 10. There is no lintel nor threshold. Therre is concrete or cement plaster on most walls in large fragments. There is a low pass-through on a tiny southwest remnant of a doorway which appears to have been added to an already plastered thick doorjam. The floor is covered with rubble, terracotta tiles and debris. The only decoration visible is on the inner face of the SE doorjamb in the east corner (red and white paint). A small piece of yellow painted plaster shows through the concrete plaster of the south corner of the SW wall. Eleven poorly preserved beam holes with terracotta tiles are high on the NW wall. A tunneling hole appears on the SW wall in the center. There is no ceiling extant, but there is an indication of a second story.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to corridor 11 to the SW and corridor 10 to the SE. Contiguous to dining 15 to the SW and 17 to the NE.

DESCRIPTION: This is the dining room. it is a rectangular space on a SW/NE axis. One enters this room from a wide doorway in the center of the SE wall from the tablinum 19. The room is in very poor condition. The walls have had very little reconstruction. There is plaster on all 4 sides of the room. Some of have early conservation but the NW wall is crumbling. Although it is difficult to determine the style of painting there is a low red dado with large panels above. In the center of the NW and NE walls, one can still make out trces of rondelles. No flooring is visible. There is no ceiling remaining. The NE wall is the best preserved. There is a small high window above the horizontal cornice. This is within a molded arch. In the north corner of the NW wall, there is a small low couch niche (3906). This niche is the height of the dado and also painted red. Like the rest of the dado, it is decorated with a delicate motif: in the niches there is also painted the hind legs and tail of the animal.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the NE to the tablinum (19). This room forms the northern most corner of the house. The dieta (20) is just further east along the northeast wall.

DESCRIPTION:
This house is not completed. It has been determined that this is a rectangular kitchen. This rectangular room has a northwest/southeast axis. The floor is obscured by the earth, lapilli and vegetation throughout. All four walls survive to a considerable height with modern consolidation. In the center of the northwest wall, there is a square plastered buttress that has been added to the interface of the wall of the room. It isolated the latrine 4541 in the north corner from the rest of the room. High above the latrine, there is a rectangular plastered window with a modern lentil tapering to the street to the north. High above the west corner of the northwest wall, there is a square window with a modern lintel. In the west corner of the room, extending along the wall to the southwest wall, there is a cooking platform 4540. There is extensive collapse in the south corner, and a doorway in the east corner with no visible threshold to atrium 27. High in the southwest wall are placings for floor joists. Undecorated plaster survives on all four walls.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Eschebach 258-259
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Atrium 27 to the east

DESCRIPTION: This is a small storeroom which is located under the stairs leading to the second floor. It is a rectangular room with a north/south axis. There are some signs of plaster on the north and east walls, but nothing on the west. The stairs are gone. The floor is pounded earth on some lapilli. This room was roofed by the stairs. There is a doorway on the west wall leading to storeroom 17.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: storeroom 17 to the east, dining garden 13 to the south

DESCRIPTION: Square room. Floor obscured by lapilli throughout. Wide doorway in the east wall opening to the street. Basalt stepped threshold with placings for a sliding door. Fragments of plaster on the south wall with a pinkish hue. High in the south wall there are two holes for floor joists between which, in the lower part, there is a restored doorway. At the southwest corner there is a rectangular base for stairs to the floor above. In the centre of the wet wall there is a basalt stepped threshold to the preparation room 2. High at the east end of the north wall there is a shallow square plastered recess. Above this, there are two holes for floor joists. In the centre of the room is a catillus 6499.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: room 2 to the west

DESCRIPTION: This kitchen which is in a state of disrepair is to the NE of entrance 18. There is a narrow doorway on the NW wall which is supported by modern boards and metal supports. there appears to have been a lava stone threshold. There is plaster on the NE NW and SW walls. The plaster on the NE wall appears to have had a lower golden register and a red border and this would now be part of the latrine wall. There is a small step up into the latrine which then is bordered byh a cooking platform support which extends from the SE wall toward the NW into approximately into the midpoint of the room. A large broken drain pipe made of terra cotta is situated in the wall toward the eastern corner. There are two small light wells on the SE wall with the one above the latrine having a much smaller opening to the street. The one over the cooking platform is square in shape. Both have modern wooden lintels inserted. On this same wall are four large holes which are below the window height, and one smaller beam hole approximately window level. The cooking platform supports jut into the room from the SE. The first to the NE as was mentioned also forms the latrine's barrier and the second abuts the SE and SW walls. On the SW wall running along the length of the cooking platform support is a deep thick groove which may have housed a shelf. The floor is obscured with rubble and vegetation. The SE wall shows a groove and building material indicating a second storey height. There is no ceiling extant.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to atrium 2 to the NW.

DESCRIPTION: This rectangular space is a kitchen. One enters this room from a doorway in the western corner of the northwest wall. an "L" shaped platform (3921) goes from the northern doorjamb to the north corner of the room and then makes a right angle to the east corner of the room. Near the center of the southeast wall are traces of another platform. The room is in very poor condition. At present the southwest wall is braced with metal and wood supports. The walls are in poor condition, however, some plaster remains on the northwest and southeast walls. The flooring is not visible and no ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The kitchen is adjacent to the stairwell at its northwest side. The southeast wall is an exterior wall to the street. Preparation room 31 is the the southwest.

DESCRIPTION:
The niche is on the southeast side of Via dell' Abbondanza at the junction with the Vicola dell' Anfiteatro.
â€ƒThe niche was restored after Allied bombing in 1943. The front of the arch is highlighted with various sized bricks and roof tiles, on the outside of which there are projecting terracotta pieces that outline the voussoirs.
â€ƒThe outside of the sill is made of cut sarno stone, while the back of the niche is made of cobbles. The area between the sidewalk and the sill of the niche is primarily volcanic cobbles. There is plaster inside the niche on the southwest wall and along that wall's junction with the rear of the niche. On one of the brick voussoirs is a mason's mark (VV?) and on one interior sarno stone is a mason't mark (X?).
â€ƒThe bottom of the niche is 0.835 m above the sidewalk. The height of the niche (from the bottom of the voussoirs) is 2.11 m. The width of the niche is 1.09 m. The depth is 1.14 m. The interior of the niche is 1.34 m in height.
L-shaped preparation platform along the west and south walls. Masonry with plastered surface.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: north end of storeroom

DESCRIPTION: Remains of a masonry cooking platform obscured by debris. Boyce and Warscher show this to be a cooking platform. Boyce also refers to a no longer extant lararium.

DESCRIPTION: Feature 6360 is a rotary hand mill. 5 round stone bases and parts of mills (not in situ) 4 have square cutout openings one, smaller, has a roundish opening cut in the top.

DESCRIPTION: On north wall, facing the south east wall of room 13, to the left is an arched recessed niche-lararium. Traces of a ledge, traces of plaster and some point exist. Surrounding the niche on wall there are traces of plaster + painting presumably a lararium painting survive. Very faded.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Lararium is located in room 13. On the north west corner on the north wall.

DESCRIPTION: Its located in the South East of the kitchen (6438). The masonry cooking platform has arched underneath storage and a tiled hearth surface
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the south east of water feature 6440

DESCRIPTION: This feature in preparation room 67 (6919) has been identified as a cupboard niche. It is a deeply set niche, fairly high and occupying almost one quarter of the eastern end of the southeast wall. It has a curved top, but there is no remaining decoration. The surface is covered with modern plaster.

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is a commercial and residential facility. This room is being identified as a dining hall due to its location, orientation, size and decoration. Colors are black and white, skin color, green and pale blue green. Figures are presented above dado. The frieze is beautiful above the figures in cloud form, totally illusionistic. There is a nicely intoxicated figure of Dionysus leaning on his wife's lap. On the next wall is the famous flagellation scene. There are 27 figures depicted on the four walls

DESCRIPTION: On the north and northwest walls are 11 figures and a sacrificial animal, a goat. A follower carries a plate of either food or ritual objects. Silenus leans on a pedestal holding a cup. On the northwest side the lady of the house contemplates the importance of this sacred rite.

DESCRIPTION: We enter through a narrow, but high, doorway and step down into the dining room. Floor is original tesserae of black and white. These are in alternating diagonal patterns of black and white. The two biclinia spaces are delineated by a square and on the north side a rectangular opening with holes indicating room for a shelf. There is a cornice going around all walls showing modern restoration and original details apparently. The west, north and south walls are decorated in the Second Style in red, blue-green, green, yellow and beige stucco. We see the usual columns and pediments and the frieze shows stucco work with two barrel vaults over the biclinia. This is a summer dining room because it blocks the sun

DESCRIPTION:

In 186 BC, the Roman Senate, on edge after the 2nd Punic War, heard from soldiers and civilians of a new and powerful religion in Campania--that of Dionysus. They panicked and ordered 10,000 followers of Dionysus to be executed and prohibited any rites to be performed by more than 6 people or a private worship.

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined structure II - 1 - 10 to be a vineyard with a pr9ocessing center and area 6 in the open garden on both the southwest and northeast sides of the house. Currently the garden is planted with grapevines, although Jashemski lists in only as a garden. There was a lot of water and irrigation in the ancient space, including basin 4280, cistern 4285, and indeterminate negative feature 4287. The southwest wall fronts the street and is heavily restored. The other walls are adjacent to neighboring properties. Garden shape is irregular (see floor plan) and all walls appear to be of opus incertum. The house structure has a series of five windows on the northwest wall of the garden, as well as one closed up window which may have become a niche in antiquity. At the northeast wall of the house in its west corner is a door accessing the garden from hallway 10. Today, room 5, which is immediately to the northwest of the door is open to the garden with a low step up and contains a staircase to the upper floor with a cupboard underneath. There is a small door in the southernmost corner of the structure.

Bibliography: Eschebach page 87; Amadio, B., 'Regio II, Insula 1,' in Rivista di Studi Pompeiana 2 (1988), 192-5.

Two of the dolia are mostly intact but one only has the terracotta on the inside bottom. Working space behind the counter is a step up from the rest of the floor. DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is a commercial and residential establishment known as the Villa of the Mysteries. This room has been identified as a dining room due to its location, orientation and size. This is a square space with a doorway on the south corner of the southeast wall. One enters from the reception area into this space through a small door but the southwest wall is also cut with a large window. There is an additional small window in the western corner of the northwest wall. The condition of this room is bare with a great deal of restoration including a modern ceiling, except for the southwest wall which is laid as opus reticulatum beneath the window. The rest is opus incertum. The floor is cut stone tesserae. The perimeter is done in white and the central square is bordered with a black band. The white central field has dotted lines of black tesserae. Although all the walls preserve plaster, there is no paint remaining in this room.
