DESCRIPTION: In bakery V-3-8 we have a very small, narrow room that was well decorated at one time. It had a low lararium or a shelf or that may have been a couch niche in one wall. The entrance is very low, arched and very narrow. From the corridor it appears there were two such low narrow arched doorways but one was completely blocked in antiquity (plaster covers the inside wall as well as the position of the lararium where that door would have been inside the room). We know the room was arched by the presence of a series of post holes on the northeast and southwest walls. Below the post holes on the northeast wall is a small square high window. Because of the location of the room, just off corridor number 5, and directly to the north of the mill room, we suggest that its function was storage when this house was turned into a bakery. Floor today is lappilli
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Opens directly to the northeast off corridor 15, to the southeast of room 9, to the northwest of room 11.

DESCRIPTION: In bakery V-3-8 we have identified room #9 as a storeroom. The room is long and relatively narrow on a northwest/southeast axis. It appears to be accessed by a single door on the southwest wall at the south end that has a stone door sill that has a step up to it from the corridor. The room shows on the northeast wall only utilitarian paintings and is currently still partially excavated. There is one window in the northeast wall high and narrow opening to the street. Directly below the window are a series of 8 post holes that appears to be in a semicircular pattern. The southwest wall is partially destroyed, making it unclear as to whether there was a second access door (I think not).
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Immediately to the northeast off the north end of corridor #15.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. We have identified the house of the Vetii as a domestic structure. Room number 15 we have identified to be a dining hall based on its large structure and its location directly adjacent to the peristyle court (11). The room sits on a north-west south-east axis with a large entry door on the south-east wall. The walls were originally made of opus incertum and were covered with a series of elaborate frescoes. The dado is black with ten human figures visible between areas of candelabra-style decoration. Directly above on all walls is a narrow band with red insets interspersed with ten small insets with black background of mythological scenes. On top of that is a black band with the very famous paintings of cupids in various occupations. Ten occupations are currently visible with probably three removed or ruined from the south-west wall. On all three walls on the north-west end of the room directly above that are main panels with central figures (usually two individuals) divided by black vertical stripes of candelabra and floating figures. four of those paired figures remain intact, one is partially destroyed, and at least two appear to have been removed, probably to a museum. There is an architectural frieze with human figures above that in the same end of the room. More painting used to exists throughout, but some of the fresco is in ruined condition (see photos). On the north-east wall high above the door height where there is no plaster we see two squared post-holes which may be from reconstruction. A matching hole appears on the south-west wall. At the south corner of the same wall above door height is a square pass-through window looking towards room (14). Below that window is a narrow doorway connecting rooms (14) and (15). The door is located on the south-east wall and has a very small square window centred above it. The ceiling is reconstructed plaster but what may be original ceramic roof tiles are visible between pieces of broken plaster. The floor is currently lined with wood and is not visible. A plaque in the room gives dates of 1894 and 1895 for the excavation.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the north-west of peristyle courtyard (11) and to the north-east of room (14).

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. This black panel above the dado figure which shows an altar which seems to be glowing. Reading from left a woman holds a jug, patera with a deer beside her. There is a man in active stance holding a short sword. A woman flees holding a patera. This panel flanks the central section of the NE wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This panel flanks the central section of the NE wall.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. In this big central panel on the left side we see cupids in a tree harvesting fruit. To the right is a cupid collecting harvest. To the left is a figure with a ladder. There seems to be two cupids harvesting fruit in the tree. The painting is in the lower centre of the north-west wall.

This is the House of the Vettii. No longer extant in the dining room is a painting which was located originally in the west corner of the room on the south-west wall. The painting depicted a baking scene of cupids working with the goddess Vesta present.

This is the House of the Vettii. This feature is a wall painting in situ on the south-west wall. The dining hall is decorated in the fourth style painting with a decorated black dado below large red panels which are divided by wide black vertical bands. Black band runs horizontally across the lower section of the red panels, creating a band below. This feature is a section of the black horizontal band. It is a vignette depicting wine making and wine tasting. Unfortunately both the left and right ends of this panel have been removed. In the remaining section we see a large group of standing amphorae, a cupid hands another cupid a bowl or cup of wine. To the right of these figures, two additional cupids pour wine from an amphora into a cup. At the right end of this panel were additional figures (now removed)...
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This feature is close to the western corner, west of the small door on the south west wall.

DESCRIPTION: This is the Houe of the Vetti. In the center of the north-east wall, above the central panels, sits the figure of a female. She is seated on a chair with an architectural background. In her right hand she holds and object that appears to be a patera. In her left hand we see a rhyton for drinking. The woman's body is seated facing out from the wall with her head turned slightly towards her left. The panel is framed on the two sides and top by red garland. This is the room's central figure as you look in the doorway directly above the central panel depicting Ixion on the wheel. Architectural structures are found immediately to her left and right.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Above and centrally located on the same wall as FS6620 and 6621.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. Another black dado figure of a woman holding a staff in her right hand. In her left she holds a tray with a hogs head on a draped plate. This painting is at the northern end of the NE wall.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Vettii. The basket is sleigh-shaped, with the tall part of the sleigh abutting the head to the right as you face the painting (the face faces right). The painting is located on the eastern end of the southeast wall.

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that structure 7, 1, 47 is a house based upon the assembly of rooms, dining rooms, etc. Room six has been determined a dining room based upon its size, its location of a large peristyle and elaborate paintings running up to an arched ceiling. Room is rectangular and sits on a west-east axis, with a broad door located on the northeast wall. The walls were originally opus incertum and show remains of highly decorated frescoes. The fresco remnants of the northwest wall culminate in an arched ceiling, level with heavily restored walls. On the same wall as the doorway is a large square window, looking on the peristyle garden. The floor, covered with dirt today, has small pieces of tiles mixed in with the dirt which indicates that might have been a tiled floor. The door sill is stone on its two ends and has a square indentation where the door was placed. Current ceiling covering is modern.

DESCRIPTION:
This house is not completed. This house is also known as House of Marcus Gavius Rufus, House of Teseo, House of the 7 Skeletons, and House of the American Admiral. This is at the back of the restaurant. It aligns with the north-south orientation of the ambulatory. It is open without doors, and it is a rectangular space. There is no threshold. The remaining four walls show some brickwork, opus incertum and plaster. On the east portion of the space you see a raised garden bed, showing modern cement and ancient garden tiles piled on top. Within this garden there is a large hole made by thieves. If this is ancient, this structure was recognized for its richness.

DESCRIPTION:
It has been identified that VII, 2, 48 is a commercial restaurant. It has been determined that the last usage of Room 8 was as a dining room. This identification is based on the room location within the structure, size, a window and doors. The large-sized dining room is entered from Space 7 to the southeast and from Corridor 15 to the northeast. The northwestern wall is pierced by a very large rectangular window to the northeast and a high small window to the northwest, which both open into Space 9 (other garden 4534). The walls show traces of red and white plaster. The walls are mostly preserved in their original heights. no traces of flooring remain. Currently, the room is used for storing roof tiles. An electricity pole is found on the northwest side of the room.

Bibliography: Eschebach p763-4 and Jashemski p175

This public fountain 4735 is on the north west side of the Stabian Gate, inside the walls (8.7) The fountain is made of volcanic slabs. Modern plaster appears to cover the floor of the basin. The interior dimensions of the basin are 1.0 m. by 0.84 m. and it is 0.61 m. deep. The pilaster is on the south west side but it is not a separate piece rather the pilaster is part of the south western slab. The pilaster is decorated with a male face ringed by what is possibly fire (Helios?) Pompeii in Pictures suggest it is a river god. The overflow is at the east corner. The drainage is possibly via the remnants of a lead pipe near the north interior corner. Worn hand recesses are on either side of the pilaster and heavily worn at the west interior corner. This is a very low spot in the city and even today the fountain is covered in moss. This fountain has no modern plumbing. Abutting the south west side of the fountain is a barrel-vaulted drainage tunnel that appears to go through the city wall.
BIBLIOGRAPHY: Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: at the north west interior corner of the Stabian Gate and 8.7.1

STRUCTURE_ID: Temple of the Genius of Augustus
DESCRIPTION:
It has been determined that this space is a sacred space around an altar in the Temple of the Genius of Augustus. Structure 7-9-2, located on the north-east side of the Pompeii forum is identified as a temple. In this temple we have 2 spaces divided at the south-west end by 2 brick walls with a wide opening between. The north-west wall is divided into 6 units with alternating triangular and arc-shaped tops. The middle opening towards the west has a slit that may have been a very narrow air access point. Walls are opus incerton partially plastered. Research says that the entire building was partially decorated at the time of the eruption. There are cornice remains across the top of the wall. Brick remains above the cornice indicate that the wall extended upward. The north-east wall is of the same structure with 2 divisions with alternating arc and triangular pediments on each end and a large masonry podium sits in the middle with a brick cella on top. Staircases are available on both sides at the back of the podium. The southeast end of the wall also contains 2 sections, triangular pediments, and arch with a small door near the podium under the triangulated unit and a narrow slit window under arced unit. The south-east wall is of the same construction divided into 6 sections with no decoration extant. No trace of the floor remains but drainage channel of cement follows all walls.

STRUCTURE_ID: House of Venus in a Bikini
DESCRIPTION: This is a rectangular room on a N/S axis. The doorway in the SW corner opens onto garden 7. High in the center of the E wall there is a plastered window. The ceiling is restored as are the lintels, the window and the door. The floor is obscured by dirt (plastered?). The room is lavishly decorated in Fourth Style with a burgundy lower register and yellow panels above. The upper register is architectural motifs, figures and animals on a white background. The central paintings survive on the N and E walls. The E wall depicts a male figure being attacked by dogs with a female figure to the left = Diana and Acteon. The N scene depicts an elderly male figure and Mercury pointing towards three female figures on the left of the scene. The female figure seated wears a turreted crown; the standing female figure wears a helmet and carries a shield = Athena.

DESCRIPTION: The oven feature is on the eastern wall of the oven room. This oven is a large elaborate structure, mostly of brick. It is rubble that encloses the inner beehive to the ceiling. Brick masonry encloses the beehive on the bottom half of the oven. The hole of the mound is laid on a stone base. The bottom course is a hard stone, better to resist blows from shovels. The oven opening is faced with lava blocks and is rectangular. Held in place above rectangular opening is the only iron door to be seen in Pompeii. The floor to the opening is a table like slab supported by bricks. Below the slab is a semicircular opening to store kindling wood, dry brush wood or charcoal. Sometimes this cavity might have been use as an ash pit. The passageway opening on the right side of the oven connects with a large preparation room. On the left (north) side, a square led container is located, raised above the surface, with a smaller round opening in the top.

The longest side parallels the Via del Abbondanza and blocks one half of the entrance. The western side of this arm has one embedded dolia. The short arm, which is perpendicular to the Via del Abbondanza contains one embedded dolia. The surface of the counter is made of broken fragments of marble as reconstructed. In the southeast part of the counter room are entrances to rooms (2) and (3). The walls have been plastered but no traces remain if it was decorated in antiquity. In the northwest corner of the room, embedded in the wall is a large drain from the second floor. DESCRIPTION:
There is a subterranean passageway on the north, east, and west sides of the garden (room 18).
WEST ARM - The west arm is on a north/south axis. The doorway is in the southeast corner (from room 27) with a step and tile ramp leading down to the lower floor level of the cryptoporticus. High in the south wall is an opening to the south. The small rectangular area to the west of the ramp (now filled with boxes of finds and amphorae) is separated from the rest of the cryptoporticus to the north by a partition wall of which the lower course survives. It has white plaster with red geometric decorations. High in the east wall are five large arched windows to the garden. Traces of second style painting survive with panels in the lower register, architectural detail above, and scenes of figures in comat above that - from the Iliad.(?) Paintings have been removed from the walls and are now in the Naples Museum, although fragments of the figure scenes are in the center of the west wall. Traces of molded relief survives on the ceiling on the northeast corner. This arm is separated from the north arm by a rough hewn and inserted doorway.
NORTH ARM - The north arm is rectangular and on an east/west axis. Plaster relief decoration survives intermittently along the ceiling. In the center of the north wall is an arch painted alcove with relief decoration and rectangular niche in the north. Second style painting survives on the southern and northeastern walls, the best preserved being that on the northeastern wall. Panels with architectural elements above with portrait masks and scenes with figures above. In the northeastern corner there is a doorway to the stairs to the peristyle garden above. At the western end of the southern wall four circular holes have been inserted into the plaster and are of uncertain use. High in the southern wall are five arched windows that provide access to the garden above. At the eastern end there is a large rectangular doorway opening to the bath suite.
EAST ARM - The east arm is divided into two by the insertion of a rough hewn wall and doorway. There are traces of plaster relief decoration on the ceiling and poorly preserved second style painting on the west wall. In the eastern wall from north to south there is a rectangular doorway to the calidarium of the baths. There are two round plastered windows opening to the bath suite and a doorway in southeast corner into the baths. The doorway in the southwest corner opens to the south. High in the west wall there are four arched windows opening to the garden.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The cryptoporticus is built on the north, east and west sides of the garden (room 18). The cryptoporticus is built on the north, east and west sides of the garden (room 18). None

DESCRIPTION:

It is a fairly wide ambulatory surrounding an open garden, supported by ten columns with plaster fluting. The space is highly reconstructed. There is a wide entrance aligned from doorway 25 and an atrium to the northeast. At the southern corner of the southeast wall there is a small low doorway. At the western end of the southwest wall is a door to the dining room (room 6). One large window looks into room 6. Another large window, located at the north end of the north-eastern wall, centered in the ambulatory. There is a large stepped shrine at the western end of the north-western wall. DESCRIPTION: This is the Villa Arianna. We have identified this space (14) as dining room due to its size and location. It opens to the northwest, however only the southeastern two-thirds of the room is preserved. While nothing can be said of its exact dimensions or entrance, there are remains of the northeast, southeast and southwest walls. The preserved portion of this room is decorated with a white mosaic floor. Two black bands define a central space. Only the lower portions of the walls remain intact with fresco. The northeast wall has a paper copy inserted as the bottom frieze. A red panel bordered by a column and pilaster depicts a kneeling male figure - perhaps a river god holding an eel. The central panel above this copy is yellow, but little survives. The rest of the wall is reconstructed. The eastern corner of the southeast wall has a filled (tunnel) hole. To the south of this hole the lower red panels continue, but are in too poor condition to discern any motifs. The central portion of the wall in the central register is a figurative panel and to the south side of this panel there is a red section with a slight suggestion of a window, with yellow panel continuing around to the southwest wall. Below the yellow panels in the south corner two paper copies of the original paintings - on the southeast wall depicting a standing female figure holding a branch in her left hand. The panel on the southwest wall mirrors the copy across the room on the northeast wall. The fresco beyond this copy on the southwest wall depicts a yellow column (originally white) and a blue-green panel for another vignette. The extant walls behind the fresco are constructed with a brick lower portion and opus reticulatum above. The room is in poor condition, with highly reconstructed walls and a modern ceiling. It is noted that the reconstructed area is delineated with terracotta tile.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the southwest of the tablinum and is presently open to the cliff face.

DESCRIPTION: From an eastern large doorway we enter a beautifully decorated rectangular shaped dining room with a northwest - southeast axis. The door is roughly axial to the main entrance of the house. The southeast wall of the dining room has a good sized window overlooking the portico of the garden (15). The floor construction appears to be concrete. The general condition of the room: all four walls are in place, the ceiling shows molding for a barreled vault, but the modern construction of the roof is a higher angled ceiling. It is not certain that this follows the ancient design but it is possible. The modern ceiling is perhaps 6 feet higher that the vaulted evidence. The placement of the banquet symposium consists of one on the south wall, one on the north wall and one center of the west wall. The banquet symposium paintings have been removed, but they commemorate feasts specific to this house and its owners. The socle represents typical fourth style paintings. On the east wall, there is a large notched area with an extrusion (painted) next to the couch niche (also painted red with the plants perhaps a aloe vera plant like the one currently in the peristyle). The second panel area has a stenciled divider with a white background. These panels have red, yellow and gold. There are large black rectangular frames with vaulted tops. There panels include interior gold stencil frames. There are eight such panels. There are three intriguing banquet scenes that have been removed. The remaining panels show winged figures (sexist and very cute). The black panels are divided by the yellow panels which there are 11. The same white boarder is across the top of this level of panels. A third level is largely obscured, but the dominant element are white stencil boarders. Above that we come to molding. Above the molding on the south wall is a circular window which appears in the center of the wall. A doorway to a small oddly-shaped storeroom is reportedly walled of in antiquity, but there is a new lintel and opening. On the southwest wall to the peristyle, there is a long high rectangular window.

The sill of the niche is approximately 1.31m above the curbstones. The extant height of the niche is 0.26m with a width of 0.52m and a depth of 0.17m

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified the structure of a Castellum Aquae as the water distribution center for all public and private water to enter the city. We have determined that the usage of the space is the Castellum Aquae based on the following criteria:

- The location of the structure, which aligns with the aqueduct which enters the city at this point, and which can be seen with a maintenance hole outside the wall which is directly aligned with the water inlet channel.
- This is a food and drink feature because it delivers drinking water to the city.

This is a domed structure with a fully plastered surface (hydraulic plaster). Three windows are cut deeply through the dome on the East side and the South, and over the door in the South West. The only door is on the South West side. This is a low doorway.
The system is designed so that water enters through the inlet at the North West side, filling the central basin. The floor of the basin slopes downwards to the tripartite outlet at the South East side. The water is channeled from the basin in three directions by raised dividers. A cutting to the North West of the divides most likely held movable doors. The water, once it is divided, is channeled downward to the three cut outlets. The perimeter from the doorway going West around to the outlet is a catwalk. This is symmetrically echoed on the North East side of the space. to the South of the door is a narrow, raised space, which is echoed on the Eastern side.
The damaged condition of the walls surrounding the outlets does not preserve the continuation of this raised platform on the South East side. A small drainhole is located through the basin wall just to the North East of the door and may have drained water into the basin that seeped in through the doorway. In general the condition of the hydraulic cement is very good.
The exterior of this building is a one storey square structure, set on a gray tufa stone socoe. The structure is brick.
The facade on the South East side to the brickwork is in the form of three arches. This decorative treatment offers an aesthetically pleasing side to the city. The building is built right into the city wall, which can be seen on the North East and North West sides.
The water outlets on the South East side are within the central archway and the stone level of the street would have presumably covered the start of the distribution pipes.

We have identified this structure as a residential house with 3 entrances. Entrance 7 is the main entrance, Entrance 3 is the secondary entrance and Entrance 9 is the back entrance.
We have identified this feature as a cooking platform due to its form as a low stone structure in parts covered by ceramic. This platform is located in the eastern corner of the atrium (2). It is clear that this was originally a rectangular platform to the east of the entry (1). This section preserves most of its ceramic tile surface. There is a raised lip along the south west end, still preserved in part. To this was added an extension to the east, as far as the north east wall. The northernmost corner of the platform curves to accommodate the doorway of (11). The surface of this platform is stone and ceramic tile.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This platform is to the south of the door to (11). It is to the north east of the door to (1).

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this structure as a residential house with 3 entrances. Entrance 7 is the main entrance, Entrance 3 is the secondary entrance and Entrance 9 is the back entrance.
We have determined that this space is the atrium based on the location directly north west of the entrance hall. This atrium has a stone impluvium with a covered well and opening to the cistern. Cooking platform (#6782) is located in the eastern corner of the atrium, along the south east wall. This is located just to the south of a passageway to house (7) (now blocked). This atrium is included in our study because of this cooking platform. Three doorways along the south west wall open to cubicula. There is also a door along the west end of the north west wall. An open tablinium is located center of the north west wall. A doorway to the north of the north west wall opens to (10). A door on the north end of the north east wall opens to (9). The condition of this space is poor, no flooring is visible, there is no roof, and doorways have been reconstructed. Very little plaster remains on the walls, with no traces of paint.

We have identified this structure as a schola type tomb. We have determined that the usage of this space is a tomb, based on the location of this structure in the cemetery area directly outside the Herculanean Gate.
The semicircular bench form of this tomb relates to food and drink by virtue of its being a place to sit, to eat, and to reflect.
One enters the semicircular space up two steps on the north side. The semicircular platform above reveals traces of cocciopesto flooring. The curved bench is fronted by decorative lions' paws at each end. This monument is placed on sloping terrain. Nineteen wedge shaped blocks are cut to form the seats with slightly sloping bottoms and tall backs. These are tufa and wew originally plaster covered, although no traces of plaster remain. Behind the most central part of the bench are large blocks identified as foundation remains which held an inscription tablet and possibly a statue or column.
Opus incertum wall supports rear of bench, upper portions are modern reconstruction. The original wall reached only the height of the bench back.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The monument is the second monument west of the Herculaneun Gate, along the via delle Tombe

DESCRIPTION: this large dining hall is in extremely poor condition. We enter through an enormous opening to the atrium (6) from the NE or a much smaller doorway on the E corner of the room from the fore room. Traces of paint and plaster are too faded and broken to precisely determine; however on the western side of the NW wall we find evidence to suggest 2nd style. There is a low yellow dado at the bottom followed by a register that is now white but could have been black with simple ornamentation, one red and one gold diamond spaced apart. Then a border of red separates the next area which forms panels. Some column figures and a man looking over his shoulder are the only discernible features. The room would have been approximately 2 stories high as indicated by plaster on the eastern corner of the SE wall. Traces of coccio pesto with tesserae which may have formed a pattern earlier are obscured by moss, vegetation, and debris. There is a large marble threshold separating this room from the atrium. Modern mantles and wood supports are in the door in the eastern corner. *Note, it appears like 3 (even though the third on the NW wall has had much plaster removed) large central paintings on each wall have been deliverately removed. No ceiling is extant.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to atrium (2) to the NE an fore room 7 to the SE.

DESCRIPTION: One enters the garden containing the outdoor dining room from the south. The garden and dining room are on a north/south axis. The floor shows evidence of white tesserae that presumably form part of a mosaic floor. Only a small area of white tesserae remain in the northwest corner. The entrance into the dining garden was possibly raised. There are fragments of marble floor at the perimeter. To the north are two columns semi-attached to the north wall. They show attached fragments of blue-green marble. Four further column remains are to the west and east - two on each side - the two on the west are reconstructed. The garden dining room was covered but the nature of the roof is indeterminate. On the east side the dining garden was open to a space that may have been planted. To the north there is a wall. Very little plaster or painting remains - a very small fragment in the northwest corner shows traces of red paint. At roof height there are four square post holes. There is evidence of a pedimental roof above, the nature of which is quite uncertain. The edges of the roof may have been supported by columns. There are three niches in the north wall - traces of marble remain in them. The central niche is apse-shaped. The two on either side are rectangular. To the west the ding room opens to a covered colonnade. Off the colonnade to the northwest there are three marble steps leading to a painted room (26) Clearly visible from the garden dining room was a mosaic on the west wall of the colonnade (Achilles disguised as a woman) To the south of the garden dining room a circular pool and fountain would be visible.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: garden 24 to the south; room 26 to the west

DESCRIPTION: The space is a dining area. It opens on the south west side to the atrium (20) which was used as a preparation area. This area of the house is associated with entrance 16 and is the commercial area of this house. This dining room as well as room 21 appear to have served as commercial dining areas which may have been associated with a bordello. This room is rectangular with a north east/south west axis. The door on the south west is almost the entire length of the room. A doorway on the north west wall opens the middle 1/3 of the wall to the dining room beyond. The condition of this room is very poor. No flooring is visible. Small areas of plaster are preserved on the south east, north east and north west walls. Red painted bands can be seen on the corners and the dado areas of the walls. A painted tableau seems to have been removed from the centre of the north east wall. A high window is located in the centre of the north east wall. No ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is north east of the atrium (20). It is south east of dining room 21.

DESCRIPTION: This is a rectangular dining room aligned on a northeast/southwest axis. One enters through a doorway with a white marble threshold, in the northern corner of the room. Directly opposite the door on the southeast wall there is a large window looking out to the peristyle 13. The condition of this room is fair. A cement floor is visible only in parts. The ceiling no longer remains. There is heavy reconstruction including the lintels, upper walls and a corrugated roof. The four walls preserve a good deal of painted plaster and parts of cornice moulding can be seen on the top of each wall. The southwest wall has its moulding preserved across the entire wall with horizontal mouldings in the corner stepping up into the centre to an arched central section. Although the paint in this room is not well preserved one can still see a dado decorated with intricate yellow bands. The central zone seems to be fourth style with large panels enclosed by red borders. The upper zone only faintly presents what may be fourth style open areas. Along the wall there is a large hole - now filled in - that may be a robber's hole.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: room 20 to southeast, tablinum 7 to the southwest

DESCRIPTION: This is a preparation room, it is aligned on a southeast northwest axis. One enters through a doorway on the middle of the northwest wall. This rectangular room is in very poor condition. Plaster remains on the northwest, southwest and northeast walls. No painted decoration survives. The floor is not visible. The ceiling is non extant, however, rows of joist holes remain in both the northeast and southwest walls. A large, heavy kneading basin is in situ in the center of the room (3871). A lead lined catillus coverted to a basin is located in the west corner (3870). A pass through (3873) to the oven cuts through the southeast wall in the south corner. A niche cupboard is located in the southeast wall just east of the pass through (3872).
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the northwest of the oven (room 6). It is southeast of prep room (9).

DESCRIPTION: Room 2 is on a north/south axis immediately to the north of counter room 6460 and west of storeroom 3 (6464). There is a north opening to corridor 4. North wall is part of counter 6468. Northwest corner is brick wall. West wall is opus incertum with counter 6462 running the entire length. South wall is brick, simply dividing off the space from counter room 1 (6457) East part of room is open to corridor 4 and storeroom 3. There is no ceiling. Floor is obscured by lapilli and dirt. Located in the room is a stone object which the tour guide describes as a phallic symbol. Its use is undetermined. At the far eastern end of the room is mortar 6465.

DESCRIPTION: This is a large Tuscan atrium which is north of street entrance 16. Its in a state of disrepair with vegetation obscuring the floor and an outline of an impluvium which has small plaster fragment which is painted black, red and white in the centre of its north west lowest portion. The structure which is gated and locked has a lava stone step up threshold from the street. On the south west wall are three doorways to adjoining rooms. The first is low and small. The second and third are the same height. All have modern wooden lintels surrounded by lead. The third doorway, which is almost in the centre of the wall also has lava stone threshold which is grounded. Today there is a locked wooden door which closes off the adjoining private bordello, with exotic pictures. Just north west of this third door is a square blocked window with brick and mortar, however a beautiful white marble windowsill is in situ and another lead and wood modern lintel has been inserted. Above the third door and the small window there is a large opening which is now roofed to protect the next room from sun and water and weather. In the extreme north west corner at the bottom is a fragment of plaster painted dark yellow. In the wall which adjoins the next corridor (north west) is a doorway with modern wooden and lead lintel. To the north east is a large room abutting the north east and south east walls is a preparation platform which is in a bad state of repair. There is no ceiling extant.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous with rooms 24 and 25 to the west, 22 and 23 to the east, a corridor to the north and the street entrance 16 is to the south.

DESCRIPTION: This is a dining room. One enters through the doorway in the centre of the south east wall. There is a stone threshold. This door is about 1/3 the width of the wall. The room is rectangular on a south west/ south east axis. The room is in poor condition, no flooring is visible. The north west, south west and north east walls are preserved to a great height. There is a high window to the street on the north west wall, a conserved area may have been a tunnel in the centre of the wall (??). two holes cut through to the entrance way on the wall probably held beams on the other side. Two small square holes on the upper section of this wall may have held a ceiling. No ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the north west of dining room 22, it is on the north east side of the atrium. The north east wall is exterior wall to the street.

DESCRIPTION: The niche is located at the south east entrance of the Macellum. The niche is set within a brick wall that is accentuated in a cross pattern of opus reticularum. The niche is on the west side of the stairs. The current sill of the niche is a large square piece of limestone. The top of the sill has a circular recess in the center from which two covered grooves come to the front of the stone. Niche shows evidence of at least two plaster linings, possibly 3. The sill stone is slightly offset within the opening. Niche appears to have been plaster lined on the sides of and below the sill stone. The top of the arch has radiating brick voussoirs. The still stone is 0.18 m thick, 0.51 m wide, and 0.44 m deep. Top of the sill stone is 1.56 m above present ground level. Height of the niche is 0.91 m above the sill stone, 0.56 m wide and 0.29 m deep. The sill stone extends 0.17 m beyond the face of the wall.

The niche is located on the Vicolo dei Soprestanti, outside the rear of the Capitolium, near the junction with Vicolo delle Terme. This niche is immediately to the southeast of the remains of a fluted pilaster which is on the back of the Capitolium. The niche is located in the part of the wall made of opus mixtum. The top of the niche is made of cut sarno stone voussoirs. The sill of the niche is missing. Plaster remains on the top of the interior part of the niche arch. The bottom of the niche is at 1.15m above present ground level. The width of the niche is 0.37m; depth is 0.26m, and current height of the niche is 0.52m. A line of vertical bricks to the southwest indicates the wall continuing in that direction has been reconstructed (probably due to allied bombing during WWII). The niche is to the northeast of the dog fountain (4819).
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Niche 4932 is almost directly backing on this niche on either side of the wall. Fountain 4819 is close by.

DESCRIPTION:
This niche is on the southwest side of Via Stabiana, on the northwest side of the doorway 7.1.26. The niche is created with vertical and horizontal terracotta pieces recessed into a brick wall. The back of the niche is the interior of the brick wall of the structure. The recess is topped by a terracotta pediment that is flush with the wall. There is no plaster inside the niche or outside it. The height from the current sidewalk to the sill is 1.84 m, while the internal height of the recess is 2.04 m from the current sidewalk. The height to the top of the pediment is 2.12 m from the current sidewalk. The maximum width of the opening is 0.18 m; the maximum depth is 0.13 m.

It appears to be made of a singe upright stone with no extant plaster visible. The top does not appear to be recessed. Behind the singular stone is a matrix of small stones and mortar bonding it to the wall. There is a public fountain across the Via di Nola (flower motif).

DESCRIPTION:
The altar is located on the southeast corner of the Central Baths on the southwest side of the Vicolo di Tesmo. This is between insulae 9.4 and 9.5.
â€ƒThe shrine consists pf a brick niche above a stone altar. The niche is outlined with brick voussoirs and has a brick back. The sill appears to be stone. Immediately below is a singular upright stone altar, partially incorporated into the wall of the baths. The sill of the niche, or possibly the top of the altar. has a raised lip on each side. There might have been a horizontal stone sitting atop the altar. A deep hole on the front of the altar stone suggests the altar was clad with a stone facing. The upright stone height above present ground level is 0.66 m; the height of the sill is 0.087 m. The stone altar is approximately 0.37 m wide and projects from the bath wall about 0.11 m. The niche width is 0.49 m at the widest point, with a height of 0.40 m and a depth of approximately 0.06 m.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Flower, Dancing Lares, p. 180. Mau p. 234.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Built into Central Baths.

DESCRIPTION: This possible altar is located on the south west side of vicolo di Tesmo where the depth of the well changes from the curb (recessed) The altar sits on the sidewalk and is constructed from a mix of stones, bricks and cobbles set in a heavy matrix, in no particular pattern. The top of the altar appears to slope down towards the street. Remains of plaster can be seen on the front towards the south east and the north west sides and above the altar. A painting of a warrior was originally reported to be above the altar but this no longer exists. A modern drain pipe is near the north west side of the altar. The height of the altar is approximately 1.5 m with a width of 0.86 m, the maximum depth is 0.39 m. Plaster is extant behind the drain pipe above the altar in the recess of the wall, and to the south east of the altar.

This is a painting on the northwest wall of the peristyle garden in the House of M.L. Fronto. It is a large painting on the central panel of that wall. The painting panels depict animals as hunters and prey (5079) (5080) (5081). In this painting we see a lion and leopard chasing a bull, deer, and a goat. The painting is on a light blue background with a red border. There is a red, yellow and white checkerboard patter above.

DESCRIPTION:

â€ƒThe face of the niche shows modern concrete, probably to stabilize wall plaster. The interior of the niche is plastered.
â€ƒThe height of the niche above the current sidewalk level is 0.33 m, the maximum width 0.38 m and the depth 0.17 m.

The most prominent feature in oven room 7 is the unusual oven. The oven sits against the northwest wall, which is an exterior wall to the street outside. The oven is beehive in shape on the interior, with wood storage in a brick-arched recess below. The access to the oven is a small square opening with a floor of terracotta. Above the beehive is another arched space leading to an opening to the street outside, perhaps for light, or perhaps as an escape for smoke. Oven construction is opus incertum with corner quoining. The beehive in the interior is shaped with narrow bricking.
â€ƒTo the immediate southwest of the oven is what appears to be a solid masonry structure that is at the height of the upper level of the beehive. DESCRIPTION:
This niche is located in the northeast far-rear of the basilica at the northern end by the exit. It is in the precinct by the temple of Venus.

The niche is carved high into the cobble of the basilica wall. There are possible remains of a crosswall to the South and a brick and opus reticulatum wall to the southwest, and a brick pier on the northwest. All of this suggests that the niche may have been in the enclosure.

There are remains of plaster within the niche.

It appears that the sill of the niche was raised several times.

The niche is near to the water tower, also on the backside of the basilica.
At the northern end of the south eastern wall of the garden (room 10) there are low masonry remains which have been identified as a garden bench. The bench is overgrown with weeds.

The niche is built into the volcanic cobble exterior wall of the tower . No plaster remains. Pompeii In Pictures reports a niche on a wall that blocked the north west end of the via di Mercurio. Their photos focus on a ramp that exists next to modern stairs which give access to the tower.

Pompeii In Pictures

This niche is on the west side of the vicolo Storto, north west of the junction with the vicolo del Panettiere (altar 4906 is at this intersection) This niche is north of doorway 43. The niche is constructed of terracotta pieces that form the sill, sides and lintel. The sill and lintel project from the face of the niche. The back of the niche appears to be a terracotta tile, with a horizontal crack about midway. Two bricks sit vertically on the sill against the sides of the niche, behind those bricks is a sizable thickness of mortar, which is topped with horizontal bricks. Thus, the sill has two levels. The side terracotta pieces have a flat face, a face that slants towards the interior of the niche, then flattens to become the sides of the niche. There are possible remains of plaster within the niche, particularly at the intersection of the walls and top. The location of the niche is recorded as a street shrine but its proximity to the crossroads altar 4906 could indicate that it is also a crossroad shrine.
Eschebach identified a water channel running around all four sides of the garden. We are not able to find any traces of it today, so we are classifying this as a negative feature

Identification of a water feature comes from Eschebach, at 1.3 m high as provided by our project measuring team today. The interior walls appear to be unnaturally high to reach into the water basin. A slot separation at the southern corner of the water basin appears to allow for some kind of water movement.

DESCRIPTION: This niche is on the south east side of the via dell'Abbondanza, on the north east side of door 2.4.6, outside the doors of the Praedia of Julia Felix. The lintel and sill are made of terracotta. The sides appear to be plaster columns in high relief. Below the sill is a band of cut sarno stones with another terracotta sill below them and two horizontal courses of bricks below that. The back of the niche is brick with no plaster extant but there is red plaster on both sides of the niche walls. The height of the sill must have been raised at least once. The niche is high on a wall above a public bench - the sill being approximately 3 m above the present sidewalk. The capital of the column on the north east side is still extant but on the opposite (south west) side the capital is no longer extant. The exterior of the lowest sill shows evidence of red paint. Niche outside the doors Praedia of Julia Felix.

This space is identified as a portico in the House of the Flamine. It is a space adjacent to the southeaster edge of the garden (5057). This is a large rectangular space on a northeast/southwest axis. There is an entrance from the tablinum (12) at the southeast, over a gray block threshold, and another entrance through the passageway which enters at the eastern end of the southeast wall. A third doorway goes from this space into the kitchen (8) which is located off the northern corner of the portico. This portico is in poor condition. No flooring is visible. Walls are of opus incertum. No ceiling remains, however, a pillar located in the center of the northwest side with a column located directly northwest of it suggests this area would have been roofed. Being open to the garden would have made this a pleasant space for summer dining. The garden is divided from this portico by a balustrae with an opening centered on the eastern half of the southeastern wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is to the northwest of the tablinum (12) and to the southeast of the garden (10).

DESCRIPTION: Room 10 is entered by one step down from two entrances located on opposite sides directly facing each other to the northwest and southeast. It is a long rectangular room which is along a northeast/southwest axis. The area is divided in two differently sized spaces. The longer side to the northeast lays on a platform about twenty centimeters above the lower, shorter side. This space, which was used to hold dining couches, is floored with an octagonal grid of white marble poised squares. What is left today is seven rows of poised squares. The three walls (northwest, northeast, southeast) have plaster fragments with small traces of red and black painting. They are preserved to the first floor height. The ceiling is not extant, but a modern reconstruction is present. The lower section of Room 10, which lies to the southwest of the couch area is more open space as it contains two entrances; one to the northwest and one to the southeast. The room has a very large square window looking out on to Room 11 to the southwest. The step to the platform of the dining area was painted in black and red but today only small fragments remain. The walls were also decorated. The southern section of the southeastern wall shows a large white panel divided by slightly recessed red bands. On the opposite wall, to the northwest, there are again traces of white painted panels with slightly recessed red bands. The lower register was divided into two bands of different colors: black and red. On the western wall in the southwestern corner there is evidence of a blocked door which has traces of plaster at the bottom. The walls are preserved to the first story. The floor is made of cocciopesto with some white marble poset squares inserted in the middle of the room toward the large window. However, as this area is accessed by a raised wooden platform it is not possible to discern if this decoration continues. The ceiling of today in Room 10 is covered by a modern wooden roof supported by four corner posts situated in each corner of the couch area with two more placed outside the walls of the room as the southwestern end.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 3 to the northwest; Room 14 to the southwest; Room 11 to the southeast; Room 9 to the northeast. Room 3 to the northwest; Room 14 to the southwest; Room 11 to the southeast; Room 9 to the northeast. None

The top of the stone is recessed, creating a lip on the sides and back; approach is from the Abbondanza. Plaster only remains on the southeast face.

This niche is on the south east side of the via dell'Abbondanza, near the intersection of 1.11 and 1.9. The niche is high on the wall above the doorway/entryway of the business. While the niche is recessed into the opus incertum wall, its exterior is raised in high relief in plaster. The interior ceiling of the niche has extant red painted plaster and a band of red plaster can still be seen t the top of the three walls.The pediment is outlined in high relief in plaster and there appears to be remains of red painted plaster within the recessed area thus created. There is a hole near the center of the back of the niche, perhaps for anchoring something. There are other possible anchor holes just above the sill toward the corners. There is a possible image centered on the south west interior wall of the niche. There is a crossroad shrine altar around the corner from the niche.

DESCRIPTION:
This niche is close to the intersection of the Via Marina and the Vicolo del Gigante, between doorways #6 and #7. Niche is on the wall inside the colonnade on the NW side of the Via Marina.
â€ƒThis niche is constructed of Terracotta tiles, the fronts of which project from the wall. The sill, the lintel, and pediment project the furthest. Below the sill are two horizontal bricks (that support the niche). The interior of the pediment is recessed but not to the depth of the body of the niche. One brick in the upper right interior corner is either a later addition or a part of an infill, intentionally reducing the depth of the niche.
â€ƒThere are plaster remains inside the pediment. Inside the niche on the right (northeast) are at least two layers of plaster. There is a terracotta projection from the top of the pediment creating an acretarium. The entire niche is created by seven terracotta pieces.
â€ƒThe plaster in the interior lower right (northeast) side of the niche appears to be associated with the second layer of interior plaster. The underside of the bricks beneath the sill are plastered, which is partially covered by mortar.
â€ƒFrom ground level to sill is 2.22 m. Maximum width of the niche is 0.49 m.

In this very large Roman house, immediately to the southeast from the fauces (12) and next to storeroom 11 is a large rectangular room (10), which we have identified as a dining hall, divided into two areas. The room sits on a northeast/southwest axis. A window on the southeast wall lets in light and a large doorway in the northernmost corner of the northwest wall provides the only entrance. The threshold shows evidence of closures but no formal remains of the sill itself. The remainder of the doorway is reconstructed. The wall construction is opus incertum and is heavily restored. The room is roofed (modern), with a high ceiling.
â€ƒWe find fresco remains on all walls with a black dado, decorated but in rough shape. Beyond slight traces of decoration in the upper register of three walls, we find elaborate paintings on the northeast wall. Two putti on fields of red bookend an elaborate fresco on a field of yellow. Outside sources suggest that the subject is Orestes fighting Neoptolemos. Between the dado and that register is a white banding with scrolling decoration.
â€ƒThe floor is intact but it appears that there were two central square decorative panels surrounded by a floor with small rosettes of white stone. The room is divided into by a masonry projection on the northwest and southeast walls. In the southwestern section of the floor an indentation indicates where the decorative panel would have been, forming a space for the triclinia. At the northeast end of the room a large central square shows a cross-hatch pattern of stones, again with space around it. We have determined this to be a dining hall on the basis of its large size and elaborate painting, as well as the two divisions of the room. Note a small square hole high up on the southwest wall that is probably just a broken area, but its shape suggests that it might have been there for venting purposes.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the south of atrium 14. To the southeast of storeroom 11. To the southwest of cubiculum 9.

DESCRIPTION: This is a wall painting at the intersection of the Via dell'Abbondanza and Vicolo dell'Efebo. This wall painting is associated with the ramp altar 4921. Originally the painting was on both sides of the altar. There are remnants of white plaster and paint remaining. Originally there were two snakes, one coming from the northwest and one from the southeast, meeting at the altar. Coils of the northwest snake are visible today. One snake coil close to the altar on the southeast side is also extant. The snake scales are visible. The snakes are represented in red and yellow. Painting and ramp altar are topped by a modern awning. At the northwest end of the painting is a vertical red painted line.

DESCRIPTION:
This space (5) is identified as a dining room in the House of M. L. Fronto. It is a rectangular space on a northwest/southeast axis. The entrance to this dining room is centered in the northwestern wall. To enter, one steps up one step to a white marble threshhold with square cuttings on each side. The finished surface of the floor is not preserved. The walls are opus incertum with the doorway and upper portions heavily reconstructed.

There is a large window on the eastern half of the southwest wall. This is totally reconstructed. There is a smaller rectangular window centered in the upper section of the southeast wall. Approximately half-way along the southwest wall, the wall slightly steps back continuing to the south.

The decoration of this room is third style painting. The bottom register is low and painted black with corner panels preserving plant motifs. Above this, the walls are divided into red and pale- green panels. These panels are bordered by strips of white depicting architectural features. In the center of the green panels on the southeast wall, the eastern half of the northeast wall and the southern half of the southwest wall preserve their small vignettes.

Above the large panels, the upper frieze has a white background with thin red and yellow patterned borders with decorative little features such as birds and tracks of architectural images.

Above this frieze, there are remains of plaster molding from which a vaulted ceiling sprang. A modern ceiling reconstruction slopes down to the southwest side.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is directly southwest of the dining hall (4). It is to the southeast of portico (6).

There is a light blue background in both paintings and a surrounding red border. There is a red, yellow and white checkerboard pattern in the upper register. There is, on the adjacent southeast wall, a painting depicting a lion.

There is a discrepancy from the plan which indicates the eastern half of the northeast wall as part of the enclosing walls of room 10. Room 10 however, does not presently exist. DESCRIPTION: This is the tomb of Eumachia. It is a large exedra tomb on the south side of the cemetery road. This is a tall exedra monument which is set back behind an enclosed terrace. It is fronted by nine cippae. The enclosure is opus incertum with brick quoining. The front wall has two white inscriptions on stone embedded in the wall. A central door opens into a small entrance with a stairway going to the left when you enter, rising to the level of the terrace. The door jambs are grey volcanic stone. The same stone is used for the decorative architrave across the full length of the enclosure wall. The surface of the terrace area has been disturbed, with no upper surface remaining. The level of this paved surface is, however, visible at the top of the enclosure walls. We have determined that this terrace would have been used for funerary banqueting. To the south west of the terrace the constructed monument rises from the floor level of the terrace. This is constructed in sixteen tuff orthostats. This is in the form of an exedra. The large orthostats form a high base supporting the floor level. The walls rise from two steps and a molded course. Above this are two rows of orthostats. The central area of the exedra forms a platform that would have held sculpture. The exedra continues upward over the two courses of orthostats with remains in opus incertum. This upper portion is in poor condition but preserves the bottoms of three niches. The burial chamber lies beneath the exedra, entered from the south east side. We were unable to enter the space but we observed from the front and the side.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This tomb is located to the south east of the cemetery road just south west of the intersection with the via Nocera.

Breton engraving (1855) and a description by Helbig (1868) and Mau (1902) describe a painting on the backing above the altar that showed four men in togas with a lute player, flanked by two lares. Flower (2017) equates this area to a small sacellum precinct.

TIME_COUNT: precious vessels on pedestals. The center has two panels with a bird on each. The eastern section has two felines
PHOTOGRAPHER: an urn

DESCRIPTION:
This is a domestic house. With the entrance on the street between insula four and insula five of Region 5, at the northwest end adjacent to the unexcavated area. Entrance 12 and 13 lead to this house. Because of extreme weeds, delicate walls, and scaffolding equipment, it is impossible to conduct a safe study of this structure.

From Eschebach and Jashemski as well as the city plan, we know this house contained both an outdoor triclinium in the garden and a kitchen. Both would have provided evidence of food and drink. The triclinium was located in room four. Kitchen was somewhere in the back.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is Northwest of back entrance 11 of the house of Marcus M. Fronto (5 4 A)

DESCRIPTION: This space is a commercial shop where pottery was made. Opening into the arcade of the shops on the upper street at the Herculaneum Gate of tombs we find a space which use was the making of kitchen pots and amphorae. This use has been determined based upon current research and the presence of a kiln in the back room. It has been reported that multiple amphorae and cooking pots were found in this space. The rectangular room sits on a northwest / southeast axis. Today it is a overgrown with weeds and a rusty chain link lock prevents us from entering. The walls are opus incertum and show traces of plaster. On the northwest wall is found a door leading to another room of this shop
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: as well as a lararium
BW_ROLL:
through a doorway on the east end. The opening to the arcade is restored brick facing.
It has been suggested that a large number of cooking vessels were made at this location and some were most likely (although we have no concrete records found in this location).
COLOR_ROLL: To the southwest of kiln room 2; to the northeast of room 3.
PHOTOGRAPHER: to the west of the door. The lararium was frescoed and remains of the offerings shelf are still in place. To the northeast the low remains of a wall lead to a room containing a kiln

DESCRIPTION: This is an altar in the rear of structure 5103. It is a rectangular altar sitting against the northeast wall. The altar is made of masonry covered in plaster with traces of red paint at the bottom. The top is slightly larger than the base, overhanging the three sides of the altar. The top appears largely reconstructed. There is another protruding rectangle above this. This top structure was also plastered but only scant traces remain. Altar is said to contain a painting of a priest's assistant holding a knife in one hand, ready to slaughter a pig with the other. Fresco is no longer visible.
F
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: In the north corner of room 8 abutting the northeast wall and the low wall separating it from the latrine (5062) is a masonry cooking platform. The front of the platform is faced with plaster. Only ruined stone remains on top.
BW_ROLL: John Mayeske
PHOTOGRAPHER: It is to the north of latrine (5062) and to the east of preparation platform 5060.

DESCRIPTION: We enter off hallway 8 into Room 16, which we are calling the mill room based upon the presence of a large grinding mill. In this room, we find a large rectangular water basin in the northeast corner area, along with a small water receptacle, fed to the southwest from the larger. The water fountains are lined with opus cementicum (waterproof cement). The North wall of opus incertum contains a series of pool holes showing a protective ceiling covering this area. A sloping passageway leads to an underground area on the northwest.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the northeast of kitchen 10. To the southeast of cellar 17.

DESCRIPTION:
This street shine is located on the south/west side of the via di Nocera.
This niche is carved into the opus incertum wall on the gate side of the doorway of 1.14.4.
The sarno stone circling the face of the niche and it's sill suggest that the niche was constructed at the same time as the wall. There was a layer of mortar originally on top of the sill stones that created the bottom of the niche, as evidenced in the south/east corner.
The sill is 0.59 m above the sidewalk, with the top of the arch at 1.51 m above the sidewalk. The interior height of the niche is 0.56 m. The width (greatest) of the niche's opening is
0.58 m, although the plastered niche was narrower. Maximum depth of the niche is 0.29 m.

This street shrine consists of a single stone masonry altar that abuts 6.1.19 at the intersection of the via Consolare and vicolo di Narciso. There are filler stones and mortar between the rear of the altar and the cistern/well. The altar is off-center on the cistern/well to the north-west. There is no extant recess on the top of the altar. The altar is not visibly resting on a platform. The ground-level platform of the cistern/well does not go under or behind the altar. Extant height of the altar is approximately 0.92 m, width of 0.65 m and a depth of 0.54 m. Some plaster is extant, on the south-west side of the altar near the junction with the cistern/well. There is possible extant cistern plaster behind the altar.

Early records show a wall painting above the altar that shows 6 individuals approaching a deity on a pedestal (Dyer).

BIBLIOGRAPHY
F. Mazois, Les Ruines de Pompeii, Second Partie, p.37, PL1 (1824)
T. Frolich, Lararium und Fassadenbilder in den Vesuvstadten (1991)
T. Dyer, The Ruins of Pompeii, p.38 (1867)
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Between cistern/well on north-western corner (4842). Water fountain 4840.

DESCRIPTION: In the north east end of kitchen 10 are two supports for a second cooking platform. The beginning of an arch tells us that this had recessed storage below although little trace remains of the top. Terracotta construction is reflected on the north east end and some tile remains on the top surface along the south east wall. The platform abuts the south east wall and would have run parallel to it from the south corner of the room.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: to the south east of cooking platform 5120

DESCRIPTION:
This crossroad altar is located on the corner of the Via dell'Abbondanza and Vicolo del Citarista, on the southeast side of Via dell'Abbondanza. It is now outside the office of the custodi.
â€ƒThe altar is a large upright stone and the space between the stone and the building is a mixture filled with small stones and mortar. The top is recessed. The inner face has red plaster visible where the altar abuts the building.
â€ƒThe altar has a height of approximately 1.05 m, a width of 0.6 m, and a depth of 0.56 m.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Flower, Dancing Lares, p. 150. no. 25.

On the northwest wall of peristyle 22 towards the north, is a large painting of animals in a natural setting. Identifiable in this painting is a stag with large antlers and a lion crouched to attack. Painting is on a light blue background outlined in red with a red, yellow and white checkerboard pattern above. The center of the painting shows two bears, one of which is being attacked by a leopard between two trees.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the southwest of painting 5082 and the northeast of paintings 5079 and 5080.

DESCRIPTION: This rectangular room on a north west / south east axis has been identified as a storeroom due to its proximity to the working area containing both the kitchens, latrine and mill room. The walls are constructed of opus incertum and frescoed although no colored paint remains. There is a large stone block in the ground in the south west corner which appears to be volcanic and/ or excavation refuse. There is only one beam hole near the ceiling indicating an upper level above. There was formerly a doorway to storeroom 12 in the north east corner of the room but today it is blocked, perhaps from antiquity, by a filling of opus incertum. High up on the walls (which were jambs in the original north east doorway) we see square inserts in the flat wall that would have been used for door closure hardware. A door today exists on the south east wall, with a free standing column on its east corner leading to rooms 11 and 10.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the north west of rooms 10 and 11, to the south west of storeroom 14.

DESCRIPTION:
This is described by Campbell p. 186-187 a possibly a podium tomb. It is a cube of opus caementicum at present with a facing of opus reticulatum in yellow tuff. A marble door (locked) remains on the northwest side as the entrance to the chamber. She reports two steps down to the chamber below ground level with a partially collapsed barrel vaulted ceiling and a bench around part of the chamber. A window remains on the southeast wall that opens to the chamber. The floor of the chamber is covered with rubble and not visible. It is reported that there was a broken alabaster urn containing bones, ash, and a gold ring, a marble urn, two glass urns, one of which was on the bench. This is PE-24.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Campbell 186-7.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is to the south of the arcade portico ( ) and to the north of via dei sepulcur, between tombs 33 and 35.

DESCRIPTION: This altar tomb is constructed entirely of large travertine blocks. There is no tomb chamber. There are levels of blocks, a cornice and then four levels of blocks with inscriptions on the southwest side (CIL 10.10.36) and on the southeast side (CIL 10.10.36). The southeast side inscription names Decimila, the daughter of M. Alleus Succus Libeller, as a priestess of Ceres and the overseer of the building of the new tomb. PE 21.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This is between tombs 35 and 40 on the north side of the via de sepulcor.

DESCRIPTION: This is a kitchen in the house 5.4.B. It is located at the rear in the north east end of the structure. In the east corner, abutting the north east and south east walls is a cooking platform (5137) that validates our identification as a kitchen. The room is rectangular with walls of opus incertum. it sits on a north east / south west axis. According to Eschebach this house was completely bombed in World War II, destroyed and never restored. The scavi wall plan thus reflects walls that are no longer present so its rooms 6 and 7 is our room 2. The north west wall contains two rectangular windows with a view into the triclinium garden. A round hole at the center top may have been for a pipe. the south west walls contain three high post holes suggesting a roof would have covered this space. These holes may correspond to two holes on the north east wall. There are faint traces of plaster remaining on the walls. the small doorway to the south west today opens to an open space which we think was the tablinum.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: in the north east corner of the house, garden 8 to the north west, the south east wall abuts 5.4.A, the house of M. Lucretius Fronto.

DESCRIPTION:
This is a large aedicula tomb formed of an opus incertum base sloping inward at the top on three sides (northeast, northwest and southeast). The front side (facing via de Sepulcor) rises flat to a narrower opus incertum block with corners formed of brick. On the northwest side of this block is an arched window or deep niche sloping upward which is presently filled with rubble. On the northeast side (the rear of the tomb) the base preserves a low doorway with a modern locked metal gate which opens to the burial chamber which is empty except for rubble and has a barrel-vaulted roof. No trace remains of what might have decorated the top of this tomb. Campbell reports the space behind and beside this tomb was an enclosure to it may have been used for funeral feasting. Walls remain on three sides -- the southwest wall being the rear of tomb 39. The southeast wall is partially preserved including a section which preserves the arched holes which retain some plaster and must have been present on the northeast wall as well, though only one each remains on the northeast and south east corners. The entrance is through the northwest wall via a wide space. The floor is overgrown with vegetation. It appears to have always been open to the elements.
PE 19
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is south of tomb 42, behind tombs 40 and 41 to the southwest behind and attached at the southwest corner to tomb 38 north of via de sepulcori.

DESCRIPTION: On the north east wall of room 16, the mill room, sits a low, half round water basin lined with caementicum. This basin sits immediately to the west of a larger water basin. The use is uncertain but we suggest that it may have been used for animals as a mill, perhaps donkey driven, sits in the same room.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: south west of mill 5121, west of water basin 5117

DESCRIPTION:
This croosroad shrine is a niche located on the via dell' Abbondanza at the intersection with vicolo dei Fugglaschi.The niche is recessed into the brick wall of 1.12.5. The header is one brick topped by radiating brick voussoirs. The sill appears to be a reused roof tile with the indentation filled with plaster. Within the niche is a large rounded blue lava stone. The area between the stone and the back of the niche is partially filled with mortar. The niche itself is plastered on the inside.
The bottom of the sill is 1.41 m above the sidewalk. The interior top of the niche is 1.98 m from the sidewalk. The width of the sill is 0.32 m and the depth of the niche is 0.25 m. The interior height of the niche is 0.48 m. There are red painted plaster fragments visible below the niche.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Flower, Dancing Lares, page 180

CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This is a fountain on the south east side of vicolo dei Soprastanti, between doors 7.15.12 and 7.15.13. The fountain cosists only of the head. There is no basin. The head is a single upright stone that tapers toward the bottom. This is embedded in the sidewalk and is fronted by a curbstone. There is no decoration on the head. The pipe opening is visible, which is much larger in the back than the front. The height of the fountain from the current sidewalk is 0.81 m, with a maximum width of 0.38 m and a maximum thickness of 0.23 m.

DESCRIPTION: An intact modern stairway takes us to a heavily restored modern upper level room/space. Fresco remains in the corners of this large space, along with its location overlooking the street, have suggested to us that this very large, upper class house would have another dining room in this location.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Immediately above cubiculum 13.

DESCRIPTION: This space is a dining room in the House of the Flamine. It is identified as space 5 and is a dining room on a northeast/southwest axis. There is a large doorway with a gray volcanic stone threshold on the southwest wall, opening to the atrium. There is another doorway to cubiculum 4 at the southern end of the southeast wall. The room is in very poor condition. No flooring is visible. The walls all preserve remains of fresco. A yellow lower register with white panels above has traces of red and yellow painted lines. It appears to be third style painting. The walls are opus incertum with the northwest wall remaining to the greatest height. No ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: THis room is northeast of the atrium and to the northwest of cubiculum 4.

DESCRIPTION: This is a small rectangular niche tomb of opus incertum. We cannot approach this as it is gated to is observed from the road. A small basalt columella (inscribed) is on the east side according to Campbell and she reports a piplet leading into the ground on the rear. PE 18.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is between tombs 39 and 41 on the north side of via di Sepulcori.

DESCRIPTION: This is a garden peristyle in the House of M. Lucretius Fronto. Jashemski tells us that (4) the peristyle garden at the rear of the house had a portico on the southeast supported by three columns and an engaged column covered with white succo and fluted above, painted red below. Part of the west wall (over northeast) all of the North (over northwest), and East wall (over northeast) were decorated with animal paintings. Today high weeds covered exposed area of the peristyle and the shaped alcove where the paintings are found a modern awning protects them. A centrally located water feature sits in the middle of the peristyle. The water feature is terracotta and stone with geometric patterns decorating the terra cotta. The terra cotta is embedded into the ground and contains two drain holes. The floor under the awning where the the paintings are is concrete with no decoration visible. On the northwest wall we see two high square windows above the paintings.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
To the northeast of Kitchen 21, Rooms 19 and 20
To the northwest of rooms 2 - 5
To the southwest of room 23 and area 1.

DESCRIPTION:
This is a shrine in the Villa of Mosaic Columns. It is located in the east end of the northeast wall of area 5. It is an arched structure with a triangular pediment. the inside of the arch is frescoed and painted. It contains an altar. The structure is brick and opus incertum. It abuts the the northwest wall of Garden 4. On the northwest side, it is attached to a descending pair of arched niches which fills in the space to a staircase to an upper level. Jashemski reports that Mau felt this might be an area for funeral feasts.

Jashemski, Tomb Gardens, p.114
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Northwest of Garden 5, north of entrance 1, east of area 6.

DESCRIPTION: This roughly square room at the rear of the house contains a working platform (5061)
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: a preparation platform (remains of) (5060) and a latrine (5062) making it easy to identify as a kitchen. Located to the northeast of portico 11 to garden 10 and to the southeast of room 9
BW_ROLL: To the southeast of room 9. To the northeast of room 11.
COLOR_ROLL: John Mayeske
PHOTOGRAPHER: this space is weed covered and of opus incertum construction. There is evidence the northeast wall was plastered and that this room was damaged by the earthquake based on repair cement in this wall. Plaster also remains in the area where the preparation platform was and wrapping the doorway to room 11. A low wall projecting at right angles from the southeast wall separates the prep platform from the latrine. Another low wall outlines the location of the latrine immediately from the doorway to 11.

DESCRIPTION: This is a shop. Space is identified as part of the pottery shop at the northern end of the arcade. It is a rectangular space on a northeast/southwest axis. It is in very ruined state. The walls are opus incertum. The lower portion of the southeast wall is preserved and only low traces of the northwestern wall remain. The southeast wall, which lies between this space and space 5086, is better preserved, perhaps due to buttressing a second kiln room (Pena and McCallum). The northeast wall is preserved against an unexcavated slope. A door into the work space (Room 1, 5086) is at the eastern end of the southeast wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is northwest of Room 1 (5086) at the northern end of the arcade.

DESCRIPTION:
This wall painting is located in the vicolo dei 12 Dei at the intersection with the via dell'Abbondanza. It is on the southwest wall of the vicolo.

Plaster and paint of the upper register of the wall painting remains showing an area noted by a small red band and an outer yellow border. Within the register, the remains of 10 of the 12 gods are extant - 9 heads extant at the northwest end and the white outline of a possible figure on the southwest end. Nine iron staples from an earlier conservation effort are visible, holding the plaster to the wall. The wall painting is topped with a modern awning. Below the northwest end of the painting are hatch marks in the stone, readying it for the plaster.

The identification of each god is not possible with current state of preservation.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Flower, Dancing Lares, p. 147
Mau, p.236
