The western most is a dolium which is surrounded by the support and remains in relatively good shape with the exception of a crack. n the western corner is also a large terra cotta water pipe which was added in antiquity to flow into the basin, probably from a second story. It is surrounded by brick and mortar behind which pre existing plaster, painted red, is evident. The second basin which is now in pieces lies to the southeast of the first basin. Only an outline on the northwest face of the support indicates its location in antiquity. Plaster remains on the wall. Behind this basin, the support, and the pile of rubble is the southeast wall on the southwestern side of the passageway through room six.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is contiguous to the oven (3867) to the northeast.

DESCRIPTION:
One enters from the peristyle garden situated by a Northeast doorway, across from a stone threshold and tall doorway. This is a large rectangular dining room with a good view, into the peristyle garden. The floor consists of lapilli and packed dirt.
Situated opposite this entrance, on the S.E. wall is another entrance with 3 steps to another room (6), with decorated walls and a small niche. There is no ceiling. The N.W. wall maintains one layer of coral/beige paint. The S.W. wall has almost one-half the wall plastered in this same coral/beige color. The S.E. wall shows brick and stone and a one third lower portion of the wall, shows plaster with gray and beige paint. The N.E. wall has a minimal amount of plaster, it is the color of dark gray.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room 7 is contiguous to the S.E., with room 6 and hallway 8.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The Video team leader is Terry Bruno.

DESCRIPTION: This large rectangular room has two entrances, one from the atrium to the east, one from area 12 to the south. It also appears to have had, on its western wall, a very large window facing the garden. The room is on an east/west axis. The room has no ceiling. The floor appears to be a combination of opus signinum and what may be modern concrete. Some of the floor is rubble, but area appears to be well covered by flooring. Starting on the east wall, the threshold in the southeastern corner is a step up. All four walls contain a fairly large amount of plaster. The lowest register shows evidence of red paint on the north, west, and south walls, but may have been black on the east wall. The upper register shows evidence of division into panels, with white, red, and blue paint still remaining. About in the center of the north and south walls, a false plaster column with blue paint and striped lines appears as an element of architectural interest. The only wall that shows evidence of second story joist holes (4 to 5) is the north wall. Under the window of the west wall is a remnant of a brick column that implies that this wall may have been a later addition. The southwest entrance is faced with brick with a spacing for a lintel up above.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 7 is to the east. Room 12 is to the south and west.

DESCRIPTION:
We enter this kitchen from room 6 on the S.E. wall. The room is contiguous to a room filled with roof tiles to the N.E. with signs of a roof. On the N.W. wall is a toilet. The floor is of pounded soil and lapilli. The space appears to be unroofed with 3 walls undecorated plaster and one-half of the wall on the N.E. with no plaster being evident. The low wall on the Northeast indicates a large opening to the room.
On the Northwest wall, there is a toilet and it is adjacent to a large cooking platform. In the South corner is a small oven. On the S.E. wall, there is a covered well. The investigator was surprised to see such a structurally significant kitchen adjacent to the decorated room off the atrium. Perhaps, the well dictated this placement.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is adjacent to room 6 (N.E.)

DESCRIPTION: This is a kitchen. It is aligned on a northeast/southwest axis and is rectangular in shape. The doorway is at the south corner of the southwest wall. There is a stone threshold. The floor in the kitchen is not visible. The south wall is brick and stone at the lower half (opus vitatem) The northeast, southeast and northwest walls are stone construction. These three walls were frescoed, with only small areas of plaster surviving. A cooking platform (3229) extends along the entire northeast wall. A latrine is located at the western corner. There is a small rectangular window in the northwest wall. Eight holes, mostly square, pierce through the northwest wall in a line roughly above the window height. To the north of the window, two holes are cut into the wall. A hole pierces through the northwest wall about a metre above the latrine. A deep hole is cut into the southwest wall near the west corner.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: entrance 31 and room number 3 to the southwest

DESCRIPTION:
Area 7 is located on the north side of the temple and is of uncertain dimension because of the presence of the remains of modern walls. The axis of the space is east west. The ground is now modern gravel and dirt but original excavation reports speak of grapevines and planting furrows. The side wall of the temple appears to have had 2 steps with a later addition of the wall above them. The bottom step is of undecorated masonry. The facing of the second step shows remains of plaster with red paint. The temple wall above that is contiguous to room #3, this section of the interior contains remains of white painted plaster. Continuing along the wall to the west, a rectangular block protrudes with plaster remaining only on the west side. To the west of the
lock, is a short wall of opus incertum, followed by round column with remains of plaster in a fluted pattern decorating the exterior only, while the interior of the column is plain. To the west of this column is an entrance way into temple room 2, followed by another similar round column also with fluted decoration on the bottom exterior. There is another short opus incertum wall. Both of these opus incertum walls appear to have been added to the portico (room 2) at a date later than the walls surrounding the sacred space. To the farthest west they are capped by another round column with no evidence of exterior decoration. The back of Triclinium (#3939) is made of opus incertum covered with plaster and directly delineates the west end of the space. The area today contains many large stone blocks that originally may have been part of the temple, likely the frieze.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Triclinia (#3939) is to the west, the temple is to the south, area 6 is to the east.

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is a preparation room. It has a low doorway in the west wall that leads to a dining room (10). A high window is located in the southeast wall. There are post holes for a second floor, in the southeast wall. There is a doorway in the northwest wall that leads to the peristyle (9). This room shows traces of a barrel vault ceiling however no ceiling remains. There are plaster patches of red seen on the east wall and other patches of plaster on the south wall. The ground is a pounded soil with weeds.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The room is contiguous to room 9 (peristyle) to the north. Room 10 (dining room) is to the east.

DESCRIPTION: This space is a tablinum which may have also served as a dining area. It is axially aligned with the principle entrance, which is (#5) and one enters from the atrium at the S.W. of this room. The entrance is one step up from the atrium onto a marble threshold. This threshold extends the entire length of the S.W. side of the room. The N.E. side of the room is bordered with a short retaining wall capped with white marble at the level of the fountain terrace. Both the N.W. and S.E. walls are intact and each has a central rectangular area where a painting has been removed. The walls are in poor condition; plaster remains with some traces of paint and traces of a horizontal ceiling molding remains on each wall. The retaining wall on the N.E. side is missing nearly all it's plaster, only preserving some in the lower N. corner. Preserved in the stone work of the wall is a terra cotta pipe near the E. end of the wall. There is no ceiling. The floor is well preserved, and it is the outstanding aspect of this room. It's a black and white tessellated floor pattern which surrounds a central square in opus sectile. There is a square towards the center of the N.E. wall that is possibly a cistern cover. The mosaic pattern with 3 broad bands of white along the N.W., N.E. and S.E. edges of the room suggest the placement of couches in a triclinium.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the N.E. of the atrium (3); thedining hall (29) is to the S.E., the fountain court (27) is to the N.E. and the stairway is to the N.W.

DESCRIPTION: Room axis is east/west. One enters through a large formal entrance from corridor 13. The floor is obscured by lapilli over most of its surface but an area on the southern side is covered by patterned marble mosaic floor containing several colours. The room has undergone several renovations (at least two) in antiquity and wall painting from two phases is visible in different plaster layers. The north wall is badly damaged. In the lower register there are traces of an original painting with overlying renovation. Behind the original plaster there is evidence of tile. Colours of the renovated layer are yellow, red and green. On the west wall the tile continues. The wall is badly damaged. There are traces of red, blue and green painted plaster on the outer layer. High on the walls there are traces of plaster moulding. Above this is a circular opening. The south wall is badly damaged. There is no tile. There is evidence of two plaster layers as elsewhere. The east wall on either side of the entrance is also badly damaged. Traces of two layers of painted plaster remain on the northeast section. There is no tile. There is a marble table in the centre of the room that may be in its original position.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: corridor 13 to the south

DESCRIPTION: This room is on a N.E.-S.W. axis, it's a dining room. It is located N.W. of the primary entrance. This room has two entrances. Entrance one, is a small doorway adjoining room no. 5. A larger doorway, on the S.E. wall, opens up to area 9. This room is in very poor condition. The walls preserve painted plaster. The S.W./N.W. wall preserves painted remains revealing a dado, a central zone and upper section. Some random blue paint can be seen. Above this, in the North corner is remaining evidence of molded vaulting. The walls are of uncut stone construction. There is no ceiling. The floors are not visible. Reconstruction in the room, includes metal brackets, holding plaster on the N.W., S.W. and N.E. walls.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The main door on the S.E., opens to are no. 9. The small door on the S.E., opens to room no. 5.
VIDEO_COMMENTS:
The run time is 2:33

Video team leaders are Capo and Wernick

DESCRIPTION: From atrium we approach a garden room from two doors. E. door has marble threshold. There is a window that looks into the garden area. As we enter Eastern threshold we see a rectangular garden. The N.E. wall shows red paint on the lower register, all across the back of the room. There is a raised bed on ceramic tile, portions of raised bed edged with terra cotta tiles, which were covered in red plaster. This garden room has opening to the dining room (10), two openings to the atrium (2), traces of plaster are found on the S.W. wall. There is a large window in the center of the S. wall. From the garden we move to Room 10, totally open to the garden's N.E. room. A gutter around the garden bed has an irrigation ditch, two drains on N. wall of garden bed that connects to the water drain, to water the garden. The ceiling is no longer extant, the floor is dirt. In the N. corner of the N./N.E. wall, about 6 feet up, is a lararium niche which had been plastered over. The open area around the garden appears to have been roofed on the N., S., W., passage ways. On the E. wall there are 4 indentations for the wall roof beams, two on the N. side, 2 on the S. side.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 10 is to the E.

DESCRIPTION: The preparation platform is in the centre of the sacred space in room three which is the innermost room of the temple (#3952). The masonry structure is made of opus incertum, and the tile pieces appear to have come from Roman times, while the construction of the temple appears Samnitic. The preparation platform is square, with a thick wall continuing from it to the north, giving it a shape of a sideways letter P. There isn't any plaster appearing on the outside of either the square platform or the short wall. The shape of the interior of the platform is uncertain, although the presence of some of the interior masonry indicates that it may have been round. The interior of the platform is now filled with rubble from about 18 inches, or 30 centimetres down.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is located centrally in room three (#3952) with the storage space (#3951), to the east.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified the Villa of Diomedes as a domestic villa. We have determined that the last usage of this room (80) is a dining hall. This identification is based on the location of the room, the marble entrance is on direct axis with the tablinum; it is raised one story above the impressive large garden (59) with a view of the bay of Naples to the south. This is a very large room. There is no ceiling and the walls have been badly damaged and reconstructed. The floor is entirely reconstructed. On the northeastern wall, on the northern corner, is an impressive entrance off corridor 44. The threshold is marble with evidence of door jambs on either side and a slight step up. At the southern end is an entrance paralleling the other, but no traces of marble remain. The entire wall is reconstructed to approximately one meter. At the eastern corner, abutting the southeastern wall, is a semi-engaged pilaster. On the southeast wall there is a large window today. The wall is mostly reconstructed. On the southwestern wall there is a reconstructed outer wall. Today the floor does not extend the full distance to the wall, but presumably did in antiquity. The view would have been to a large garden one story below (59) and to the sea beyond. This wall would be had an opening on axis with the dining feature and water feature in the garden (79) below. The northwestern wall is reconstructed, with an apparent opening at the western end of the wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The room is contiguous with walkway (44) to the east. The dining garden (59) is to the west.

DESCRIPTION: This space in the Villa of Diomedes is identified as a dining room This identification is based on its size, location, and character. This room is a large rectangular space on an east-west axis. The location is garden level, with a large window opening to the west, allowing for a view of the garden through the colonnade. This large window may have been arched. The entrance to this room is in the southwest corner of the western wall. The window opens onto passageway 68. There is a small window in the center of the east wall. There is no visible original flooring. The ceiling was barrel vaulted and remains of this are present along the north wall. The walls are opus incertum. Plaster and frescos remain on all four walls. Presently one can see some red dado and the panels above are shades of blue and cream colors with details in red. The character of this room conveys great elegance. This room was only observed from the upper floor level.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the east of colonnade 63.

DESCRIPTION: The dining room (3) is on a North West axis and is rectangular. It is entered from the door from the atrium on the East corner of the North East wall. The doorway is not exceptionally wide, however the sight line would run through the atrium to the garden behind. The doorway has slight remains of a cement threshold. The South East wall was originally covered with scored plaster; but no painted plaster remains. The South West wall runs along the street-side of the building and contains a high rectangular window as well as two post-holes indicating a second story or a shelf. Most likely a second floor. The wall has signs of plaster and scoring. The North West and North East walls are patched, but otherwise identical to the first 2 with no windows or post-holes and scoring is present. A faint trace of what might be red plaster remains on the North East wall next to the doorway. The floor is lapilli.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The dining room is located West of atrium (2). It is South West of cubiculum (4). It is North West of fauces (1).

DESCRIPTION:
This is a large ornate lararium located in the southern end of the garden (4-3977). This has a large apsidle niche with a pedimented front. The niche is flanked at the corners with plastered, molded, fluted corinthian columns and the interior of the niche is topped by a large plaster sea shell.
The niche is flanked with smaller (possibly cornthian with a patera) columns supporting the niche arch. A band of molded floral decoration runs across the interior of the niche. The front surface is painted with an unidentifiable sea serpent in the right hand corner of the front with red and blue floral vine below.
The pediment of this structure has egg and dart molding. The pediment has one patera centered, with a torch (?) to the left.
The painting within the niche preserved a yellow background with birds and flying puti. The alter is in situation. It is square brick with a white stone top.

This room has a NW/SE axis. We enter this preparation room from the Southwest from room 8, across a large stone threshold and step down approximately 1 foot. The floor is obscured with vegetation and debris; however, remnants of 2 supports for a preparation table lie several feet from each end of the room on the axis. A small portion of a concrete floor with scattered white tesserae appears near the support, situated nearest the North end. There is evidence of plaster painted with a red lower register and a white upper register is present on the Southwest, Northwest and Northeast walls. The walls extend to an indeterminate height, and no ceiling is present. However, on the Northeast wall, approximately 2.5 meters high are 6 large beams, holed above which some red and white painted plaster survives. There are 2 square shaped smaller holes situated lower on the S.W. wall to the West of the threshold.

* A terracotta roof tile juts into the room from the S.E. wall at the top, probably in order to preserve the oven which forms the other side of this wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to the dining room 9, to the N.W. and the oven room #8, to the S.W.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Performed by Lisa Wernick and Fran Capo

DESCRIPTION: Sales room is entered from the street to the south and, on its north/south axis, has a central doorway opening to preparation room 2. Entry and doorway sides are of brick, remainder of walls are of opus incertum. There are only faint traces of plaster on the walls. On the west wall one finds eight existing post holes for shelf 6509. The bottom of the wall shows some areas that are impressions of dolia or other objects which were there in the past. The north wall has two post holes, one in the brick to the west one higher up in the masonry to the east. The east wall has six shelf/post holes and one tiny square window to the street next to it. Floor is obscured by dirt and lapilli. Streetside entrance has a stone threshold with door placements. There is no ceiling. Large dolium 6507 is embedded in the southwest corner of the room. Eschebach suggests this was an olive oil shop.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: street is to south, preparation room 2 (6500) to the north

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that this is a dining room based on it's location off of the atrium to its southwest side. Also the large size of this room suggests a dining room as does the white marble threshold. This room is roughly square in shape with a northeast/southwest alignment.
The entrance to this room is located at the south corner of the southwest wall with a fairly high doorway. It is adjacent to another doorway in the south corner of the southeast wall. There is no original floor surface visible; the room is in very poor condition. No ceiling remains. The walls are preserved for two to four meters in height. The walls are constructed of opus incertum. Plaster and paint remains indicate Fourth Style, however, there is very little paint remaining. This room would have had two stories.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the northwest of a small room possibly a preparation room. It is to the northeast of the atrium and ala.

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that the structure at 6.10.1, is a large food and drink shop. We have reached this identification due to the following visible characteristics: (1) location on a street corner, (2) the presence of an L shaped counter and cooking platform, (3) a large opening to the street. One enters from the southwest. The L shaped counter blocks part of the opening, leaving a narrow passageway by the south corner of the threshold. The threshold is at sidewalk level. The cooking platform directly abuts the south corner between the southeast and southwest walls. Situated directly above the cooking platform about 70 centimeters from the cooking platform surface is a narrow rectangular indentation. Seen much higher up on the same wall is a fairly square opening, topped with a piece of terra cotta which may indicate the presence of an upper story. There are several other scattered cuts, jutting into the wall, but its impossible to determine if they are identical or due to site destruction. The northeast wall contains five doorways with stone thresholds. They lead to back serving rooms and are constructed of large blocks. Each doorway has a course of bricks and stone situated above, giving it the appearance of an arch. A little plaster remains on this wall and it was originally painted red. The northwest wall appears to be mostly reconstruct-ed. Remains of red painted fresco are found on the bottom, running under the storage in the northwest corner. A rectangular opening indicates something inserted into the wall, it's situated directly above some of the red plaster. Stepped shelves, are stretching from counter (6704) to the southwest wall. These provide an outline for a semi arched storage area situated below. The floor is made of lapilli rubble. There are no ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The counter room is to the southwest of serving rooms 2 and 4, and is situated to the northeast of the street.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this structure as a tomb attributed to Arellia Tertulla based upon its location immediately outside of the Vesuvius gate and from traditional literature. We have determined the type of tomb to be a schola or semicircular bench tomb.

The tomb sits on a northwest to southeast axis with access from the northeast. At the center of the bench is seen a square base from which the inscription plaque is missing with a tall column on it. The square base sits upon another square base of opus incertum that raises the column itself above the back level of the bench. The opus incertum base is considerably larger than the more visible column base. The bench itself is semicircular with drapery type curvature on either side of the column. There are two steps accessing the bench area from ground level. The seating area runs the full half circle sloping down with the northeast ends. At the southeast end of the tomb on the east corner there is a masonry support rectangular in shape that appears to have had some sort of wooden structure attached to it based upon the cuts in the stone.

Some restoration is noticed at various areas of the bench particularly along the northwest end of the semicircle. in addition at the same end, one of our features is located on the down slope of the seat (6586) as well as another a couple of seats away (6587) that we hypothesize may be libation tubes. Traces of yellow are visible on the bench but we think this may be natural weathering. The floor of the seating has remnants of coccipesto paving. The tomb appears to be made of tufa stone.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: stand alone

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this structure as a residential house with 3 entrances. Entrance 7 is the main entrance, Entrance 3 is the secondary entrance and Entrance 9 is the back entrance.
We enter from a corridor from the garden. The door is on the north west wall of the preparation room. We turn towards the west into a preparation room. There is some evidence of plaster on all of the rock walls. There is no evidence of a ceiling. The floor is pebbles. We identify this as a preparation room by its location near the kitchen and by the size of the kitchen, which is made smaller by the addition of a bath furnace. This is a villa urbana with five dining rooms, which would have required a large preparation space. We leave the south west portion of portion of this room and step up one step into the north western portion. This is adjacent to a stairway down to a root cellar. The south east wall and south west wall show niches for lights. In the north corner, there is a preparation platform with a niche on the north west wall for a light.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
Preparation platform on north corner.

Located near kitchen.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified Oplontis A as a villa. We have determined that Room 78 is a diaeta room. Identification is based on the unique location at the southwest corner of the pool complex. We note that we can see outside walls on the north side of the pool, that duplicate this arrangement.

The east wall of this diaeta has one very large window, one average sized window, and two very small, mid-level windows, all looking out to the east, overlooking the garden, sculptural display, and pool. The south wall is divided into three sections. One portion, on the east end, has a mid-level large window. The second portion is a curved, convex wall that cuts the corner of room diagonally, and includes a door that leads to a highly decorated corridor. The final part of the south wall contains a small high square window. The west wall centers the room. The north wall duplicates the three sections of the south wall. the door in it opens to the pool complex of colonnade via a highly decorated corridor.

The doors in the western corners of the south wall and the north wall have marble thresholds. The ceiling has modern plaster, but has cut-aways showing a decorative style incorporating roof tiles. The main area of flooring has a diamond shaped pattern in colored marbles. The area between the edges of the protruding walls of the north and south convex entrances and the west wall is patterned with squares and triangles.

There was marble floor molding all the way round the base of the walls, only some of which is extant on the east wall. We are pleasantly surprised at the coolness of the room.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Rooms: Corridor (85) to the south, corridor/anteroom (66) and colonnade (60) to the north, corridor (77) to the west and garden/pool to the east.

DESCRIPTION: This space in the Villa of Diomedes is identified as a vestibule associated with the apsidal dining room (33). This is a square room on a north - south axis which one enters from the peristyle (21) located to the northeast and leads into the dining room (33) to the south as well as a preparation room (32). The entrance to this room from the peristyle is a high doorway located near the northeast corner of the north wall. There are remains of the threshold blocks. No original flooring remains in this room. The walls are in fair to poor condition. The painted decoration seems to be Third or Fourth Style and is mostly red with pale yellow details. Two small painted sections were removed from the eastern wall and a third painting was removed from the south wall. The west wall may have merely been a partition between room 35 and this space and may have had a very large central window. There is also a small window at medium height on the north wall. There are no remains of the original ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is north of dining room (33) and is west of storage room (32)

DESCRIPTION:
We enter this square room, #2 from a low wide doorway, seen from the Southeast, on the Southern end of the partitioning wall. In antiquity, it appears that this room was a Tuscan atrium, as we note the small square impluvium, situated in the center of the room. There is little evidence left of plaster and paint on the walls. This, suggests, a structure may have been neglected. It appears, the last usage of this structure was for cooking because, I note a large cooking platform is situated on the Southwest wall in the southern half. It appears that this former house was re-conditioned, for commercial use. A large high window or opening in the wall is situated between rooms 1 and 2, it interrupts the Southeast wall and could have been used for passage of goods between the 2 rooms.

Abutting the Southeast, situated along the South and Southwest portions are 2 large stone structures, these appear to have been cooking platforms that were joined together by a grill. One-half of this structure, the Southernmost, contains an arch underneath, for storage. Above this portion of the structure, lie two holes and an indentation that housed a shelf which was probably related to cooking.

Situated above the 2nd structure, which was probably the base for the other grill, is a large hole located high on the wall. On the Northwest wall, are 2 doorways. The Westernmost leads to a store room (3) and the Northernmost to andron number (4). The Northeast wall contains more mortar than the other walls, and toward the East end of the Northeast wall, we note a small indeterminate structure. There are 6 beam holes situated approximately 2 meters high that may have been used for support, possibly of a shelf. The floor is obscured with lapilli and an overgrowth of vegetation. The walls indicate an indeterminate height, but a 2nd story. (Esch.) noted a terracotta puteal which has now been found in another room. There is no ceiling extant, present.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
Room 3 (storeroom) is situated to the N.W..
Room 1 (salesroom) is situated to the S.E..

DESCRIPTION:
From the entrance, go to the S.E.. Enter the large atrium with a shallow impluvium with two channels. Situated directly beneath the impluvium is a slightly raised dining tablinum with an elaborate fountain, situated behind it. Enter, the large square dining room. There is a black and white tesserae, with interlocking white capital. I's outlined in black on diagonal to room- double black tesserae border, on the entire floor. There is a large white marble threshold eating room, #35. Room 75 is remarkable because of the wooden reconstructed ceiling.

On the N.W. wall, we see a very large window with a marble sill and a very high zone. Two windows, on the S.E. high zone are currently shuttered. All 4 walls, show painted plaster, likely completed 62 centimeters in 'deep' perspective. There is dado, divided by a stenciled band of the middle zone. The Dado shows a yellow background with 10 large black rectangles. The middle zone has stencils, dividing the space into sections; mostly with a red and yellow background. A double Greek key stencil demarcates the top and bottom of the middle zone. The high zone has lost most of its plaster. On the S.E. wall, at the high zone, a faint red border is evident. 5 small and 2 large sections have been removed.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: With room #35
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Done by Lisa Wernick and Fran Capo

DESCRIPTION: We enter this mill work room of a bakery, from the East door. The door has 2 steps and animals could be moved through this door. This almost square room contains many openings. The floor is pounded earth, and lapilli and lava stones placed around the 4 mills. This mill room has a South entrance to a wall (4). There are minimal signs of plaster seen on the walls and there is a window to the Dining room and ? against the wall, (3790). T he S.W. wall has an entrance to a small rectangular room, that is stable (6). There is a lararium (3791) situated about 10 feet high on the wall with a discernable shelf; it's still plastered with no sign of paint left. There is a well, situated on the ground; adjacent to this wall. This West wall, in the year 2013, extends only 4 feet high, and we can see into the adjoining preparation room (7). There is a stone threshold, there to aid movement into this room with a door opening. On the N.W. wall, there is a wide opening, and we can see the baker's oven (13). It also opens to a processing room (14). The N.E. wall, on the street contains 11 large post holes that are about 10 feet high and some remaining dark colored plaster. The base of each of the 4 mills has been built up as a mill platform. There are no lead sheets. 2 mills are complete, one has a meta only and one is missing a meta and a catillus. We can see a catillus (3812) toward the N.W. corner. The asses have plenty of room to move around the mill stones. Mills (3798, 3794, 3795, and 3793)
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This mill room opens on to the street entrance (20), onto hallway (4), onto the stable (6) and onto the preparation room (7), onto the oven (13) and onto the processing room (14).
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Terri Bruno.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified property 6-10-6 as a house and room 14 as a dining room. We have determined this based upon a large open threshold entrance to the peristyle garden, large size of the room, and elaborate painted decoration. To the northeast, alternating courses of brick and stone frame the large the large threshold opening. Only a small portion of the stone threshold remains. A second opening to the room is found on the south end of the southwest wall and is a narrower although still fairly high doorway. The northwest wall contains remnants of First Style painting. The very top of that wall contains a series of small postholes, too small to be beams for an upper story. The northwest and southeast walls each contain two horizontal rows of two postholes each; one at ceiling level and one at about the wall's midpoint. The walls are opus incertum with some reconstruction, and no plaster remains. The doorway to Dining Room 14 is at the north end of the northeast wall. Along the floor level at the southwest wall we see remains of a white and black mosaic border.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This Dining Room is to the southwest and the peristyle garden is to the northeast. Atrium 5 is southwest of Dining Room 14.

DESCRIPTION: The semicircular couch is made of solid masonry construction. The couch is shaped like a 'C' with the opening facing the south west direction. The couch has a high arched back covered with masonry on all sides. The back of the couch, to the north west, is covered with red plaster. The center back of the couch directly abuts a protruding rectangular pillar from the temple building. The back to the north east and east is also stucco with red plaster. Overall the construction is of concrete. The interior of the bench has a seat. Above the seat the concrete is covered with red plaster. There is little plaster remaining on the seat itself. From the seat to the ground there appears to be a black and white striped vertical fresco pattern. The two ends of the couch are also frescoed, but only the south east end has any remaining red-covered plaster.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is contiguous to the dining couch, #3940, to the west.

DESCRIPTION:
The horticultural area is to the south of the temple structure and is in an east west configuration. It contains a semi-circular dining couch (#3938) and a negative feature (#3942) of vine plantings. The current area is in a triangular shape which narrows towards the east end. The temple wall runs along the north edge and contains a lower masonry step. A second plaster covered step is covered in red paint. The upper wall with white plaster remains in pieces. The upper wall is recessed from the second step with the exterior remains of two to three columns showing. Currently there are pieces of the upper metope construction. The ground is now covered with modern gravel. Jachemski says when excavation occurred planting furrows and root cavities
were visible.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This horticultural area is to the east of space 4 and to the south of the temple.

DESCRIPTION: In the Roman Villa of Oplontis A, we have determined that the last usage of room 20 was an enclosed garden. The room is on a north - south axis with a large window opening to dining hall 21 and a columned low wall opening towards portico 4 and atrium 5. A water channel runs completely around the exterior walls encircling a raised planting bed. Walls are brightly painted and originally contained garden paintings per Jashemski. A highly decorated cornice is visible on the east and west walls with an egg and dart pattern carved below and faces with water spout mouths carved above. The north wall is not as intact with only slight traces of the egg and dart pattern visible. Entrance to this garden room is in the north west corner. The room has been determined to be a feature based upon Jashemski's report of cavity indicating a stake, " propping up the limb of a tree... heavy with fruit or nuts." No ceiling is present. The water spouts indicate that the room was open to the sky. Columns in southeast and southwest corners not round - on the outside edge, they square to the wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the north of passageway 4. To the east of hallway 3. To the south of dining hall 21. To the west of hallway 6.

DESCRIPTION: In the Roman Villa A at Oplontis we have identified room 11 as a Diaeta based upon its location off peristyle 13. The room is L-shaped with doorways on the north and south walls. A shuttered window (shutters fossilized and still remaining) opens on the east wall. The room is elaborately painted in the third style with architectural elements, including columns, gateways show perspective, and landscapes along with one human figure faintly visible. Decorative elements including winged figures, gold pots and wreaths crown these panels. There are also two series of squares painted to look like marble at the same height. The painting is fully colored. Above the painted walls there is a cornice, with a painted frieze (subjects unidentifiable) topped with an even more elaborate carved wooden cornice. The ceiling consists of two arches, both with geometric designed, plastered surfaces. The L-shaped room is divided by these arches into two niches with a square connector. Inside the niches the arches have remains of painted ceiling plaster. The subject of paintings in the arches cannot be determined. The square portion of the room is also topped with cornice molding. A small protion of the floor remains, showing it was constructed of black and white mosaic with a geometric pattern dividing the south niche area. The west niche may also have had this, but no floor remains. The doorway on the south wall, and the doorway on the north wall, have partial in situ remains of their original doors.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
To Room 12 to the south
Portico 13 to the east

DESCRIPTION:
Proceeding through the long hallway #4, we enter room 6, situated at the door in the East corner on the S.E. wall of this. The N.E. wall is a restored high wall. This abuts onto the House of M. Lucretius Fronto. Esch, says there is a door in this wall, giving entrance to the House of Lucretius. Staff sees no evidence of the door today. Situated on the same wall, there is a high rectangular window with an uneven top frame. The well shows minimum remains of stucco. The floor is composed of pounded dirt and lapilli. On the Northeast wall, there is one high rectangular window, seen at the same level. On the N.E. wall, there is one high rectangular window, at the same level on the N.E. wall, there is an opening with a wooden lintel. On the Southeast wall, there are small traces of plaster.

There are no ceiling walls, there are signs of heavy restoration.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 5, (storeroom) is present to the N.W..

DESCRIPTION: Enter this room from a doorway in the Southern end of the Southwest wall. The L shaped room is on a Northeast S.W. axis. There is an entrance to the street on the S.E. wall. We see a large bakery work room. A second entrance #12 from the via degli Augostli (street) is on the South end of the Southeast wall. The walls are up to a second story height. There is no roof. A lararium is on the Southeast wall. There is evidence of plaster on the Northeast and S.E. walls. A beehive oven occupies a central spot in the bakery's Northeastern part of the room. A storeroom to the Northeast and an animal stall located to the N.E. flank the baking latrine space. 4 mills and 4 catilli are extant. A 6 foot high wall bisects a small portion of the N.W. side of the room, on it are traces of red plaster. Adjacent to this wall, to the North are 3 steps leading up to room 10(garden).
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Done by Lisa Wernick and Fran Capo

DESCRIPTION: On the southern most exterior wall of the podium is a large wall painting of seven individuals seated on a dining bench (it appears to be a stibadium rather than a triclinium). The second individual from the west side appears to be drinking from a rhyton. There is a table in front of the diners on which we see dish ware similar to that in the tableware fresco on a different wall (6580). In front of the table there are blue and yellow flowers. On the eastern end of the wall there is another individual who may be holding a tray with service ware who seems to be standing behind a table which appears to contain various foodstuffs with possibly a pig in the center. In front of the diners we see faint remains of another standing figure, but the condition of the painting doesn't let us know what that is. This painting is separated from the dado by a wide strip of red paint. The dado contains a nilotic scene with pygmies and water animals and boats. I should also mention that the top of the painting has a peacock on either corner with a medallion with garland descending in the center.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: On the short southern end of the rectangular tomb structure to the northwest of platform 6582.

DESCRIPTION:
This feature is a large fresco on the southeast wall of the ambulatory (10).

The fresco, which is in second style, depicts a harbor scene. The right side of the painting reveals a harbor with a boat inside and another outside. A figure crosses what appears to be a bridge to the harbor works. it carries a stick, with what might be fish, over its shoulder. Another figure is fishing on the banks. The left side of the painting is architectural with a small temple or shrine at the far left. Another structure, which may be a house or a temple with tower, is seen behind this. These buildings are on a podium.

In front of this, there is a space with three figures. A female figure at the lower left holds a jug in her right hand and a large basket or bowl in her left hand. There is a large male figure and a smaller figure to her right. The small figure may be a pygmy or a mythological figure with a tail. He is holding a platter/tray with objects that may be cups. This appears to be a scene of a visitor to the temple being served refreshments.

Although the fresco is in poor condition around the edges, most of the central area is well preserved.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
This fresco is to the southeast of the fountain.
This feature is south of corridor (9).

DESCRIPTION: We have identified Oplontis A (Villa of Poppaea) as a villa structure. We have determined that the last usage of this room is as a dining hall. We have identified this as a dining hall because of its location within the structure. Also, the characteristics of the room that identify it as a dining hall include: large mosaic floor with a white background, grey stripe border and chips of green, red, yellow and black in the main area. On the north side is an interior circular garden that serves as a light well. On the south side are the shutters of large windows within the remnants of a massive volcanic strike. The windows on this wall open to a view of a mosaic floor and three columns. The easternmost of the three engaged columns is painted with a spiralling egg-shaped motif in reds and brown. We see a rectangular garden beyond the colonnade. One quarter of the room along the west side, is obscured by volcanic deposits which are held up by modern masonry. The southern end of this obstruction, along the western wall, has a bench. This gated portion is holding sound and light equipment. On the north wall, there is one doorway on the eastern end and a small painted wall between that and the large opening to the round garden. The floor of the smaller door shows post-holes for door furniture and a square geometric, black and white mosaic. On the east wall there is a wall painting covering the full wall. This painting is majestic and contains Apollo's Tripod in the central zone, flanked by painted columns,and zones of architectural elements with theatrical masks and peacocks. The doors opening to views of interior gardens on the north and south also help identify this as a dining room. On the southern end of the east wall is a door to a triclinium for overflow guests. This has a concentrically striped rectangular mosaic floor and two post-holes for door furniture. The room is protected by a modern ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: round garden light well ( ) to the north, colonnade ( ) to the south

DESCRIPTION: This space in the Tavern of Tertius has been identified as a dining room based on the size and location of the room. This room is in very poor condition, having suffered through bombing. It also appears it was never completely excavated. This is a rectangular space on a northeast-southwest axis. The entrance is a wide doorway at the western end of the southwest wall. This doorway leads out towards the atrium [3]. The walls are opus incertum, with traces of plaster on all four walls. This is in such bad condition that no paint is preserved. Seven post holes are aligned horizontally across the upper portion of the southeast wall, but the northwest wall is not preserved high enough to see these. There is a large, gray stone threshold. The quality of this doorway and threshold with channels to support a door support the identification of this room as a dining room. No ceiling remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the east of the atrium [3]. It is directly northeast of corridor 5 and is opposite storage room [9] across the corridor.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified room VI-8-20 as a commercial structure whose primary use was an industrial property/fullery. We have determined that room 7 was a dining room based upon a large entrance to a peristyle garden, very high, well decorated walls and a mosaic floor. The room is roughly square and is entered on the southwest from the peristyle of the fullery The floor is white mosaic tile with black edgelines running around the perimeter of the room. The threshold is of the same tile in a straight geometric key-type pattern. Currently there is no evidence of any door or curtain attachments. There are two low doors connecting this room with rooms directly to the northwest and southeast of it. There are also two windows along the northwest wall high up which also make the same connection. All three walls contain remains of fresco painting with the northeast wall in particular showing the breakdown of the dado and the central panels.
No trace of what was painted there really remains, just faint lines. The top of that same wall contains an indentation in the fresco which could show molding or roof line for an upper story.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the southeast of room 6, to the northwest of room 8, to the northeast of peristyle 3

DESCRIPTION:
This rectangular room is identified as a dining room because of its proximity to the counter room.

The north wall is extensively restored with a modern window high in the center of the north wall. At the west end of the north wall there is a partially preserved recess with a down pipe of a drain.

Extending along the north wall to the east there is a shallow recess (4133) with traces of undecorated plaster. Undecorated plaster survives in the center of the wall. Extensive restoration exists on the east and south walls; there is no visible decoration.

Only the lower courses of the west wall survive, with a supporting pillar.

The doorway to the sales room (1) is at the south end of the west wall, with a partially preserved threshold.

The floor is obscured by lapilli and earth. The room has a northeast / southwest axis.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 1 is to the southwest.

DESCRIPTION:
One enters the room through an entrance in the East wall. There is a raised stone threshold. The entrance is on an axis to the entrance of the house. The floor is obscured by capilli. There are 2 post holes situated on the North wall. They are arranged one situated above the other. There are poorly preserved fragments of painting on the North wall. The style is not discernible. There appear to be 3 distinct painted panels, where the predominant color is yellow, separated by borders of white. Traces of red border around the yellow panels are also visible. Seen, on the West wall, there are 2 post holes, arranged horizontally relative to each other and situated at a lower height than those on the North wall. At the northern end of the West wall, situated above the level of the post holes, there is an opening; it appears to be an opening; perhaps a window or entrance with a threshold, situated on the 2nd floor.

There are 4 yellow painted panels situated on the West wall, in a similar style to those on the North wall. On the Southern wall, there are 3 yellow painted panels, these are separated by thick white borders. Above my head height and placed centrally in the wall is an opening, possibly a window which is recessed. There are traces of white paint in the recess and perhaps a thin yellow border. (The recess appears to be circular in shape)

On the Eastern wall, the pattern of yellow painted panels continues. There are possibly 3 in number. The plaster on the wall is too badly damaged to be sure. At the intersection of the South and East and South and West walls, there is a vertical painted border, extending above head height.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Garden (15), seen to the East
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Cavila

DESCRIPTION:
We enter the dining room from the Southeast. The room is sitting Northeast from the main entrance of the property. The room lies on a Northeast-Southwest axis. Upon entering the room, one feature worth noting is; on the Southwest and Northwest walls, there are unusual features of a coping or curb which juts into the room along the lowest level, but it does not appear on the other walls. It was painted red in the fashion of the plaster which can be found on all 4 walls, along the lower register. Evidence of plaster painted white, still exists to varying heights in varying amounts on each wall with the greatest concentration on the North and East sides of the Northwest and Northeast walls. There are faint remnants of a green dividing stripe situated between the red and white portions exist on the Northwest, Northeast and Southeast walls. Evidence of plaster crown molding is preserved on the Northwest and Northeast walls. The height of the room is indeterminate. No ceiling is extant. Remnants of white tesserae are mixed into a cement floor and can be seen under debris and vegetation.

* Note, on the Southwest wall and even possibly the Northwest wall windows may have present, looking into the garden.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to room 8, seen to the Southwest and the prep room, as seen to the Southeast.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: Taken by Lisa Wernick and Fran Capo

DESCRIPTION: This Prep room, 12 has two low doorways. One is situated on the N.E. and the other is on the S.W. wall. Situated in the middle of the room is a stone which may be the remains of a preparation table. There are remnants of plaster painted red, seen on the bottom and the colors of light yellow or white. Seen at the top, there are remains on all 4 walls. There are 9 circular holes on the S.W. wall situated about 2 feet above the doorway, in a line. There are 9 poorly preserved brick lined square holes, situated across on the N.E. wall. On the S.E. wall, at the level of approximately 5 feet high is a small vertically positioned rectangular window, the top of which aligns with the top of the previously mentioned support holes. The window is plastered on the inside, there is a tiny piece of ancient blue window glass, situated in the South corner. Centered along the N.E. wall is a small low sloped terra cotta lined pass through to the oven room. The floor is covered with vegetation and lapilli. Only 2 pieces of lava stone remain on the N.E. threshold and there is no ceiling. There are modern wooden lintels, on both doors.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous to the prep room, is room 11 to the S.W. and the oven room (13) to the N.E..
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The Video team leader is Terri Bruno

DESCRIPTION:
This is a prep. room. It is a rectangular room, that is oriented on a N.W./S.E. axis. One enters this room from the Northern end of the Northeast wall from the mill room (5). Another entrance is located on the Southern half of the S.W.
wall. This room is in very poor condition. The floors are not visible. The ceiling has not survived. The Southern end of the S.W. wall is of indeterminate length and may have extended to the stone threshold. Rough plaster remains on all 4 walls, without any trace of paint. The characteristic of this room, as a prep room; is supported by the presence of a large dolium (3808) seen in the Western corner and a stone basin (3807) situated in the South corner. A small window is located in the center of the N.W. wall, opening into room #12.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is located to the S.W. of the mill room (5) Room 12 is situated to the N.W. Room 6 is situated to the S.E. and room 8 is at the S.W..
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Terri Bruno

DESCRIPTION: We have identified VI.10.10 as a food and drink shop. We have determined the last usage of this room as a sales room (1. 6528) We have identified this feature as a puteal on the northeast side of the room. It is cylindrical. It has been repaired in antiquity. It appears to be made of terracotta. It is filled with lapilli and modern trash. There are 14 metal staples in situ used for repairs. The base is round with two bands that have very worn decoration. The rim is lipped and approximately 6 cm. wide. The rim slopes to the straight sides. It is not apparent that it is in situ.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: the puteal is to the east of 6529 (dolium), 6530 (dolium) and 6532 (kneading basin)

DESCRIPTION: This structure is identified as a granary. This identification is based on literature, location, and character. From the literature we know that granaries were constructed where the upper stories of the Imperial villa had been. This structure is a very long rectangular building which is divided into eight large vaults. The construction is opus reticulatum. Remnants of plaster coating are visible on the barrel vaults of the two western most vaults. The southeastern facade was also plastered and probably painted. The first vault is actually a half vault. The second vault has a support to its southwestern side going the length of the vault. These vaults are not fully excavated, but each vault clearly has a doorway on the southeast side, raised quite high from the ground level (loading docks), and there are holes at the floor level of the southeastern wall that appear to be ventilation holes. The present condition is poor.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: These granaries are located to the east of the Imperial Villa as it rises up the hill.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified structure V-1-28 as a shop-house based on the description of Eschebach, who has described this as a jeweler's establishment. Room 5 we have identified as a dining room based upon its size and large door opening to the atrium. The floor is rubble. The walls are opus incertum, somewhat reconstructed towards the top. Fresco traces remain on all walls with red plaster evident. The northeast wall and the southwest walls have a series of post holes at the top indicating a second story. The axis of the room seems to be northeast/southwest, with the doorway taking up most of the southeast wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It is to the northwest of atrium 6.

DESCRIPTION: Beginning in the east corner and running along the northeast wall we have identified two masonry structures as ends of a preparation platform. One end is approximately one meter high (see measurements on drawing) and immediately abuts the east corner of the room. The other masonry support is in a more ruined state and only sits about half that height today. The second support is approximately midway of the northeast wall. Both structures are rough masonry. Pieces of broken terracotta are visible in each.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
to the southeast of latrine 4130
to the east of cooking platform 4129
to the northeast of prep platform 4131

DESCRIPTION:
There is a large wall painting on the north wall. Running along the top is a partially reconstructed cornice/moulding. The lower register as been damaged and partially restored with yellow, red, and black architectural features similar to First Style. The entire wall above shows architectural features with six painted pilasters, which have corinthian capitals. The color scheme appears to be yellow, blue, red, and black.
From the eastern side, the first three of seven panels are damaged. The fourth central panel has traces of a pedestal with a domed serving cover presumably protecting the food. The fifth panel in the middle register has traces of possibly a bowl leaning against the pilaster. The sixth panel from the eastern side has a well preserved pedestal base painted with geometric design in borders. The pedestal holds a platter of fruit, possibly pomegranates, covered by a very sheer veil, possibly silk. From behind the painted pedestal is a painted staff with some type of decoration and possibly grain. The seventh panel is badly damaged. Sitting on top of the architecture directly above the second panel from the east is a ribbed rimmed glass bowl with handles on either side. The fruit is not easily identifiable but may possibly be apples, pomegranates, and grapes.
Above the fourth central panel from the east, sitting on the architecture, is a large glass bowl without handles, containing fruit possibly figs and apples. Over the sixth panel there is a third glass bowl sitting on the painted arhitecture. This bowl matches exactly the glass bowl above the second panel with ribs, rim, and glass handles. The painting is better presented with a fig, possible pomegranate and apple.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The wall is on the north side. The entrance to the room is on the west side.

DESCRIPTION: The western-most room of the series of food processing rooms on the south excavated area of the villa has been identified as one of the processing rooms with size unidentifiable, it has been excavated on three sides and is quite small. Plaster remains on all three walls. Decoration is not visible. The north and west walls appear to have been divided into two horizontal areas by a slight ridge at dado height. On the west wall an arch with slight remains of plaster is very small and located at the base of the wall. It appears to lead into this room via a sloping floor from Room 83 which could channel liquid through the arch into what may be an excavated drain in Room 84. The east wall has a bricked column attaching it to the Villa area 81/91 and to the column's south is a marble window sill or threshold leading into this room. Opening size is not determinable. The floor and ceiling of the room have not been excavated.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Opening from the west area 91. Attached via a small arch. Room 83 to the east.

DESCRIPTION:
The Dining room is situated on a N/S axis, with the door in the S.W., opening to atrium #4. The opening has a marble sill with door fittings. Also, situated in the West wall is a blocked in window with a marble sill and what appears to be an original wooden lintel. The wall was painted and plastered in antiquity. Evidence remains of a red dado with yellow panels located above a small section of crown moulding that remains in the N.W. corner. On the North wall, is exhibited, and is seen the best preserved plaster painting containing a ribbon pattern in red and yellow background with possibly a bird situated above. The panels appear to be outlined and white with diamond shapes. Dado was bright red on this wall and the frieze was white with yellow divisions and inset painted panels. A large portion of ceiling moulding remains situated in the N.E. corner and 9 post holes appear directly above. The East wall was made of large tufa blocks and it faces the street. The plaster is in a ruined state but occasional colorful traces show continuity within the other walls, in design. 2 higher openings seen in the wall, appear to face the street.
The South wall is mostly covered with remains of plaster, but the color is almost completely washed away. There may also have been a small high window, facing the fauces situated in that wall. There is no ceiling to the room. Most of the floor is lapilli, but a small bit of Opus signunum, primarily in a clay color remains in the S.E. corner and along the East wall. A long indenta-
tion is present in the West wall, beginning about 1 meter to the North of the doorway. It may have provided fittings for a dining couch.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: East of atrium #4

DESCRIPTION:
I enter this large rectangular dining room from the N.W., over a stone threshold, with evidence of a door. The floor is lapilli and compacted dirt, covering portions of terracotta, in cement. There is no ceiling. The 3 walls have been reconstructed to about 12 feet. On the West corner, is situated a doorway with a large lintel and stone threshold with evidence of a door jamb. Situated, on the S.W. wall and rebuilt to a high level, there is a small segment of plaster. The dado is the color of Coral with a yellow, double striped border. It contains a coral gray band, with topped with a yellow band. From there, plaster painted black extends almost to the height of the wall.

On the SouthEast wall, the lower one-fourth repeats the border colors of the South wall. Seen, at the center is evidence of a filled in good sized doorway, that's missing a large lintel. This wall is mostly plastered. The N.E. wall has about one-quarter plaster with a large rectangular niche situated near the East corner. The plaster color repeats itself, in the niche.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 15 is contiguous with corridor 8, situated to the N.W. and corridor 5 at the S.W..
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The Video team leader is Terry Bruno.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified this room as a dining room in Villa Oplontis A. This identification is based on the size and shape of the room as well as its location in the east wing of the villa. The shape of this room is unusual, essentially a square space with a rectangular niche stepping out from the north wall and an apsidal space stepping out from the south wall. The only entrance to this room is in the center of the east wall. The walls are highly reconstructed. There is no original ceiling remaining, but two high concrete beams span the space across the north and south ends of the room. The walls preserve a fair amount of plaster and a tall ochre-painted dado is preserved although the upper walls are cream colored. The decoration is no longer visible, or may have not been completed. The apsidal wall on the south side is pierced with a large curved window. There is a second, independently carved window seen directly above the much larger window situated in the middle of the south wall. This window has a marble sill and looks out into the light well with little garden with rich paintings. The floor is marble. It is a white field with a double black border delineating the central square of the room. The apse and sides are defined by a single black line. Over all the condition is fair.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is north of the garden light wall. This room is east of the large garden fronting the villa.

DESCRIPTION:
It is determined, this space is the front room of a food shop. It is a rectangular space, located on a S.E/N.W axis, that opens up to the street at the S.E. end. This food shop or Caupona has a street front L shaped counter (1-3980). The threshold of 3 large blocks of Tuf has a channel situated down the center for shutters, and it is seen across the entire front of the shop.

The counter occupies the Southwest half of the front of this room. The N.W. portion of the room provides access to the rear of the room, as well as the space situated behind it, (#2). No original floor surface is visible. The condition of this space is poor with conservation on the walls and counter. The walls are opus incertum, with brick seen at the front of the shop. The walls preserve plaster and are painted in red and yellow. These colors are visible in some places on all the walls. The back wall at the N.W. side of the this space is only partially preserved, on the N.W. side. Seen there, are 5 blocks of limestone creating a threshold, and one can step up to the room behind it (2-3981).
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is situated N.W. of the street and it is S.E. of room (2-3981)

DESCRIPTION: We have identified Oplontis Villa A as a domestic villa. We have determined that the last usage of this room (74) is a dining room. This identification is based on: A) The room location within the structure, it faces west with a wide entrance and view of the large pool; B) The characteristics that suggest a dining room are the mosaic floor, large entrance with view, possible serving passage on eastern side; and C) Previous research indicates a salone. There are no clearly obvious food and drink features. The floor is mosaic, white with black border, defining the space within the dining room. The ceiling is totally reconstructed. Traces of original stucco molding have been inserted in the reconstruction. The ceilings is divided into nine areas, four with recessed diamonds, two a piece; four plain, yet arched slightly. The central panel is defined by geometric recessed areas. Along the east side of the room there appears to be a separate area defined by the wall structure, mosaic floor and niche attached to the west wall. The area to the west is clearly accessible to the main room. On a north/south axis, there are two large openings on the north and south walls, each with well panned views of planted areas and garden paintings. The entire room was purposely planed with views on all sides. Remnants of a base molding of stucco painted to look like marble remain in a few areas around the room. In total there are five entrances to other rooms. The east opening is a large monumental opening, with a few small pieces of the marble threshold remaining. The interior of the east wall is reconstructed, partial plaster with no wall paintings. The south wall has an entrance to (72). Area (72) appears to e an ante room. The center of the south wall has a large opening with a marble ledge. Evidence of door jambs present to close it off. This is directly onto (70). This appears to be a garden area with water feature. There is a smaller window higher up which is also looking into (70). Room 70 is painted with elegant garden paintings of fountains and birds. The color scheme is gold, yellows, red, blue and green. The view to the south through (70, 69, 68, 65) is of a fountain (65), identical to the fountain on the north wall of (74). The wall is restored with stucco, but no paint. On the west side of the south wall there is an entrance to corridor (71). The west wall has no openings. In the center of the wall is a large niche on a base projecting into the room. It has been reconstructed. At the top of the ceiling there is reconstructed stucco cornice/molding in red, white and blue. The north wall has an entrance to (87). Area (87) appears to be a garden with water features. There are door jambs present. In the center of the north wall is a large opening. This opens to an unusually shaped garden area. The walls are covered with elegant garden paintings of similar style, design and color. To the northwest is an opening to room 88.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the west is portico (60). To the southwest is room 72. To the southeast is corridor (71). To the northeast is entrance (87). To the northwest is the entrance to (88).

DESCRIPTION:
The large rectangular sales room sits on a north/south axis. There is a wide open doorway to the street on the southwest wall with a step threshold. The floor is obscured with earth and lapilli. A masonry counter (4124) extends from the northwest corner to the center of the room.

The upper register of the north wall is restored. At the east end of the north wall is a lararium (4126).

A low wall and supporting pillar are all that is left of a collapsed east wall. Facings of the wall survive on the north wall.

A doorway with a fragmented threshold enters dining room 2 (4127) in the center of the east wall.

A corridor extends west from the southern end of the east wall.

Traces of plaster survive on the east wall while the south wall shows extensive restoration. Traces of undecorated plaster survive in the southwest corner. At the southern end of the west wall there is a circular window, tapering from the street outside.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
Room 2 (4127) to the east
Corridor 3 to the east

DESCRIPTION: We enter the Temple of Dionysus from a ramp that slopes upward towards the east. Over our heads there is a pediment. The room is a portico in the most ancient part of the temple. There are 8 very large columns - which are probably doric - and supporting the temple roof. The floor shows minimal evidence of concrete. Columns show evidence of concrete painted with red paint. Between the columns there are benches. Benches would be part of any eating and drinking ritual. There are 3 benches between the columns along the south wall. There is 1 bench between 2 columns along the western wall, south of the entrance ramp. There is an additional bench between 2 columns along the western wall to the north of the ramp. Columns show tiny portions of marble fluting. There is a possibility of a doorway previously existing on the north wall. There is a bench on the north wall. The huge ashler walls surround the back portion of the oldest part of the temple. Most benches have been finished with modern cement and show traces of red paint on the south west limits of the portico. There are 2 prepared threshold stones leading to the sacred space area, and other. There are blocks of worked architectural components within the room that have fallen from architrides.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To sacred space is to the east, the ramp is to the west, room 7 is to the north, room 5 is to the south

DESCRIPTION: We have identified the Imperial Palace as a domestic villa. We have determined that the last usage of this room [2-4094] is a reception room. This identification is based on the room location within the structure. The entrance to dining hall 3 is on the northwest wall. It served as an anteroom to the dining hall. The reception room opens directly onto the ambulatory on the northwest side. The entrance is large and tall, and centrally located. The floor is marble as is dining hall 3. There are no remains of a door jamb or threshold. The walls are tall. There are tall arches defining lateral recessed areas spanning the southeast to northwest walls forming an area approximately one-eighth of the main room on each side. There are entrances to hallways on the north and south corners of the southeast wall. The northeast wall has traces of yellow paint in the middle register. On the southeast is the grand opening to dining hall 3. On the southwest wall evidence of plaster and painting show a dado, a middle register and several higher registers. The panels are yellow with red and white spindly borders and one single small architectural panel in the higher middle register. The top remaining register has a cream background. The northwest wall cannot be viewed but contains the large opening to the ambulatory.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The entrance opens to the northwest with a view of the ambulatory and presumably planted garden.

DESCRIPTION: This counter room is entered through a wide entrance from the northwest via a sidewalk. It is on a northeast-southwest axis. We do not see a threshold. Instead we see a series of flat stones which define the entrance as a step up from the sidewalk. This counter room is dominated by a large L-shaped counter located on the northwest side of the room across the entrance. It has a step-shelf and two small circular openings for amphoras or other containers. The size of the room is adequate for serving and for drinking customers. The ceiling does not remain. We see one post hole on the southwest which may indicate a second floor. The walls and the counter show evidence of painted plaster. The floors are not visable due to mud and lapili. There is no window. The door would open to the counter and to the entrance.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The atrium [room 3-4102] is to the southeast. The dining room [2-4097] is to the east.

DESCRIPTION:
Aligned with the entrance corridor and corridor 8, one enters this space at the very back of the house. This is a small storage area in the Western most corner of the house. This small rectangular area is aligned S.W./N.E. and half of this space contains the arched cella penaria, which is preserved to approximately 4 ft. in height. The interior space is preserved plaster facing.

At the Northernmost side of this room, there seems to be only a low partition, separating this space from the kitchen. This house is in poor condition and the walls in this space are only preserved to 8-10 feet. No flooring is visible and no ceiling survives.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is N.W. of area 8. The kitchen room 9, is situated to the N.E..

DESCRIPTION:
This great oven, once had a full arched entrance, now only one-fourth of the arch, shaped with brick, exists. This was restored in 2005, and its portions are being held up by 4 rusty rods.
We can't get close to the entrance to describe the baker working in the oven. We must stand 3 feet away from the arch. We look directly at the rubble beehive enclosed portion of this oven. At the base is a basalt post and lintel entrance. The West side of this oven has a pass through to a preparation room. (3800) There is no pass through to the large processing room (3799), but the Baker could remove the loaves and hand them to a slave who would take them to the processing room. (3799)
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Terri Bruno

DESCRIPTION: We enter this square salesroom from a large entranceway, #19. The floor is pounded mud and lapilli. The East wall shows on the plaster, once; a stairway existed. On the East wall, there are 6 holes for shelves. The North wall shows a large entrance to a Dining room and a tall hallway to a mill room. Seen on the North part of the wall, are 4 holes for shelves. On the West wall, there is a large entrance equal in height to the entrance to the other Dining room, on the North wall. There is no sign of a roof. There is some plaster residue, but only on the West wall, where we see red colored plaster. Situated to the East wall, are 2 catilli. These catilli, appear to be the top parts of the 2 mills, from the mill room.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Contiguous, on the North wall, is a rectangular dining room, #15. Next, on the North wall is a hallway #4, which leads to the mill room. On the West wall is an entrance to a Dining room.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader is Terri Bruno.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified the Villa of Diomedes as a domestic villa. We have determined that the last usage of this room 28 (4075) was as a dining room. This identification is based on the location within the structure as it is off a frigidarium, and the room has a large opening to a small peristyle around the frigidarium. This dining room is in the southwest corner of the portico and frigidarium (room 22) The entrance is on the northwest wall of the room. There is no evidence of a threshold. The floor is currently pounded mud with traces of concrete at the southeast corner. There is no ceiling extant but wall painting remains that suggests a very tall room. The room has modern reconstruction. On the northwest wall traces of painting, stucco and plaster remain on either side of the entrance but no identifiable subjects remain. Centered above the doorway is a window opening to room 22. On the northeastern wall traces of concrete and stucco remain but no painting is discernible. Most of the wall is modern reconstruction. On the southeastern wall (reconstructed) traces of stucco remain. No identifiable paintings remain. On the southwest wall are large sections of modern reconstruction. Little plaster and stucco remains. There are no traces of paint.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Door opens to room 22 to the northeast.

DESCRIPTION: This room in the Villa of Diomedes has been identified as a dining room. This identification was based on the size, shape, and the exterior view associated. This space is apsidal. It is approximately aligned in a north/south orientation. The room is in poor to fair condition. The floor is not visible except for a small threshold block, which has white mosaic remaining beside it. The walls are mixed opus incertum and brick. Plaster remains on all of the walls, preserving a red dado with red and ochre panels above. The condition of the fresco work is very poor and the style is unidentifiable. There is no ceiling remaining. The north wall is divided in three sections. To the western side is the entrance, which is narrow and partitioned by a tall wall. Along the western wall of the entranceway there is a thick rubble and plaster addition which terminates in alignment with the partition wall to the east of the entrance. The entrance partition sets off the central section of the north wall and is matched at the east side of this space by the projection of a stone feature, which seems to be some kind of double basin, but usage is undetermined. The space created in the center of the north wall would be appropriate to hold a couch or other seating. The apse of this room is fairly large, with the wall punctuated with three large windows. These three windows could be the focus of the room, with a view out to the garden.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is south of room 34 and north of an exterior garden.
