DESCRIPTION: We have identified this space as a dining room in the house of IDC Felix. This identification is based on the size and location of the room as well as the character of its decoration. The overall condition of this room is poor to fair. It is a rectangular space on a northwest-southeast axis. The floor preserves several traces of opus sectile, with a round piece of red marble in the center of the room and several other pieces visible to the southeast of the centerpiece. The rest of the floor is cocciopesto. All four walls preserve fresco revealing a high black dado, a middle zone with alternating red and yellow panels, and an upper zone of cream color. This paint is too weathered to reveal further details. The door to the room is a tall opening on the east end of the southeast wall. We noted that Eschebach indicated another doorway in the eastern corner of the northeast wall, but this does not seem to be accurate. No ceiling remains. The walls are opus incertum. The north corner along the northeast and northwest walls have not survived to any great height so no windows are observed.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the northwest of the peristyle (22). It is to the north of room 40.

DESCRIPTION: In the Roman Villa Oplontis A, we have identified a small space to the east of kithchen 7 as room 100, storeroom. We have made this determination based on the room's size (small, almost square), location off the kitchen, and the fact that the west wall appears to have had an arched opening that was blocked into a traditional rectangular door in antiquity. The wall above the arched opening is made of opus reticulatum with vaissoirs delineating the arch, indicating a later construction date than the opus incentum in the remaining walls. The room was plastered and painted with remnants on all four walls. The west wall contains a small doorway, centrally located, and the possibility of a window opening high above. Behind some of the plaster can be seen indications that the west wall may also have been arched at one time. High square post holes in the north, east, and south walls suggest some sort of upper story on the structure above. The reconstructed west wall appears to have stopped and been capped mid-point. The floor is clay. The current ceiling is a reconstruction and is extremely high. The ceiling height is based on a line above the arch on the west wall, 123 centimeters above the existing door.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The storeroom is situated to the east of kitchen 7, and to the west of dining room 15.

DESCRIPTION: Dining room 3 is in the northwest corner of the property. It is entered from atrium 2. The room is large and rectangular and on a northeast - southwest axis. The doorway is extremely high and located on the northeast wall. The north part of the wall shows evidence of black painted decoration and frescoing with a piece of white crown molding at door height with 3 round post holes below it, running in a vertical direction. The east portion of this wall contains cupboard niche (3965) with plastered wall above. At about the height of 5 feet, there is a cut out in the masonry which may have been an attachment for the door. Another round cutout appears to be close to the same location but on the door jam instead of the wall. Turning the corner to the southeast, plaster remains through most although no decoration is evident. The southwest wall was also plastered covered with reminisce still remaining today with square post holes indicating an upper story. The northwest wall also would have been plaster and contained a high rectangular window. The floor is rubble. Room is identified as a dining room despite the narrow doorway because of the size of the room and the view through the atrium, tablinum, and peristyle beyond.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room is to the southwest of cubiculum 4, west of atrium 2, and northwest of fauces 1.

DESCRIPTION: We have decided that the House of Pomponius was a house but may have had some form of production activity. The presence of a vat room, trapetum, and an underground cellar, possibly for storage,may indicate the possibility of non-domestic activity. This room has been identified as an atrium due to its location, features, and previous identification in the literature. The atrium (room 5) contains a well and was listed by Jashemski as the findspot for the trapetum. The atrium opens on a northeast - southwest axis from the fauces in the southwest. A stone impluvium is centered in the room and we see typical Vitruvian construction in the symmetry of the cubicula on either side. Two alae flank the atrium and a tablinum is on the northeast end. A vat room opens off the east corner. The well is immediately to the southeast of the impluvium. A floor is no longer extant. Some traces of yellow and white paint remain on the southwest, southeast and northeast walls. The area is open to the sky. A cistern mouth is at the center of the southwest end of the impluvium.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: fauces 1 to the southwest, vat room 13 is to the east, tablinum 11 to the northeast.

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that this is a small food and drink shop because of the following two reasons: first, it's location is on Via D'Dabbondanza; and the presence of a counter with dolia inserts, and a hearth. The room runs on a northwest/southeast axis, off the street at the south corner of region 9, insula 7. The southwest side of the space contains a food counter (#3992) in an L-shape, with a preparation platform (#3994) situated behind. The southwest wall also contains a series of holes indicating a shelf (#3993) or an awning, it was fixed to it. A beam hole high above may indicate an upper story, but it is uncertain based upon the remains. The wall has remnants of plaster covering it with traces of red paint. There is a tag stating that parts of the wall were restored in 1985. The northwest wall also has some traces of plaster with red paint and is made of opus incertum. There may have been an ancient doorway to the room behind. We believe that the fill in the door area is modern, but it is not labeled as such. If it is modern, there would be a step up to the door. The northeast wall has traces of red and white plaster and is made of opus incertum.
The southeast wall has a high doorway to the street, it is reached by a high step up. The threshold is granite with a deep cut where the closed shop door would have been. The door appears to be connected on the northeast side. Inside of the doorway, there are traces of decorated plaster. There is some plaster on the exterior wall as well, facing the street. The floor was tiled with cocciopesto, but very little remains. No ceiling, remaining.

Enter, pass thru an old peristyle, it was last used as a fabric drying area. We pass an entrance on the Northwest. We pass through to a 2nd entrance on the Northwest. The N.E., determines this room. From the N.W., it was formerly a dining room, by virtue of location, orientation toward painted and plastered walls. The room is on a N.W./S.E. axis, to the entrance hall. There is no lintel. The room is on a N.E./S.W. axis. The rectangular room has no ceiling, this is evidence of a high zone. The floor is pounded dirt and lapilli. The S.E. wall, overlooks the garden, there is a window, positioned nearly 4 feet from the floor. A niche, on the N.E. wall, was for a dining couch. On the N.E. wall, 6 feet above ground, a window overlooks their neighbor. All 4 walls, retain evidence of plaster, the West corner sign of yellow with an aqua border. This appears to be a 4th style painting. The East corner shows signs of black dado. Seen on the middle zone, is an aqua border.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Situated to the S.E. is room 9, which contains a 1st style architectural wall design. Seen, at about 5 feet, there is a lararium. (nediCulara)
VIDEO_COMMENTS:
The running time is 4:18

Done by Fran Capo and Lisa Wernick

DESCRIPTION: We have identified a residential structure. We have determined the usage of this room as a dining room. This identification is based on the location within the structure, the size and shape of the room, the great height of the doorway opening to the atrium, and the ample light from a large window as well as from the atrium. This room is on a northeast/southwest axis and is rectangular in shape. The doorway is at the west end of the southwest wall. There is a narrow marble threshold flanked by square cuttings. The floor preserves seven rows of randomly shaped colored marble, with a gray rectangular piece of stone in front of the doorway. The floor matrix is pebble with random white tesserae lavapesta. The large window is centered in the upper area at the northeast wall. It is glazed (modern). The frescoes are preserved, in most areas, to the plaster molding with voids mostly on the northwest wall. The painting is fourth style, possibly third. There is a decorated low red dado. The walls are white above with architectural decoration and small vignettes at the center of the panels. The two vignettes on the northeast wall are food related, as is the one in the east corner of the southeast wall (6569, 6570). The ceiling is a modern reconstruction. Two pairs of beam holes are aligned on the northwest and southeast walls. The northeast wall preserves the arched end of the vaulted ceiling. This room is a smaller echo of room 27.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP:
6570 wall painting
6567 wall painting
This room is to the east of the atrium (4) and to the southeast of the entrance (1).

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that room number 3 at the back of shop 6.10.1 is a serving room based upon the elaborate third style decoration on the walls. Serving room 3 opens from the south west to serving room 2. Both serving room 2 and serving room 3 are behind a locked gate for which the key is not available. The square room is on a north east/south west axis and has a red bordered dado which contains rectangular paintings that cannot be identified today. Directly above the dado is a narrow band or register of paintings that appear to be of four-legged animals. Above that were white frescoed walls with unidentifiable paintings that are very worn today. The room has a square window in the north east wall which appears to have been a doorway that was sealed in antiquity (before the final decoration of the room) On the two sides of the window are some round indentations. On the south east wall near the east corner is a small rectangular window. On the exterior of the room on the south east wall is another doorway, walled up in antiquity, that was covered up by plaster (in the interior of the room) in the final phase of the structure's life.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: to the north east of serving room 2

DESCRIPTION: In the Roman Villa of Oplontis A, we have determined that the usage of room 17 is a dining room. This identification is based on a location that includes a large window overlooking the peristyle garden, 33, on the north wall, as well as remains of painted decorated plaster work. Access to the room is through a fairly wide, although not exceptionally tall, doorway from hallway 6, in close proximity to the very large dining hall, 21. The room may also be accessed through a doorway in the southwest corner of the west wall. With three large steps coming up from tepidarium 18. Currently there is also a rectangular opening at ceiling level in the southeast corner of the south wall. The walls have a black dado at floor level, red panels directly above, and what appears to be a fourth style, cream based, painting above. No decorative elements, besides outlining are visible. The floor is black and white mosaic. The threshold of the west door had a geometric pattern with door inserts on either end. The north two thirds of the floor is delineated by two horizontal blue black stripes. The remaining one third of the floor to the south has a black, double striped, rectangular pattern. In the northeast corner of the room there is a short cylindrical, cement object with a wooden central piece, held together currently by thin wire, that we cannot identify as either ancient or modern Much of this room appears to be reconstructed.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the east of hallway 6. To the north of portico 33. To the west off tepidarium 18.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified the House of the Working Painters as a house. We have determined that the last usage of this room (4043) was as a dining room. This identification is based on: a) the location of the room off the peristyle and colonnade; b) characteristics of the room including a monumental entrance aligned with a view of a pediment at the entrance to the colonnade, peristyle, and garden. The pediment suggests a temple facade. There is an elaborate mosaic in the center of the room and elaborate wall paintings. In addition to the large entrance in the center, there is also a smaller entrance at the west end of the southwest wall where there appears to be traces of door jambs. The exterior of this wall, along the colonnade, shows traces of plaster and paint which has been reconstructed. The floor of this room is mosaic, white with a black border. The center of the floor is paved in opus sectile in geometric designs in varying colors. The ceiling no longer exists; however, the walls are tall, with paintings in three registers. The wall has been reconstructed. There appear to be three registers with traces of painting in the middle register on the south side of the wall. The color scheme is black, yellow, green and red. There is a figure set in painted architecture on the south side. On the same wall, west side, in the upper register, there are traces of decoration. On the northwest wall there are fine paintings in the middle register. The paintings contain architectural structures. The central panel is a picture that we cannot identify, however there is a sketch showing the legs and feet. Along the border at the bottom of the central panel there are cupids racing in small carts with goats or deer. On the north end of this wall there is a tondo painting of Mars and Venus. Below the Mars and Venus there is a scene showing six figures. The northeast wall is in three major panels separated by architectural design. On the north side of this wall there is another tondo but it is unidentifiable. The central panel has been cut out. The central panel is flanked by architectural features. The north panel is painted, the east panel was in the process of being painted, with the artist's original sketches in situ. On the easternmost side in the middle register, there is a painting of Ceres holding a staff. Possibly the southeast wall is reconstructed. In the middle register there are traces of painting of the east side. There is another tundo, possibly of Venus and Mars. There is painted architectural design. In the upper register of the northwest wall there is a sacroidyllic paining which is badly damaged.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: It opens on the southeast side of peristyle/corridor 12.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified the Imperial Villa as a domestic villa. We have determined that the last usage of this room [3-4090] is a dining hall. This identification is based on the room location within the structure opening with a view to a large ambulatory and possible garden to the west. The general condition of the room is partially restored. The size of the room is very large and impressive with a barrel vaulted ceiling. There are very fine and large paintings of mythological scenes on the northeast-southeast and southwest walls. There are smaller dimensional architectural paintings in relief upon the ceiling. It appears that the there was a marble floor because of definition remaining on the floor but no flooring remains. Previous research refers to the room as an oceus. All the walls are painted in Third Style in fine painting. The lower register is red with scenes bordering the middle register. Each wall has a middle register with a large impressive panel in the center. Above the red middle register panels there are painted scenes on a white background. In the upper register there appear to be painted architectural scenes on a black background. Only fragments remain on the southwest wall. The ceiling is painted and stuccoed in small to medium sized panels with central figured motifs. The upper section of the southeast wall finishes the barrel vault. It has architectural painted stucco relief molding around all edges.

We have identified this space in the Tavern of Tertius as the atrium. This identification is based on the location, character, and previous descriptions of this property. The large entrance [21] directly enters this space at the south corner of the southwest wall. In the center of the space is a large impluvium. This has four columns and traces of built up wall surrounding the basin. The basin is not visible. No original flooring is visible. No ceiling remains. The walls are not well preserved. On the southwest wall there is a square lararium about two meters up the wall in the western corner. There is a small window adjacent to this lararium in the western corner. She southwest wall also preserves some plaster with traces of fresco, but is too minimal to identify details. A platform is located in the west corner. Per Eschebach, this may also have been a cooking platform. Overall this space is in very poor condition, having been bombed in World War II.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The atrium is southeast of the shop [1] with a doorway connecting the two. At the north corner of the atrium there is a doorway at the northwest into dining room [2] and a wide opening into the southeast wall into area [5].

DESCRIPTION: We have identified Shop 6.10.10 as a commercial food and drink shop, small in size. We have one room opening to the street to the southeast, located on the corner of another street to the southwest. The shop contains several items of kitchen equipment (two dolia, a puteal probably over a cistern and some sort of stone mixing bowl). The opening to the street on the southeast is a high step up from the sidewalk and the stone threshold contains evidence of doors and hardware. Similar evidence is found on the opus testaceum door jamb about 100 centimeters up. The eastern most door jamb contains remnants of plaster. The southwest wall of the shop is primarily made of large tufa blocks. It contains a lararium and post hole evidence of an upper floor and a very very high window. Two other post holes are also located horizontally in what appears to be a reconstructed opus incertum area high up on the wall. The northwest wall contains remnants of scored plaster and may have had two doorways in on earlier construction period. There is one small hole near the center near the center top of the wall which may have been some sort of attachment. Much of this wall has been reconstructed. The northeast wall and the southeast wall to the east of the threshold all contain evidence of painted plaster. Two holes midway up the wall indicate perhaps a shelf attachment. The floor today is rubble and no ceiling remains. The southwestern most door jamb has evidence of frescoed insert very high up, square in shape, like a lararium. Immediately below this feature there is an L-shaped cut out and a rectangular cut out indicating some sort of attachment.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This is to the northwest of via della Fortuna.

DESCRIPTION: This is a Dining room, aligned on a N.E./S.W. axis. This rectangular room is entered by a doorway, at the Northern end of the N.E. wall. There's a window in the Center of the S.E. wall, opening to room 2, and there is a window situated in the center of the S.E. wall, it's opening to room 2. There is a window in the center of the N.W. wall, opening into the Mill room, room 5. This room is in fair condition with heavy reconstruction. It's reconstructed with a ceiling sloping downward from the S.W. to the N.E. side. The high ceiling, situated above the S.W. wall allows for a very high painted wall. The painting in this room is 4th style, with a red dado with plants and tall central zones. Figurative central panels and present on the S.W. and the N.E. walls. The upper zone shows windows and outdoor spaces. Earlier researchers were able to identify figures in this room, however the present room condition does not allow this. No flooring is visible. The threshold is stone and has some cuttings for a door. One steps up into this room.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 5, is to the N.W.. Room 2 is situated to the S.E..
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The Video team leader is Terri Bruno.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this structure as a house. We have determined the usage of this room as a dining room. This identification is based on the dining room location within the structure as it has an imposing doorway overlooking an ambulatory and a garden area with gorgeous frescoes and a mosaic fountain. In this room there is a food and drink feature, it is a dining couch niche. The very wide entrance to the rectangular room allows entrance to the north east corner. There is a couch niche that indicates of portion of a triclinium. The walls show minimal evidence of painting. The ceiling is modern and probably too high. The floors of this room are of dust. Some remnants of a marble threshold exists. There is a door to the room to the south east which is a large tablinum. Previous excavation reports include Eschebach and Jashemski.
No other features. Couch Niche northwest corner.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This is contiguous to a large tablinum to the south east corner.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified the House of the Small Fountain as a domestic structure. We have determined the usage of Room 28 as a storeroom. This identification is based on a) the small narrow size of the room, b) the presence of a series of post holes on two of four walls. The room is on a north west, south east axis with a door on the S-E wall. The room is narrow and rectangular with a high ceiling. There are no windows but the N-E and S-W walls contains high post holes as an indication of an upper story above. Ceiling is reconstructed, the walls are made of opus incertum with the lower portions covered with ruined frescos. The S-E and N-E walls contain two rows of square post holes, one at shoulder height, one of a couple of feet above that (see measurements on drawing). The S-W wall contains a cupboard niche 6571 in the south west corner of the room. The floor today is dirt, but currently is unidentifiable. The door on the N-W wall has a stone threshold with door indentations and is quite high.
Opens to the south corner of atrium 22 adjacent to the S-W entrance of room 20 to the S-W and alae 5 to the S-E.

This is a large open area running the width from N.W. to the S.E. axis. Situated on the N.E. side of the establishment, according to W. Jashemski, this area was badly damaged during the 62 A.D. earthquake. At that time, rubble was removed and subsequently the entire area was made into a garden. We see a large entranceway that is entered from corridor 1 on the S.W. side. There is no floor, for the walls there are fragments and there is no roof.
At the S.E. wall, seen to the right upon entering there are badly damaged traces of plaster.
The N.E. wall is badly damaged. There is some reconstruction with traces of plaster, the color is indiscernible. In the middle of the wall, there is an arched and recessed niche; it is possibly a lararium at one time. There exist traces of plaster and white paint -present- inside the niche.

The N.W. wall is badly damaged, there is evidence of a stairway seen to the right. It is facing the West wall, it is badly damaged. There is sign of some reconstruction and no trace of plaster. As you enter the garden space, the wall situated on the left side of the garden contains some traces of plaster with possible paint, on the plaster. The Western wall is badly damaged!
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The garden abuts on the far N.E. corner. Situated there, are 2 rooms; possibly a kitchen and a storeroom (7). To the S.W. corridor #1, adjoins the garden. The entrance is on the S.W. side, to room #5.
VIDEO_COMMENTS: The video team leader it Carlos Avila

DESCRIPTION:
We have determined that this is a dining room. This is based on the character and location of the room as well as previous attribution by the excavators. This is a large rectangular room aligned on a north/south axis. One enters the room through a wide entrance the width of the room on the south, which is open to a portico (13) to the south of the room. On the southeast corner of the wall is a door to a prep room (10A). In the southwest corner of the west wall is a doorway into the large dining room (15). Room 14 has been highly conserved and the condition is excellent. The floor is mosaic with a rectangular space defined in the entrance section of the room (south end of room). A Greek key pattern in polygonal mosaic crosses the east/west axis of the room just north of the entrance area. The dining space is denoted by a central panel placed on the floor, which indicates the three seating areas. This panel is a polydrome lattiae pattern.
The east and west walls are richly decorated in second style frescoes, with the frescoes revealing internal spaces with doors, ornate columns separating the panels, and elaborate cornices and friezes above. These spaces provide glimpses beyond the wall, of exterior spaces.
On the west wall a small tholos (round building) rises in the center with a statue of a female figure within. The north wall continues this scheme with a basket of fruit at each side in an upper window (feature 14-4002 and 14- 4003). Portions of an upper molded cornice remain, and the ceiling is reconstructed.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room is to the east of the large dining room (15) and to the west of the preparation room (10A).

DESCRIPTION: We have decided that room number 5 is a dining room based on its large size and a series of arched windows overlooking a garden. The room is on a northeast-southwest axis and can be entered from a door in the west corner of the southeast wall; a door in the east corner of the southeast wall; or another door in the east corner of the northeast wall [this last door is slightly larger in width than the other two]. The room is very high and barrel vaulted. Elaborate paintings remain on the southwest, northwest, and northeast walls. The southeast wall is divided by three tall arched windows. The ceiling is reconstructed. The room is decorated in Fourth Style with large red panels with plain narrow borders on a yellow ground above a lower black dado. In the center of each wall is a landscape panel. The floor is of black and white tesseraeted mosaic but is largely covered with dirt. Doors do not appear to have threshold remaining except for the door on the southeast wall which is stone [today covered with gravel].
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 3 [4090] is to the north. Room 4 [4091] is to the west.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the House of the Vettii. We have identified this space as a dining room. this determination is based on the location of the room just off the peristyle, the very large entrance across the entire south-west side of the room, and the formal decoration of this room in fourth style painting.
This is a rectangular room on a north-east/south-west axis. One enters the room through the large doorway on the south-west side, across a broad tufa threshold. This threshold is two large blocks with cuttings for screens. The floor of this room is in very poor condition with sections of smooth plaster preserved near the centre and south-west side of the room. The walls are frescoed and preserved almost to the ceiling on sections of the south-east and north-west walls. The frescoes on the north-east wall are only preserved to about the middle of the wall.
These fourth style paintings depict a red dado with large yellow panels above, which are divided by red bands and thin white ionic columns. The centre panel of each wall depicts large mythological scenes. The side panels on each wall are openings looking out to architecture beyond. The upper levels are white and are also architectural vistas. The upper part of the wall and the ceiling are reconstructed.

We have determined that V-1-2 is a small food and drink shop based upon (1) Escheback and (2) it's wide opening to the street. We have decided that room 2 is a kitchen based upon the presence of a slight raised platform defined by Escheback as a cooking platform. The room is rectangular with an opening to the SE to shop room 1 and it sits on a SE / NW axis. There is a small window on the SW wall high up. The NW wall has a series of large beam holes indicating an upper story. The walls are mixed open incertum and brick courses with a relieving arch in the western most corner of the room where Eschenback says a latrine was located, however it is no longer there. On the NW wall, almost directly above the cooking platform is a small recess with a flat tile that forms a possible shelf, possibly for a lamp. The floor is rubble, and one stone indicates the previous presence of a threshold. Room is open to the sky.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the SE is sales room 1

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified this structure as a residential house with 3 entrances. Entrance 7 is the main entrance, Entrance 3 is the secondary entrance and Entrance 9 is the back entrance.
We enter this dining room from the atrium's north east wall, through a very tall doorway with a marble threshold. It is a small rectangular room with plastered and painted walls. The top of the plastered north west wall shows an arch in the plaster that suggests a possible barrel vault. The painted walls have an almost continuous lower zone of cream with black border. The middle zone on the south east wall show a central shuttered window with a painted scallop shell motif on top. There are two framed rectangles of cream, turquoise, red and yellow - flanking a central panel. The themes and colors are repeated on the north east wall, where there are two shuttered panels. There are twenty small holes above the upper zone. Above the upper zone in the eastern corner of the north east wall there is a robber's entry hole. On the north west wall the colors and themes are repeated. The painting is of a large window with big red shutters. It has triangular, peaked top that shows depth. Above the painted upper zone there are nine small holes in a line. On top of the upper zone is a plastered arch. On the south west wall is one similar window motif. The floor is opus, a cement matrix with random fragments of colored marble.

We have identified a domestic structure. We have determined the usage of the room as a dining room. This identification is based on: the location of the room opening on the peristyle colonnade (29); the size and dimensions of this room, which is a fairly large rectangular space on a south west/north east axis. A wide opening almost the entire width of the north east wall would have provided a view of the colonnade (29) with the two fountains between the columns towards the eastern end of the peristyle columns. A smaller doorway opens to the corridor at the northern corner of the north west wall. This doorway has a white stone threshold and is restored to a lower doorway than the main door. The present condition of this room is very poor. The floor is completely gone, exposing the lower level of the house (6789, root cellar). The walls are opus incertum with plaster remaining at the south corner of the south east wall, and the eastern corner at the north east side of the doorway, and on the north west wall. There are two lines of holes cut through the south east wall with the lower row comprised of three large round cuttings and with the upper row comprised of two smaller cuttings. The cuttings align with each other above. There are also two rows of holes cut into the south west wall. The bottom row comprises one rectangular hole in the south corner, a square hole in the middle and a square hole in the west corner. The upper row comprises a central rectangular hole and a rectangular hole in the western corner.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The room is to the south west of area (29) of the peristyle and is south east of the corridor. Dining hall (24) is to the east.

DESCRIPTION: The dark is presently a dark floor. We have determined that the structure at 6.10.1 is a large food and drink shop. We have reached this identification due to (1) location at street corner, (2) present features of serving counter, hearth, as well as multiple frescoes on the walls, (3) previous research. One entered room four from the north corner of northeast wall (counter room). Threshold raised four inches of concrete and stepping back to level of shop in front. The sides of walls entrance are rubble masonry with traces of plaster and faded red paint on the northwest side. The ceiling and wooden lintel over entrance door are modern. Inside the room facing southwest wall (entrance) is rubble work with traces of plaster. On northern side of southwest wall fresco remains (6711) pertaining to dining. Facing northwest - on northwest wall entrance (19) near middle of the wall there is a raised threshold and step up to level of room (rubble concrete). The northwest wall has traces of plaster and painting. Painting is divided in three main areas. The lower portion has a band of red paint at the same level around all four walls separating the scenes. On northwest wall and all walls the mid region contains frescoes. The upper painted level on all walls is gone. On northwest wall, western side of entrance (19) no fresco remains but traces of red, black, yellow border. We conjecture two frescoes that are no longer extant on western part of northwest wall. On northwest wall, eastern side of entrance (19) there are traces of red border paint and two frescoes. Closest to entrance feature (6712) of wine delivery and on eastern side of northwest feature (6710) a fresco of a man pouring wine. On northeast wall there is rubble interior with traces of red border paint and stucco and traces of fresco with a mans feet only remaining on northern side of northeast wall. One the southeast wall with rubble interior there are traces of stucco and painting as well as five original frescoes with a red border separating the low register from the mid register. Traces of red border define the five separate frescoes. On the eastern part of the southeast wall the first fresco is too badly damaged to identify. Moving form east to west on same wall is fresco feature (6709) showing a tavern scene. The next fresco moving west feature (6798) is a man serving wine. Feature (6707) shows people eating with sausages presumably hanging above. The fresco on western side of southeast wall is too badly damaged, but appears to be a face.

This small dining room overlooks the impluvium of the atrium. This atrium is now connected to the great atrium of Obellius Firmus. It has a very tall opening for a dining room. The floor is soil. The walls are partially decorated with dadoes. The low dado is grey wall, the middle and upper are beige with red outlined rectangles. The south wall is a demarcation line that extends 3 inches out and delineates the lower from the upper wall. This line has cut-out lines (dentils) which are also beige. Near the ceiling on the west wall are two long rectangular windows that are now blocked.
The south wall has a level of molding that runs the entire length. It is a repeating small rectangular form. Traces of the molding can be seen on the southeast and the southwest walls.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: ESCHEBACH PAGE 451
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room opens on its north side to the atrium (secondary) and two alae.

DESCRIPTION:
This public fountain is Northeast of 9.10.2 and it is on the south side of the Via di Nola below a modern bridge. It is constructed of volcanic stone slabs. The basin floor lining is missing, revealing stones of the street. The interior dimensions of the basin are 0.95 meters by 1.35 meters and it is 0.96 meters deep. The pilaster is centered on the southeast slab and is decorated by a patera or plate in relief. The fountain has no modern plumbing. The overflow is in the center top of the northwest slab. The drainage hole is at the bottom of the southwestern slab. All of the metal clamps have been removed. Worn hand recesses are primarily on either side of the pilaster and near the eastern interior corner. There is a less noticeable worn hand recess at the southern interior corner.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This public fountain is located on the south side of the Via di Nola and northeast of 9.10.2.

DESCRIPTION: This is a small room on the southeast corner of the temple complex. It is entered from the kitchen area understairs. In the southwest corner of the room is a structure made of three parts. On the right is what appears to be steps leading to a platform, most of which is taken up by a vat-like construction which has been plastered by white plaster. The vat-like structure is rectangular in shape. As extant, the vat is about 2.5 inches deep. In the south of the structure below the vat is a recess that goes back under the vat and seems to end at the wall at the northeast.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Kitchen (room 9) to the northeast. Kitchen (room 9) to the northeast. None

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so-called House of Championnet, also known as the House of the Geometric Mosaics. We have identified this section as a separate entity which one enters through entrance (13). This room (6) is identified as a dining room. It is a rectangular space on a northeast, southwest axis. The entrance to this room is at the west end of the southwest wall. The identification of a dining room is based on the size location and decoration of the space, and view of atrium (2).The floor is very poorly preserved. only underlying cocciopesto remains and it missing a section along the northern half of the northwest wall. The walls are constructed of opus incertum, with remains of plaster and fresco on the northwest, northeast, and southwest walls. Fresco remains with trace of a high dark dado, as well as alternating yellow and red panels in the center zone. The southeast wall has two rows of postholes, four upper and three lower. No ceiling remains. The overall condition of the space is poor.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room (6) is to the southeast of the atrium (2), as well as southeast of room (5).

DESCRIPTION:
Tomb 7 viewed from the street looks simply like a wall with 3 lava blocks projecting at various levels which Campbell conjectured was used for access to the chamber itself. The tomb enclosure has no roof. It is quite square in shape. There is a hygeum chamber in the south-east corner of the enclosure. To the south of that chamber is a masonry block which we have identified as feature 4913. The walls of the tomb are opus incertum but much is modern reconstruction. The hygeum chamber would have contained the burials. This open area we suggest may be used as a space for funeral banquets.

BIBLIOGRAPHY
Campbell P.N.C. 31
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the south-west of the tomb 9. To the north-east of tomb 5.
DIGITAL_IMAGE: 109-0400 A, 109-0401 B A is north facing, B is inside enclosure

DESCRIPTION:
Against the south corner in the exterior walled space (feature 4912) sits a small block that appears to support a small masonry block that appears to support a table or altar which could have been used for food offerings to the deceased.

BIBLIOGRAPHY
Campbell P.N.C. 31

On the north-east end of the rectangular tomb (42), attached to the south-east and north-east walls are 2 remains of a masonry platform, that may have supported a table or altar. Both are today are 'L' shaped with the central area broken away. This is suggested by V. Campbell. Further exploration and interpretation makes us question this attribution as plaster extends behind these masonry pieces. We suggest perhaps a stair base?

BIBLIOGRAPHY
Campbell P.N.G. 23

This feature is identified as a lararium located in the eastern portion of the southeast wall of the kitchen (5072) in the House of M.L. Fronto. This is in very poor condition. It is missing its back surface. Remaining plaster defines a rectangular space.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This is to the east of the doorway to the kitchen and to the southeast of the latrine (5074).
PHOTOGRAPHER: Amy Borden

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so-called House of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14, 16) and part of the complex of L. Aelius Magnus which includes entrances 14 to 20. This is also known as the House of the Geometric Mosaics. Tis area was under reconstruction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This feature (7021) is a lararium. It is a rectangular podium of cut grey stone. Plaster molding surrounds the base, however, the plaster sheathing no longer exists anywhere else. The top surface is of terra-cotta tile. Its location is centered along the southeast wall. The remains of an aedicula above the platform suggests that there had been a semi-enclosed space. Only the southern narrow wall remains, but cuttings at the west end and extending above both these areas indicate a tall enclosed space. At the upper portion there is a cutting suggesting the removal of a fresco from the center.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This feature is located directly southeast of the doorway of room 30 and opens to the atrium (17).

DESCRIPTION: We have identified this room as a serving room. This room is almost square. This is on a northwest/south east axis. The floor is covered by weeds, lapilli, and rubble. On the northwest wall is a low doorway in modern cement. Seven feet from the floor is a line of nine holes running across the entire wall. There is slight evidence of plaster, but most of the wall is opus incertum, appearing to be heavily reconstructed. The northeast wall has remaining areas of plaster, but no fresco is visible. About two feet from the ground are three round holes across the wall. On the southeast wall is a is a very wide opening with a step down into room 2 (4524). Both sides of that doorway have only small portions of the wall exposing the opus incertum. On the southwest wall, centered on the wall, is a small window approximately five feet from the ground. Directly above is another rectangular window which was probably located in the second floor room. There is no evidence of a ceiling.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 2 is to the southeast and room 4 is to the northwest.

DESCRIPTION: In the commercial processing shop, room 7 has an oven, a water feature and some in-ground dolia, which lead us to identify it as an oven room. The room is rectangular and sits on a north/south axis with walls of opus incertum. The room directly abutts hallway 10 to the northeast, which leads to side street entrance 8. As visible today the room is completely overgrown. Features are located on the northeast and southwest walls. A small doorway in the southwest corner leads to storeroom 6 (5034). A larger doorway enters the room from hallway 10 on the southeast. No remains of doors are present. The only plaster remaining is a tiny bit of red and black above the oven. Note the unusual shape of the oven, feature 5036. There is a small window above the latrine (5037) on the northwest wall. Water feature (5038) occupies much of the southwest wall.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the northeast of storeroom 6 and to the southwest of hallway 10.

DESCRIPTION: We can enter this mill oven room from two entrances. The Southeast entrance is low and goes into a large mill room paved with stones. The East entrance is wider and leads to three remaining mills and a great oven. In the rectangular part of the room are three platforms for three mill bases (4596, 4597, 4598). There may have been a fourth mill, indicated by the pattern of floor stones. The problem is, this fourth mill would have been very close to the wall. There is a small door to a back room behind 4598 and there is a small prep platform 4587. The custodi have covered oven in green styrofoam probably portions of another platform or dolium.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Open into processing room 4582 (room 3).

DESCRIPTION: This dolium is located in Room 5 of the Food and Drink Shop / Food Processing establishment. This is a very large dolium. It is embedded to its shoulder into the ground. There is debris in the bottom, or else it appears empty. This is a globular form with a very wide rim that turns outward and then downward. The rim is stamped and seems to be hand inscribed, COINVSIVS and to the right of this inscription is stamped GNAIVI VITALIS. The stamp name is flanked by two circullar emblem stamps. The dolium matches dolium 5030.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This dolium is in the west corner of Room 5. It is north west of dolium 5027 and south west of dolium 5029.

DESCRIPTION: In the eastern corner of store room 5 , abutting the north east and south east walls is an embedded round dolium. Only half of the lip of the dolium remains but we are able to identify a slightly flared body extending upward to an inward turning carinated shoulder and culminating in a horizontal rim. The dolium shows that it had been repaired on its body in ancient times. On the carinated shoulder appears an incised inscription which is difficult to read but appears to be the numerical characters V or X, IXVII.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: To the east of dolia 5027, 5028 and 5029; to the south east of 5030 and 5031; to the north east of dolia 5026 and 5033.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so called House of Championnet, also known as the House of the Geometric Mosaics. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14 and 16) and part of the complex of L. Aelius Magnus, which includes entrances 14-20. This area was under reconstruction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This space (30) is located in section of the house closest to entrance 16. It is a small room off the southeast side of the atrium (17). It is rectangular and on a northeast, southwest axis. The space is identified as a lararium, as is the actual feature (7021) within. The entrance is located in the center of the northwest wall and preserves a broad white threshold. This threshold preserves cuttings for double doors. There is also a small marble fragment with preserved metal posthole at the north end of threshold. The floor of this space is mixed red and white cocciopesto . The northwest walls flanking the doorway are brick, as are the north and west corners extending along the northeast and southwest wall. The rest of the walls appear to be opus incertum, although barely visible due to the preserved plaster. No fresco remains. The upper portion of this space is reconstructed and supports a rectangular ................. tile top surface. A cutting above the altar suggests that a fresco has been removed.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Eschebach
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 30 is to the southeast of atrium (17). It is directly northeast of ala (29).

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so-called House of Championnet. Also known as House of the Geometric Mosaics. We have identified this area as a separate entity which one enters through entrance 13. We have identified room 3 (6990) as a dining room due to the view of the impluvium in the atrium (2), its size and its location in the house. It presents as an L shaped room in its late usage, but shows evidence of having been three rooms in an earlier usage due to the presence of rudimentary walls remaining. The floor is covered with grey gravel. The four walls we see are heavily rebuilt in opus incertum. The only remaining plaster is on the northwest and southwest walls, and some on east walls. No paint remains. There is no ceiling extant. Modern steel girder construction to maintain the walls is placed on the northwest to southwest corners.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is north of the fauces (1), south of the third public building facing the forum, and northwest of atrium (2).

DESCRIPTION: Altar with niche. This street shrine is a rectangular recess within an arched niche on the south side of the Porta Marina. It is located outside the Porta Marina gate opening. The sides of the rectangular recess are of various sized stones, while the back is of large cut ashlars. There is a space between the top of the rectangular recess and the top of the niche. Three is a step up to the altar from the gates paving. The base of the altar is made of various sized stones, topped by a concrete layer. Some plaster remains within the rectangular space. The niche appears to be made of large ashlars. A terracotta statue of Minerva was found when originally excavated.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Porta Marina

DESCRIPTION: F
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This structure is a food and drink shop/food establishment. Room 1 is identified as a sales room. This identification is based on the streetside location and the very wide entrance from the street. The threshold is gray
BW_ROLL: which is clearly not in situ. The entrance to this room is street number 6.
COLOR_ROLL: This space is to the northwest of the street and to the southwest of space 13 and to the south of room 2.
PHOTOGRAPHER: volcanic stone. This is a rectangular space on a northwest/southeast axis. No original flooring is visible and the floor is also covered with heavy weeds. The construction is opus incertum. The south corner is constructed of masonry blocks. The northern half of the northeast side of this room opens to space 13. The northwest side of the room has a wide opening divided into two by a central pillar. This wall and doorway is heavily reconstructed. The upper walls and ceiling are non-extant. Of note is a very small meta (mill bottom) in the south corner of the space

DESCRIPTION:
The commercial property of 1.13.13 is a wine-handling facility and we have identified Room 7 as a processing room, based on its location off of working area 12 with its large door to the street, which Jashemski suggests may have been a cart area and stable, The room is rectangular in shape and sits on a northeast/southwest axis, It has 2 doors: a small door near the north end of the northwest wall, leading to Kitchen 8, and a high larger door on the southwest wall, leading to Space 12. Interior walls are opus incertum. Traces of plaster remain the northeast and southeast sides. The southwest wall appears to be reconstructed with a brick opus mixtum pattern. Centered on the southeast wall is an arched niche or lararium with red plaster interior, with a lower shelf which is also plastered. The southwest wall has a couple small square openings that may have held posts, but the use is undetermined because of the irregularity of their placement. The room is open to the air and the floor is lapilli.

Bibliography: Jashemski 96-77; Eschebach 70.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This processing room is to the southeast of kitchen 8 and to the northeast of Space 12.

DESCRIPTION:
We have identified 3-4-3 as a domestic structure based upon the layout of rooms and previous scholarship. We identify room 4 as a dining room based upon a wide opening facing an atrium and elaborate paintings. The room is rectangular on a NW/SE axis. Most of the northeast side is doorway, with an unusual pebble-stone sill. There are no windows. All walls in the room are heavily frescoed and the southeast wall in particular provides evidence of elaborate decorations. The dado is black with remains of plants decorating panels divided by red vertical stripes. The central register is bright yellow with lace-like horizontal decoration on the southeast and northwest panels. The central panel contains a rondo with an unidentifiable center and framed with ribbons in an arced pattern. The uppermost register is similarly divided with trellis-like structures with small inset pictures of flowers and fruit scattered throughout. Walls are constructed of opus incertum and the ceiling was also frescoed in a yellow paint and bordered in red. Floor was paved with inset tessarae.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Eschebach 105; Jashemski 157.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Dining room 4 is to the southwest of atrium 3, to the southeast of dining room 5, and to the northwest of cubiculum 2.

DESCRIPTION: It has been determined that this is a domestic structure known as the House of the Moralist. Room 5 is identified as a dining room due to its form, location, and decoration. It is a rectangular space on a NW/SE axis. A tall wide opening is the only entrance to this room in the center of the northeast wall, with a white marble threshold. A large square of opus sectile indicates the placement of the triclinia along the northwest, southeast, and southwest walls. Other than the central square, no other flooring remains. The walls are highly restored. The upper portions are modern restoration with a modern door lintel and ceiling. Surviving remains of fresco are only on the southeast side of the room; across the southeast wall, turning a bit on to the southwest wall, and on the small wall on the east side of the door. The fresco style is Third or Fourth. There is a low red dado with vegetation; large black panels above the dado separated y red vertical bands with horizontal black panels with architectural reliefs above the central zone. The center of the southeast wall has a large void in the plaster. Above the painted plaster there are traces of horizontal plaster molding.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Dining room 5 opens up to what may have been a passage (6) and garden (7). It is directly northwest of dining room 4.

DESCRIPTION:
This public fountain is on the north side of the Via di Nola. It is in front of 5.1.3-5.1.4. The fountain consists only of a pilaster with no basin. The pilaster is limestone and decorated with a patera or plate in relief. It has no modern plumbing. The pilaster sits atop the sidewalk/curbing. The Northwest side of the pilaster has a pipe recess.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This public fountain is located in front of 5.1.3-5.1.4.

DESCRIPTION: We have identified this as the House of the Moralist. We have identified this space as a dining room due to its location and its decoration. We step into the room from passageway 8 on the southeast, which connects to an old atrium (3) on the south. The doorway opens into a light well garden that adjoins passageway 8. Yashemski reports "set in a doorpost and enclosed by glass was a lamp which lighted the passageway at night". This remains on the south end of the southwest wall and would have also lit the dining room. The floor is reduced to stone and cement, but eight hexagonal marble tiles remain around the base and possibly outline the placement of the triclinia couches. The dado is lack with green floral arrangements. The central register is black, with three visible rondos showing elegant architectural landscape scenes. The upper register was also black and decorated with elegant garlands. Two elegant ladies are depicted in the center panels of the northwest and northeast walls. The lady on the northeast wall appears to be broadcast sowing grain from a billowing cloth bag. The lady on the northwest wall appears to be carrying a patera of fruit in her left hand and possibly a knife, and her draperies in her right. A large window is in the center of the southwest wall looking onto a small garden (7). The window is outlined with a red border within a larger stencilled border. The lintels of the window and doorway are modern. The ceiling is modern.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Dining room 9 is entered from passageway 8 to the south.

DESCRIPTION:
This is a rectangular room on a NE/SW axis. The western three-quarters of the room is occupied by triclinium #4376. The east and north-east opens directly to the garden, with a low plastered wall or bench. In the east end of the south wall there is a doorway with stepped threshold and modern lintel to room 10. At the east end of the south arm of the couch there is a drain running from the couch along the floor through the low wall into the garden (13) to the east. The floor is opus signinum with marble inserts. In the center of the northwest wall there is a window looking to the garden directly contiguous with the triclinium. Between the arms of the triclinium there is a rectangular table. The north, west, and south walls are decorated in 2nd style with black lower register and alternating red and black panels above. The red panels are decorated with garlands. The black panels depict birds and admonishing inscriptions (4378 and 4382). The center of the southwest wall does not survive where inscription 4383 would have originally been located.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Eschebach p105-106; PPM p406-407; PPP 1, p249-252; Clarke 2006, p233-239; Jashemski p134-135.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 10 is to the southeast. Garden 13 is to the east. Garden 12 is to the north-northwest.

DESCRIPTION: This is the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche. This plaque/inscription is located on the top of the tomb (number 7). This elaborately decorated tablet is situated on the north face of the altar. The front/north side depicts a bust of the tomb occupant. A rectangular inscription (CIL X 1030) is surrounded by a garland/frame of acanthus leaves and flowers. Of primary importance is the relief sculpture below the inscription. This relief depicts individuals coming to honor Naevoleia Tyche, freedwoman, and Gaius Munatius Faustus. Moving west to east the rectangular relief depicts six men in togas with refined features; a smaller male figure (slave) adjacent to a mound of grain; then a bent figure measuring grain into a modius; then nine individuals, some looking forward, some looking back, carrying baskets. A carved tablet on the west side of the altar depicts a ship. A carved tablet on the east side of the tablet depicts a bisellium. BIBLIOGRAPHY: CAMPBELL p 172

This space has been identified has a processing room. This is a rectangular space which presently is open to passage 10 and out to mill room 9. It may have been divided into smaller spaces as indicated on an earlier plan. The main feature of this room is the pass through to the oven (4588). This is an opening at the North corner of the Northwest wall. This space has no visible flooring. The walls are opus incertum with some conservation. There is no Northeastern wall. Plaster can be seen on all the walls with traces of red paint on the Southwestern wall at the south corner. No ceiling remains. There is a high window in the center of the Southwest wall. The enclosure of the oven (4588) is preserved to a higher extent than the rest of the wall towards the western corner. Traces of features in this room are unidentifiable. There may have been a platform beneath the oven pass through in the northern corner of the space where we can see some stones remaining.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This space is to the Southwest of corridor (10) and mill oven room (9) and southeast of the oven (4588).

DESCRIPTION: This water tower is wedged between 9.10.2 and a modern (?) bridge. It is on the southeast side of the Via di Nola. It abuts the bridge's support on the northeast. Only the northwest side of the tower is visible, as it abuts the corner of 9.10.2. There is a pipe recess on the western corner of the tower, with a heavy calcium carbonate accumulation to the north of the pipe recess on the northwestern face. The tower is constructed of tufa masonry.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This water tower is 2.10 meters southeast of fountain 4833 and abuts the corner of 9.10.2. It is on the southeast side of the Via di Nola.

DESCRIPTION: This is a commercial establishment with a shop, vineyard, and processing room. We have determined that is the House of the Wine Handler, also known as the House of the Isis Lararium. We have determined that this is a dining room due to its large door and position off Atrium 2. There is a high small window in the southeast wall. Some traces of plaster and paint remain. The floor is lapilli and weeds. No roof remains.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Atrium 2 is to the north.

DESCRIPTION:
This water tower abuts the outer southwestern wall of the basilica. It is in between the basilica and the Temple of Venus, but abuts the basilica. It is constructed of tufa masonry. There is only one pipe recess and that is on the northwestern face. No album carbonate scaling is visible in the recess. It appears that the extant top of the tow4er tilts slightly to the west. There is no access to this water tower.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: The water tower abuts the southwestern wall of the basilica.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of the Geometric Mosaic in the the so called complex of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14,16) and part of the complex referred to by Eschebach as the complex of L. Aelius Magnus, which includes entrances 14 to 20. This area was under reconstruction in 79 CE. The area has since had modern reconstruction, including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This space (3) has been identified as a cubiculum/reception space. We have determined that rooms such as this may have been used as additional dining spaces. Due to its location, opening to the atrium (2) this would have been a convenient reception space. /this is a rectangular space on a northeast, southwest axis. There is a wide doorway in the center of the southwest wall with a grey stone threshold. The remaining floor is cocciopesto which may have been a mosaic surface, however no mosaic remains. The walls are opus incertum on the southeast and northwest walls. The corners and southwest walls are brick. The northeast wall is opus reticulatum, supporting a high rectangular window in the center of the wall. All the walls have some plaster remaining but with no trace of fresco. No ceiling remains. The room is in poor condition.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This room (3) opens to the north corner of the atrium (2), it is to the northwest of the fauces (1).

DESCRIPTION:
This is the so called complex of Championnet. This is identified as a double house (entrances 14,16) and part of the complex referred to by Eschebach as the complex of L Aelius Magnus, which includes entrances 14 to 20. It is also known as the House of the Geometric Mosaic. This area was under reconstruction in 79 CE,. The area has since had modern reconstruction including the insertion of conserved and reconstructed mosaics. This feature (7011) is a large preparation platform in room 10 (kitchen). It is heavily reconstructed in opus incertum to the same height as 7010. There is no evidence of fuel storage or upper surface, which has been replaced by terra-cotta pieces and cement. It is a broad square and extends from the doorway in the southwest wall almost to the western corner of the room.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Eschebach
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Preparation platform 7011 is to the southwest of 7010 and shares a wall with alley (15) to the southwest.

DESCRIPTION: This is the House of M. Pupius Rufus. We have identified this room as a dining room (11). the space is approximately square. The extant floor appears to be cocciopesto with colored stones imbedded in it. Remains of frescoes are on all walls. The roofing appears to have slanted from east to west as evidenced by small holes and the disruption of plaster. The dado appears to have been colored bands. The central zone is red bands divided into panels. The upper register is extant only on the north and south walls and shows colored bands. There are incised circular designs at the upper frieze on the south wall. There was a low door on the west end of the northwest wall leading to the tablinum (10).The main entrance to this room was on the southwest wall, opening to the corridor (12) along the peristyle.The thresholds of both doorways are basalt. The narrow space along the exterior of the southeast wall was identified as a service area.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This dining room is to the southeast of the tablinum (10) and northeast of the peristyle(14) and corridor (12).

DESCRIPTION: This public well is immediately southeast of the open plaza in front of the Castellum Aquae. It is inside doorway 6.16.22. The well has a modern square concrete superstructure with a metal top. The actual dimensions are not discernible because of fencing due to the excavations in Region V. However, the modern superstructure appears to be approximately 1.40 meters square.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This public well is located inside of the doorway of 6.16.22 and southeast of the open plaza in front of the Castellum Aquae.

DESCRIPTION:
This is the House of the Vettii (room 19). This room is identified as a cubiculum/small reception space. It is a small room decorated in fresco. This feature is one of a group of seven and is a small vignette located at the located on the northern half of the northwest wall. It has a red border on a white background.
There is a blue ground with a bird depicted facing to the left. There are cherries in front and in back of the bird. It is in poor condition.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Feature 4693 is located to the west of this feature (4694) on the northwest wall. Feature 4695 is to the northeast on the northeast wall.

DESCRIPTION:
This public fountain is at the intersection of the Via Consolare and the Vicolo di Narciso. It is constructed of volcanic stone slabs. There is a round lining at the wall/floor junction. Part of the lining on the floor is no longer extant, revealing the street pavers below. The interior dimensions of the basin are 0.88 meters by 1.25 meters and it is 0.73 meters deep. The pilaster sits atop the northwest slab and is undecorated (although there could have been a patera or a plate that is no longer visible). The overflow is on the top of the southwest slab with the drainage hole below at street level. There are deep worn hand recesses on either side of the pilaster, particularly on the northwest. There is a slight hand recess on the interior west corner, but a deeper one about 0.25 meters in from the southern corner. On the northeast slab there is a hand recess near the interior northern corner, another about mid-slab, and another one near the interior eastern corner. It has modern plumbing but is not operational.

BIBLIOGRAPHY:
Pompeii in Pictures
F.Mazois, Le Ruines de Pompeii
Second Partie, Paris: Firman Didot, 18. p. 37 PL 2,1
T.Dyer. Drawing of fountain and deep well with altar and lararium
painting London:Bell and Daddy, 1867: p.38
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This fountain is at the intersection of the Via Consolare and the Vicolo di Narciso. It is southeast of 6.1.18-19. It is 3.06 meters southeast of barrel-vaulted well/cistern (4841) and water tower (4842).

DESCRIPTION: This feature is a painting in the House of the Vetti. It is a small detail on the wall located at the western end of the northwest wall. It is north of the western doorway to the peristyle. This is a small vignette at the bottom of a narrow section of wall. There is a red field on a yellow panel. Against this red background is a figure depicted holding a large two-handed drinking cup (Kantheros). It is in poor condition.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This feature is directly below feature 4672, a painting. It is to the north of the western door to the peristyle and to the west of the central door to the peristyle.

DESCRIPTION:
The commercial property of 1.13.13 is a wine handling facility and we have identified Room 8 as a kitchen, based upon the presence of a low tiled platform, a latrine, and a narrow window to let out cooking smoke. The room is rectangular and sits on a southeast/northwest axis. There are 3 features in the room: platform 4994 in the north corner, latrine 4996 in the east corner, and water cistern 5009 in the south corner. The room is currently open to the air. The walls are opus incertum with traces of plaster on the northeast wall. Wooden beam holes are present in the north and west corners of the northwest wall. An indentation above them runninging from one to the other indicates where a wooden beam would have lined the ceiling. Three postholes remain above the preparation platform at ceiling level. A narrow, rectangular, slit-like window sits on the same wall above the latrine (4996). A narrow doorway on the southeast wall provides access to processing room 7 and a wide doorway on the southwest wall provides access to space 9, and a narrow doorway with a modern lintel on the northwest wall is the only access to storeroom 10. The floor is lapilli. A continued-wall above the ceiling level indicates the presence of an upper floor.

Bibliography: Jashemski 96-97; Eschbach 70.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: This kitchen is to the southeast of Storeroom 10; to the northeast of Space 9; to the northwest of processing room 7.

DESCRIPTION: We have determined that this is the House of Lesbianus and that it was used as a restaurant. This room (3), oriented on a southwest-northeast axis, is determined to be a dining room because of its position in the house and the large window along southwest wall to the vineyard (4363). We enter the room over a small step but no threshold remains. The northern end of the doorway retains colored plaster that shows the original finish. There is a modern lintel. The room is decorated with a red dado, with green foliage. Yellow central register with white borders but no paintings. No upper register remains. A window to the vineyard (4363) is on the southwest wall with modern metal grille. A window on the southeast wall was filled or blocked, probably in antiquity, as plaster remains in situ, though the lintel is modern. The floor is covered in mud and weeds and fallen plaster. The ceiling is modern wood.
CONTIGUOUS_RELATIONSHIP: Room 3 is to the southwest of Room 1, and steps to the vineyard (4363).
